session_name: Drones: How Commercial, Security and Defence Demands Are Shaping an Industry
title: Drones: How Commercial, Security and Defence Demands Are Shaping an Industry
authors: Simon Bachelor; Sofia Stayte; TBC
abstract: Uncrewed Aerial Systems (UAS) - or Drones – are presented as a huge commercial opportunity by some, a security capability or liability by others and, with the Russia-Ukraine conflict front of mind, a profound defence challenge. Bringing together a manufacturer building dual-use systems, a police force flying beyond visual line of sight over national infrastructure, and the department shaping UK policy and industrial capability, the panel asks how an industry takes shape under these varied conditions. Where regulation decides what is feasible as much as technology does, where sovereignty and supply chains matter as much as capability, and where what works today is contested tomorrow.

session_name: Public Policy and the Digital Stack
title: Public Policy and the Digital Stack
authors: Diane Coyle; Annabelle Gawer; Helena Malikova
abstract: Online platforms have become essential infrastructures of modern capitalisms. In recent years, a few hyperscalers have shifted from consumer- to enterprise-oriented services, and from asset-light service providers to asset-heavy orchestrators of a multilayered digital stack. As digital technologies transform legacy manufacturing industries, this evolution is reshaping entire production systems. Unsurprisingly, the digital stack has become a central feature of international political and economic conflict. It has also risen to the top of national agendas for economic security, sovereignty, resilience and competitiveness. But how did we get there? And what does it portend? Are the two countries that own their own digital stacks set to dominate the global political economy? Can mid-sized economies with real technological capabilities become countervailing forces? Can these middle-powers leverage existing specializations in complex manufacturing industries to build innovation in critical areas of technology to protect their interests and remain relevant in the global arena? And can they do so without compromising existing commitments to fair employment and environmental sustainability?
panelists: Diane Coyle; Annabelle Gawer; Helena Malikova

session_name: Market Power, Competition, and Social Outcomes
title: Supplier Grievances in Concentrated Markets: The Case of Australian Grocery Supply Chains
authors: Medo Pournader* (University of Melbourne); Andrew Kach (Willamette University); Stephanie Eckerd
abstract: The world economy is increasingly moving toward concentrated markets. It has been documented by OECD that between 2000 and 2019, industry (market) concentration, measured as “the combined market share of the leading four firms in terms of sales within each industry” has increased from 25.78% in 2000 15 OECD countries to 31.4% in 2019 . Industry concentration is not limited to a geographical region but is quite growing globally from Asia to Europe and North America (Bajgar et al., 2026). Industry concentration is also not limited to superstar firms (Autor et al., 2020) but it can encompass a wide range of industries from grocery to banking and finance (Fels, 2024). The implications of industry concentration, mostly explored in Economics scholarship, can vary from unfair pricing (Feldman, 2006) and reduced innovation (Den Hertog, 1993) to higher consumer costs and dissatisfaction (Poghosyan, 2013). Despite such prevalence and impact of industry concentration on businesses, their consequences for supply chains and interfirm relations have not been studied. What prompted this research has been firsthand observation of high market concentration in Australia, which has since 2024 caused major controversies as to how to protect consumers and suppliers from the implications of dominant firms wielding their powers in the market. These controversies, at least in the grocery sector in Australia, resulted in Parliamentary inquiries as well as mandatory codes of conduct. Yet how effective such policies are in protecting suppliers and hearing their grievances remains to be explored. We embraced this research opportunity and conducted extended qualitative investigation in the sector interviewing major stakeholders and collected key public and confidential documents on how supplier grievances are managed and acted on in the sector and whether the current mechanisms enforced by the government are effective. We accumulated over 60 primary and secondary documents to this end, and conducted critical discourse analysis to understand how authoritative entities (e.g., government and regulatory bodies, supermarkets) and non-authoritative entities affected by (e.g., suppliers and their associations) grievances understand and discuss supplier grievances in grocery supply chains in Australia, where do these discourses overlap and where they diverge. A grand challenge facing this industry has been associated with operational de-scaling and market exit from the suppliers sourcing to the major supermarkets. More specifically, suppliers have over time pared back operations, sold land, and left the market entirely due to various pressures economically and otherwise. The purpose of this study is to shed light on how engagements with large buyers, such as supermarkets, may influence these decisions; and likewise, how the suppliers’ voice is heard (and understood) throughout the process. In the following sections, we will outline the context of the study, data collection and analysis phases leading to discussion of our main findings and their implications for future research on concentrated markets and supplier grievances.

session_name: Market Power, Competition, and Social Outcomes
title: When Peers Fail: Data Breach Signals and the Competitive Advantage of Non-Breached Firms
authors: Domenika Uskova* (Warwick Business School and Nova School of Business and Economics)
abstract: Drawing on signaling theory, this study examines the competitive effects of data breaches that consist of personal information and sensitive personal information. This research classifies such incidents as negative signals resulting from corporate social irresponsibility, triggering a stakeholder, in this case, customers, shift in demand toward non-breached firms. Analyzing 29,511 observations from 3,575 U.S. publicly listed firms with 368 officially reported data breaches between 2007 and 2025, this study finds that while nationwide breaches result in only modest sales growth, state-level incidents drive a 6% increase in sales and a 4.4% profit boost at non-breached focal firms in a subsequent year, as customers perceive localized incidents as personally relevant triggers that activate an ethnocentric bias toward non-breached firms within the same state. Focal firms capture this value by increasing their cost of goods sold as a costly commitment to prove their superior stability compared to breached peers, which, therefore, establishes a separating equilibrium between the two. Ultimately, while data breach incidents drive significant financial performance gains for non-breached focal firms in the following year, they fail to lead to a structural redistribution of market share, which remains resilient to such failures.

session_name: Market Power, Competition, and Social Outcomes
title: Product Vulnerability, Executive Incentives, and Sustainability Performance: Evidence from Three Industries
authors: Saurabh Ambulkar* (University of Texas at Arlington); Jinguo Wang (University of Texas at Arlington); Li Cheng (Michigan State University)
abstract: This study examines how product vulnerability influences firm sustainability performance through the mediating role of sustainability-based executive compensation (SBC), and how these relationships vary across industries. Drawing on agency and stakeholder theories, we argue that product-related risks shape the design of executive incentives, which in turn affect sustainability outcomes. Using a multi-industry sample of digital, manufacturing, and retail firms, we operationalize product vulnerability using cybersecurity-related exposure for digital firms and product recall measures (frequency and severity) for manufacturing and retail firms. The results reveal significant cross-industry heterogeneity. For digital firms, product vulnerability is negatively associated with sustainability-based executive compensation, suggesting a substitution toward short-term, innovation-focused incentives. However, SBC remains positively associated with sustainability performance, indicating its effectiveness when adopted. In contrast, manufacturing firms exhibit a positive relationship between product recalls and SBC, reflecting the use of sustainability-linked incentives as a corrective governance mechanism. Consistent with this, SBC is positively associated with sustainability performance, supporting a mediation effect. For retail firms, neither product recalls nor SBC show significant relationships with sustainability performance, suggesting a decoupling between product-level risks and sustainability governance in intermediary business models. Overall, the findings highlight the contingent role of executive compensation in linking operational risks to sustainability outcomes and demonstrate that the effectiveness and adoption of sustainability-based incentives depend critically on industry context. This study contributes to the literature on corporate governance and sustainability by integrating product risk into the design of executive incentives and offers practical implications for boards and policymakers seeking to align managerial incentives with sustainability objectives.

session_name: Market Power, Competition, and Social Outcomes
title: Financial Inclusion: Exploring ROSCAs and the hidden economy of community finance
authors: Teslim Bukoye* (University of Bath); Olayinka Oronigbabe (Communomics CIC); Emmanuel Omotosho (University of Bath); Serumun Biam (Communomics CIC); Wuraola Durosaro (Communomics CIC)
abstract: Rotating Savings and Credit Associations (ROSCAa), known across communities as Ajo, Susu, Pardner, and related forms, remain an underexamined yet highly consequential part of urban financial life. This study investigates the role of ROSCAs in advancing financial inclusion among ethnic minority communities in London, particularly where trust in formal finance is weak and access to mainstream banking remains limited. In 2024, around 0.9 million adults in the UK were unbanked, while estimates suggest that between 200,000 and 260,000 adult Londoners do not have a bank account. Drawing on an ongoing mixed-methods study supported by Trust for London and undertaken with Communomics, the paper examines why ROSCAs persist, the functions they perform, and whether formal recognition could strengthen financial inclusion without undermining the flexibility, trust and community accountability that make them effective. Emerging findings indicate strong participant support for greater recognition of ROSCAs, not as marginal informal practices, but as socially embedded financial infrastructures that help households save, smooth consumption, manage emergencies and sustain economic participation. The paper contributes theoretically by repositioning ROSCAs within the wider architecture of financial systems, showing that ROSCAs are a vital part of the hidden economy of community finance, through which trust, access and economic participation are sustained among ethnic minority groups. Practically, it speaks to policymakers, regulators and financial institutions by demonstrating why culturally embedded community finance should be taken seriously as part of a more inclusive financial system. In doing so, the study opens a timely conversation on how financial inclusion policy can become more effective, more contextually grounded and more responsive to underserved communities.

title: The AI Dividend in Early-Stage Experimentation: How Generative AI Reshapes Capital and Time Requirements for Initial Idea Validation
authors: Sebastian Höflich* (HHL Leipzig Graduate School of Management - Chair of Strategic Entrepreneurship); Maurice Steinhoff (HHL Leipzig Graduate School of Management - Chair of Strategic Entrepreneurship); Dominik Kanbach (HHL Leipzig Graduate School of Management - Chair of Strategic Entrepreneurship)
abstract: Early-stage ventures face a pre-validation funding gap. Traditional early-stage investment instruments are associated with high transaction costs, making small investments required for initial hypothesis testing unprofitable. Consequently, low-stakes entrepreneurs outside established ecosystems face the challenge of mobilizing resources and capital. At the same time, Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) and cloud computing reduce cost and time required to develop a Minimum Viable Product (MVP). In this study, we examine the “AI dividend” in early-stage entrepreneurship. Specifically, we investigate the impact of AI tools on the capital (ticket size) and time required for initial idea validation and MVP development. Therefore, we are conducting a quantitative survey targeting early-stage entrepreneurs across diverse entrepreneurial ecosystems. By comparing high- and low-AI adopters, we measure how the intensity of AI adoption affects financial and time-related costs of experimentation. To distinguish between the two groups, we introduce an AI adoption index. We hypothesize that AI reduces initial validation costs to a small fraction of those associated with traditional business angel investments. In providing empirical support for a significantly reduced “affordable loss” threshold, this research contributes to the literature on entrepreneurial finance and innovation. It demonstrates how AI democratizes entrepreneurship, empowering marginalized founders to bypass existing early-stage investment constraints and efficiently achieve either venture validation or failure.

title: Agentic AI and Complementor Adaptation in a Platform Ecosystem: Evidence from Salesforce AppExchange
authors: Marco Ceccagnoli* (Georgia Institute of Technology); Chris Forman (Cornell University); Thien Dong (Pennsylvania State University); Weiting Wang (Cornell University)
abstract: How do platform-driven AI innovations reshape complementor dynamics and entrepreneurial opportunity within digital ecosystems? We study the introduction of Agentforce, Salesforce’s agentic AI platform that enables developers to embed autonomous agents into applications, as a technology shock to the AppExchange ecosystem. We construct a novel dataset covering the universe of AppExchange applications at monthly frequency between 2024 and early 2026, which we combine with external data on firm characteristics and business focus. Using these data, we track when Agentforce-related features first appear in complementors’ listings, which we interpret as a measure of observable commercialization and market-facing availability within the platform, rather than precise technical adoption. The introduction of Agentforce unfolds through multiple stages, including early announcement, the emergence of marketplace features, and subsequent improvements in functionality and deployability. We leverage this evolution to examine how complementors respond over time and across different dimensions of the ecosystem. Our preliminary analysis identifies three broad patterns. First, visible commercialization is limited in early phases and increases substantially only as Salesforce provides the tools, integration, and enablement needed to deploy the technology at scale. Second, responses are heterogeneous across complementors, with a higher propensity to commercialize through the platform among applications more closely aligned with data-intensive and automatable workflows. Third, adaptation appears to occur primarily among incumbent complementors, while entry patterns also shift as new capabilities become integrated into the platform. Together, these preliminary findings suggest that the impact of agentic AI in platform ecosystems is shaped not only by the technology itself, but also by the timing of platform enablement and the alignment between new capabilities and existing complementor activities.

title: Beyond Productivity: Evaluating the Hidden Costs of Generative AI in Software Development
authors: Edward Anderson* (University of Texas at Austin)
abstract: AI-assisted programming tools are increasingly adopted to enhance developer productivity by automating routine tasks and accelerating software development. While early evidence highlights short-term productivity gains, our study shows that excessive reliance on AI can unintentionally accelerate the accumulation of technical debt, leading nto escalating maintenance costs and eventual revenue erosion. Drawing on interviews with software engineers and insights from the literature, we build a dynamic simulation model to examine the long-term impacts of AI-assisted coding under varying conditions of project horizon, legacy-system interaction, developer skill, and market dynamism. Our results reveal that productivity benefits follow an inverted-U pattern: there exists a “sweet spot” where AI assistance improves overall performance, but beyond this threshold, compounded technical debt undermines system maintainability and profitability. We further show that greenfield environments and fast-evolving markets can tolerate higher levels of AI assistance, whereas brownfield (legacy) settings and teams with less skilled developers are substantially more susceptible to long-term decline. We identify technical-debt retirement as a strategic guardrail that can help sustain AI benefits over time. These findings demonstrate that AI-assisted development is not simply a choice of productivity tool, but a strategic decision that must consider programming environment constraints, system longevity, skill composition, and market factors.

category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
title: The Implications of the Interplay between Global Value Chains and Technology for Labour Productivity and Demand
authors: Sotiris Blanas* (University of Warwick)
abstract: Leveraging a new sample of 34 industries, covering roughly the entire economies of 80 developed and less developed countries in 1995-2019, we study the implications of Global Value Chains (GVCs) and their interplay with technology for labour productivity and demand. We find evidence of labour productivity and value added losses and employment share gains of high-skilled workers associated with participation in GVCs through linkages with suppliers (i.e., backward), and of labour productivity, value added and aggregate employment gains and employment share losses of young workers associated with participation in GVCs through buyers (i.e., forward). Distinguishing countries by income status and industries by technology and R\&D intensities yields results pointing to complementarities among backward or forward GVC participation, utilisation of communication technologies, information technologies, software or robots, innovation, and domestic output, employment, and skills in high-income countries. By contrast, in lower-income countries, forward GVC participation complemented domestic output in industries of different technology and innovation intensity statuses, but less skilled workers only in more technology- and innovation-intensive industries. The skill bias of backward GVC participation and its substitutabilities for domestic aggregate output and employment were concentrated in less technology-intensive industries, especially those that are also less innovation-intensive.

category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
title: Career Similarity and Post-Acquisition Employee Outcomes in Technology M&A
authors: Junyan Lu* (National University of Singapore); Weiyi Ng (National University of Singapore); Lisa Tang (National University of Singapore)
abstract: Acquisitions bring employees with diverse backgrounds into acquiring firms, yet little is known about how such heterogeneity shapes post-acquisition outcomes. We examine this question through the concept of career similarity, defined as the extent to which acquired employees (AEs) resemble incumbent employees at the acquiring firm. We unpack career similarity into two dimensions: professional affiliation similarity (overlap in prior employers) and job experience similarity (overlap in functional experience). Combining these two dimensions, we distinguish four similarity profiles, and theorize that their effects depend on the nature of work across job roles. Where work relies more heavily on coordination, similarity may facilitate communication and knowledge transfer. Where work is less interdependent, similarity may instead signal substitutability and intensify competition. Matching data on 2,114 technology acquisitions by S&P 500 IT firms (1995–2020) with 8.6 million LinkedIn resumes, we operationalize affiliation and experience similarity using cosine similarity measures and estimate deal-stratified survival models of turnover and promotion. Results reveal a striking reversal across role types. In business roles, similarity increases turnover and reduces promotion, consistent with substitutability. In technical roles, similarity reduces turnover and enhances promotion, consistent with coordination benefits. Effects are strongest when both similarity dimensions overlap. Our findings advance research on corporate strategy, careers, and strategic human capital by showing how ex-ante career similarity shapes post-acquisition mobility depending on work structure, with implications for AEs navigating career disruptions as well as for managers seeking value creation from their acquired human capital.

category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
title: It All Adds Up: Immigration Policy Multiplicity and the Eroding Education Advantage in Ownership
authors: Alfred Marcus* (University of Minnesota); Gal Blatman (USC)
abstract: Using 2001–2020 ACS microdata on immigrant business ownership across U.S. states, we find that the positive association between Interpretive Capacity (IC) and the ownership of businesses by immigrants weakens as cross-domain contradiction among public policies increase. When prescriptions across policy domains are misaligned—a condition we term residual institutional ambiguity (RIA), measured as state-level entropy in enforcement, integration, and benefits regimes—additional interpretation reveals that coherent expectations cannot be constructed. Policy-domain contradictions matter especially for business ownership, which requires sustained multi-domain engagement and thus forecloses selective decoupling. High-IC actors rationally defer making a commitment, a pattern we term competence-induced caution. We also find that co-ethnic density independently compresses IC returns. Research on entrepreneurial cognition assumes that greater interpretive capacity (IC) reduces uncertainty and promotes business ownership. This expectation, we argue, holds only when uncertainty is informational and yields to additional interpretation. We contribute to entrepreneurial cognition and institutional theory by distinguishing informational uncertainty from specifying a boundary condition on the view that institutional contradictions are generative, and recasting dense co-ethnic communities as collective interpretive systems that compress returns to individual interpretive capacity.

category: Operations, Supply Chain, and AI-Enhanced Industry 4.0
title: Sourcing for Safety
authors: Andrew Balthrop* (University of Tennessee)
abstract: Over-the-road freight transportation kills more than 5,000 people annually in the United States. The US has attempted to reduce these crashes through a regulatory and liability-based approach focused on transportation suppliers (i.e., motor carriers), the locus of operational-level control. While this approach has been successful at incentivizing operational safety at the intensive margin (fewer crashes per unit of freight), it fails at the extensive margin (total crashes). We argue that vicarious liability for transportation buyers (i.e., shippers) is needed to address this margin. As evidence, we examine safety data aggregated from millions of roadside motor carrier safety inspections for a sample of 192 buyer firms, including third-party logistics brokers. We find that liability exposure reduces accidents. Buyers have consistently safer records for owned-assets, liable under the doctrine of respondeat superior, than for contracted assets, where liability is more tenuous. Additionally, we find that buyer firms with more assets, greater visibility, and more logistical dependence contract with safer suppliers. We conclude with commentary on the safety repercussions of recent U.S. legal proceedings and case law.

category: Operations, Supply Chain, and AI-Enhanced Industry 4.0
title: Learning curve effects in outsourcing: Evidence from the medtech industry
authors: Ilkim Güneri (ETH Zurich); Oliver von Dzengelevski* (ETH Zurich); John Gray (Ohio State University); Torbjørn Netland (ETH Zurich)
abstract: Outsourcing in medtech manufacturing has been observed to grow about twice as fast as the industry overall. Given the public health and safety implications, understanding how outsourcing can be managed successfully is crucial. Yet unlike pharmaceutical manufacturing, little data is publicly available, despite oversight by the same regulatory bodies such as the FDA. We therefore draw on a decade's worth of unique panel data covering quality test results for parts of high-runner medical devices produced by an industrial company. Using a quasi-experimental design, we examine how the probability of failing physical quality tests evolved for parts relocated to be outsourced relative to comparable parts relocated in-house at the same time. In particular, we analyze learning curve effects and theorize about the roles of the focal firm's outsourcing experience, suppliers' experience in the outsourcing relationship, as well as part-specific experience over time.

category: Operations, Supply Chain, and AI-Enhanced Industry 4.0
title: Transforming Healthcare Service Supply Networks: Integrating Digital and Physical Infrastructures
authors: Lishu Xia* (University of Cambridge); Jagjit Srai (University of Cambridge)
abstract: The integration of digital technologies with traditional systems is radically reshaping the healthcare sector. Incumbent providers and supply chain partners are embedding digital platforms into established physical service networks, while telemedicine firms are investing in hospitals, clinics, and pharmacies (WEF, 2024; 2025). This bi-directional transformation — digital-to-physical and physical-to-digital — is especially visible in China, where recent regulatory innovation of Internet Hospitals as dedicated medical institutions delivering remote care has reshaped national outpatient care (Wang et al., 2026). Motivated by this context, we conduct a multiple-case study of six leading Internet Hospitals (three operated by incumbent healthcare institutions and three by private tech firms) drawing on 60+ hours of interviews, 10 site visits, and informed by five years of industry engagement. Framing both as hybrid platforms that evolved from previously digital or physical infrastructures coordinating service supply networks (Joglekar et al., 2022), we explore how these networks are reconfigured in terms of network structure, processes, network relationship, and product value structure (Srai and Gregory, 2008; Anderson et al., 2022). Cross-case analysis shows that although integrating digital and physical infrastructures widens the scope of operations, the extent and direction of widening depend on each platform's inherited baseline. Contrary to prevalent belief, scoping across both supply and demand networks is consistently easier for born-physical platforms. This asymmetry suggests that integration in regulated service industries is bounded less by technological investment than by institutional inheritance. Industry policy may therefore need to prioritise enabling partnerships between digital entrants and incumbents over subsidising infrastructure investment.

category: Operations, Supply Chain, and AI-Enhanced Industry 4.0
title: Learning From Those Who Walk Away: A Censored Newsvendor Approach to Risk Segment Volume in U.S. Subprime Lending
authors: Shingirai Kwaramba (Virginia Commonwealth University); Jeff Shockley* (Virginia Commonwealth University); Shashank Rao (Auburn University)
abstract: Consumer finance lenders in the United States face a censored feedback problem when adjusting for risk segment volumes in their credit models; they observe outcomes only for funded borrowers, making it difficult to distinguish deterioration in the broader credit environment from payment strain caused by their own loans. In this research, we show that Approved Unconverted (AU) applicants, those borrowers who are approved but decline the loan offer, help to resolve this identification problem when they are incorporated into the models. Because AU applicants rarely take on new debt elsewhere, their subsequent delinquency reflects environmental credit stress rather than loan-specific payment burden, a decomposition that portfolio data alone cannot provide. In this study, we develop and validate a risk-based forecasting model using segment-month panel data from 169,190 applicants observed over 12 months at a U.S. subprime installment-loan originator. Our analysis yields three contributions. First, we identify the conversion filter as a distinct source of censored feedback, distinct from the approval filter studied in reject inference. Second, we demonstrate that AU delinquency distinguishes between environmental stress and loan burden. Third, we show that incorporating the AU signal into volume decisions improves firm profitability while reallocating lending away from segments that subsequently underperform. We show that the AU signal reduces prediction error and improves performance at longer forecast horizons. When implemented, we estimate the model will yield a 4.7% revenue gain for the provider with reduced default risk for its customers.

title: Do Government Subsidies Promote Global Value Chain Upgrading? A Difference-in-Differences Analysis of Cross-Country Industry-Level Evidence
authors: Jing Yuan* (University of Reading)
abstract: Government subsidies have long been a central instrument of industrial policy, yet their effectiveness in shaping countries' positions in global value chains (GVCs) remains contested. Proponents argue that subsidies correct market failures and support functional upgrading, while critics contend that they distort competition and generate limited spillovers. Existing evidence is largely confined to firm-level studies within single countries, leaving the causal relationship at the cross-country, industry-level underexplored. This paper investigates the causal impact of government subsidies on GVC participation at the country-industry level across 35 countries and 17 manufacturing industries over 2012–2022, a period marked by heightened geopolitical tensions and systemic shocks including the COVID-19 pandemic. Drawing on the Global Trade Alert (GTA) Corporate Subsidy Inventory and the OECD Trade in Value Added (TiVA) database, we construct a country-industry-year panel dataset and employ a difference in differences (DiD) strategy, treating industry-specific subsidy interventions as policy shocks and comparing GVC trajectories between treated and untreated country-industry pairs. We capture forward and backward participation as well as relative GVC position, and incorporate controls including domestic value added in gross exports and capital intensity. Heterogeneous effects across industries of differing technological sophistication are examined to test whether subsidy impacts are conditional on absorptive capacity. Robustness checks include parallel trends tests, placebo tests, and alternative measurement using the ADB MRIO database. By providing systematic cross-country causal evidence at the industry level, this study contributes to debates on industrial policy design and offers implications for policymakers seeking to leverage subsidies as a tool for GVC upgrading under conditions of global uncertainty and structural disruption.

title: Enhancing Global Competitiveness Through Cross-Country Research and Innovation Partnerships
authors: Muthu De Silva (Birkbeck, University of London); Dize Dinckol* (Birkbeck, University of London)
abstract: This paper examines how public investments in international research and innovation (R&I) collaborations generate economic returns for the home country, focusing on UK-funded cross-national partnerships led by academic researchers. While prior literature highlights the importance of knowledge flows, spillovers, and global production networks in shaping innovation outcomes, it offers limited insight into how such internationally distributed activities translate into domestic economic value. Addressing this gap, we explore the mechanisms through which international R&I creates and returns value to the UK. Drawing on 20 semi-structured interviews with UK-based academics leading impactful international collaborations, complemented by archival data, we conduct a qualitative, cross-case analysis. Our findings show that international R&I collaborations enable access to unique and complementary expertise, datasets, infrastructures, and real-world environments unavailable domestically, allowing the production of globally distinctive and economically valuable knowledge. Contrary to linear models of innovation, these collaborations evolve iteratively across technology readiness levels, integrating technical, regulatory, and market feedback. We identify key mechanisms of value creation, including enhanced research quality, accelerated commercialization through global resources, talent development via international exposure, and improved industry and public sector performance. Importantly, we show that economically impactful collaborations are inherently multi-actor, involving a range of stakeholders. We also highlight critical moderating factors that shape value capture, including strategic alignment with UK needs, funding continuity, and cross-border institutional frictions. Overall, our study contributes a nuanced understanding of how international R&I generates domestic economic benefits and advances a broader perspective on return on investment that incorporates foundational knowledge-building alongside measurable economic outcomes.

title: State-Led Path Creation in Emerging Industries: A Comparative Study of China’s Electric Vehicle Hubs in Shenzhen and Hefei
authors: Jun Sun* (East China University of Science and Technology)
abstract: The rapid ascent of China’s electric vehicle (EV) industry represents not only a notable national achievement but also a compelling regional phenomenon, marked by the emergence of new manufacturing and innovation hubs such as Shenzhen and Hefei. These cities, despite possessing weak or even non-existent traditional automotive industrial bases, have successfully achieved industrial path creation and upgrading during the transition from internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles to EVs. This puzzle challenges established predictions in evolutionary economic geography, which emphasize the advantages of incumbent industrial regions and the difficulties for peripheral areas to leapfrog. Grounded in the theories of regional innovation systems and industrial path creation, this study employs a comparative dual-case methodology to unpack the distinct roles and mechanisms of local governments in fostering successful EV clusters. The analysis draws on extensive primary data, including in-depth interviews, policy documents, and a comprehensive database of Chinese EV manufacturers and models. The analysis reveals that both Shenzhen and Hefei’s governments acted as pivotal institutional entrepreneurs, constructing system-level agency to enable new industrial paths. However, they pursued divergent paths. Shenzhen exemplifies endogenous cultivation, where the local government systematically built entrepreneurial infrastructure—encompassing physical, knowledge, capital, and institutional dimensions—to nurture and empower a homegrown champion, BYD, from its early startup phase. The government’s role evolved from providing risk capital and R&D support to orchestrating lead markets through public procurement and, eventually, to shaping institutional frameworks for intelligent vehicles. In contrast, Hefei demonstrates exogenous leveraging. Faced with the stagnation of its local automotive incumbent, the government pivoted to act as a sophisticated, market-savvy strategic investor. Utilizing state capital platforms refined through prior industrial reforms, Hefei executed a high-stakes, timely equity investment in the faltering new entrant NIO. This decisive intervention served as a catalytic anchor, attracting a cascade of complementary investments from firms like Volkswagen and BYD, thereby rapidly assembling an EV industrial ecosystem.The comparative study yields several key insights. First, successful regional path creation in a complex, capital-intensive industry like EVs requires proactive governmental agency to address systemic coordination failures and early-stage investment risks. Second, the local state can effectively play this role not through picking winners or direct substitution of the market, but by building neutral, enabling infrastructures and acting as a de-risking partner for innovation. Third, the choice between endogenous cultivation and exogenous leveraging depends on region-specific conditions, including legacy industrial structures, institutional capabilities, and access to external resources. This research contributes to the literature by detailing the micro-mechanisms through which local governments in China build system-level agency for industrial path creation. It moves beyond national-level explanations to show how sub-national institutional innovation and strategic action are critical to understanding China’s EV rise. The findings offer relevant policy implications for other regions, both within and outside China, that seek to cultivate new growth paths in emerging industries amidst technological disruption.
