title: The snow must go on: Theorizing the climate adaptation conundrum in expiring industries
authors: Juliane Reinecke (University of Oxford); Paolo Aversa (King’s Business School, King’s College London); Alberto Nucciarelli (University of Trento); Edoardo Trincanato* (University of Trento)
abstract: The climate crisis has pushed industries worldwide to innovate for adaptation. While adaptation can sustain short-term viability, the range of responses can also narrow: successful near-term fixes may crowd out broader strategies needed for long-term transformation. We call this the climate adaptation conundrum. Our study of the Italian alpine snow-based industry shows how technology-intensive investment in snow production infrastructure has become the dominant response to declining snowfall, sidelining diversification and structural transition even when these alternatives are known, occasionally pursued, and increasingly urgent as ecological decline outpaces technological compensation. By focusing on what we term expiring industries—industries that remain economically viable while the ecological conditions they depend on are foreseeably disappearing—we advance a model explaining how shared frames justify technological continuation while material-institutional dynamics lock actors into the chosen pathway. We contribute to research on climate adaptation, framing and industry evolution by theorizing how expiring industries become trapped in narrow adaptation through self-reinforcing frames.

title: Lands of Opportunity! Social Movements, Opportunity Context, and Paths to High Adoption During Market Formation
authors: Panikos Georgallis* (University of Amsterdam); Todd Schifeling (Temple University); Brandon Lee (University of Melbourne)
abstract: Because of their unique potential for social change, markets that address grand challenges are often supported by broader social movements. Research has shown, for example, that social movements engage in collective action to stimulate firms’ entry into markets such as renewable energy, green buildings, or organic food. But are there synergies in having movements, new entrants, and incumbents operating in the same market, or are their contributions to market adoption substitutable? And how do social movements and industry combine to shape market adoption in different national contexts? In this study, we treat market adoption as a configurational phenomenon, arguing that the influence of social movements on market adoption rests on the configuration of industry, political, and cultural opportunities that they face in a given country. Empirically, we study the adoption of solar photovoltaics (PV) across 28 European countries over two decades by employing a multi-method approach. Using fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fs-QCA), we uncover three different ‘recipes’ for high adoption during market formation, each representing a different combination of conditions; we then rely on Sequence Analysis and qualitative case evidence from exemplar countries to identify when and why these recipes emerge. Our results reveal that social movements can shape adoption by leveraging either cultural or industry opportunity, and that their influence wanes once policy renders adoption economically attractive. Overall, we highlight the crucial nature of the opportunities that the country context affords for market adoption, and point to the relevance of studying market formation more broadly as a configurational phenomenon.

title: Formalising social legitimacy: A two-phase process model for social license in a case study of a hydropower public-private partnership in an emerging economy
authors: Seokhoon Ko* (University of Bath); Omid Maghazei (University of Bath); Jens Roehrich (University of Bath); Michael Lewis (University of Bristol)
abstract: Large-scale infrastructure projects in emerging economies frequently face failure due to a “social license gap,” where local communities withhold legitimacy. While literature frames the social license to operate (SLO) as an informal, relational agreement managed by private partners during implementation, this research addresses critical theoretical gaps regarding how social license is formalised during project initiation and the under-researched role of the public partner as the primary "social licensee". Using a qualitative, longitudinal case study of the Tina River Hydropower Project in the Solomon Islands (2009–2015), the study develops a two-phase formalisation model. Phase 1 focuses on securing a “social license to plan” (SLP) through transactional legitimacy and documented mandates, which permit technical investigations. Phase 2 transitions to a foundational SLO, establishing structural legitimacy through culturally authentic identification of customary landowners and the codification of unwritten norms into legally binding agreement. The findings demonstrate that the public partner acts as an institutional anchor, sealing social legitimacy into formal governance before private sector engagement. However, the research identifies an “exclusion paradox,” where formalising rights for a narrow group of landowners can recursively withdraw legitimacy from the wider community, driving social unrest. Ultimately, the study theorises that SLP is a structural prerequisite for SLO and suggests that formalisation should serve as a mechanism for integrating local stakeholders as institutional partners in public-private partnership governance. Keywords: Social License to Operate, Social License to Plan, Public-Private Partnerships, Formalisation, Customary Land, Infrastructure Governance, Utilities.

title: Examining the relationship between organizational action and stakeholder group action: A justice norms perspective
authors: Hanzelle Kleeman* (University of Oxford)
abstract: As organizations increasingly experience stakeholder group action, managers are informing, involving, interacting with, and compensating stakeholder groups in the hopes of preempting oppositional and fostering supportive stakeholder group action. Yet research has not examined the relationship between such organizational action and stakeholder group action. Moreover, research on stakeholder group action treats it as inherently oppositional. I therefore examine the relationship between organizational action and stakeholder group action and conceptualize stakeholder group action as having the potential for both support and opposition. I argue that organizations preempt oppositional and foster supportive stakeholder group action through greater adherence to organizational justice norms. I evaluate this argument by analyzing community group action following developer-community engagement wherein developers inform, involve, interact with, and offer compensation to community groups. The analyzed dataset includes 75 major solar farms proposed across England (~70% of the population of proposals), each with a distinct developer-community group pairing. The findings suggest that developers preempt oppositional and foster supportive community group action through greater adherence to procedural and interpersonal justice norms; that high adherence to informational justice norms becomes beneficial in contentious contexts; and that compensation offers may be expected in contentious contexts, but may, under less-contentious conditions, and in the absence of adherence to interpersonal or procedural justice norms, trigger oppositional community group action. I discuss the implications of these findings for policy and practice in England's solar farm development context, as well as the applicability of these findings for alternative contexts.

title: Coffee Break

session_name: Opening Plenary: Industrial Policy in an Era of Geopolitical Competition
title: Opening Plenary: Industrial Policy in an Era of Geopolitical Competition
authors: The Rt Hon Lord Hague of Richmond
abstract: Lord Hague joins Dr Monica Gorman for a wide-ranging conversation on the geopolitical forces currently shaping industrial policy. Drawing upon his experience in international affairs and public life, Lord Hague will reflect on how geostrategic rivalry, rapid technological change, and growing national and economic security concerns are influencing decisions made by governments and business leaders. Dr Gorman will bring complementary insights from her recent White House work on manufacturing, supply chain resilience, and industry competitiveness. Together, they will explore the implications for industrial strategy on both sides of the Atlantic, including how policymakers and companies may respond to a more contested and fragmented world. This opening plenary will connect high-level statecraft with the practical realities facing industry, offering a forward-looking discussion of the forces transforming national policies and modern industrial systems.
panelists: The Rt Hon Lord Hague of Richmond

title: Tariffs Favor the Prepared Firm: Capability Thresholds and the Uneven Distribution of Talent after Liberalization
authors: N. Ricardo Laverde-Cubillos* (Insper); Carlos Charris (Universidade Catolica de Brasilia)
abstract: Debate over globalization’s uneven consequences has renewed interest in whether trade and investment opening fosters technological upgrading in emerging economies. Drawing on absorptive capacity and technological capability theories, we argue that liberalization operates as a simultaneous competitive and knowledge shock whose upgrading effects are conditioned by absorptive capacity and sectoral technology intensity. Firms with greater pre-shock absorptive capacity are better positioned to recognize the technological gap revealed by import competition and respond through deliberate investment in technical human capital. The minimum capability required rises with the complexity of sectoral knowledge, so that firms in low-technology industries can clear the threshold at lower prior endowments than those in knowledge-intensive sectors. Using quasi-experimental variation from Brazil’s reforms of the 1990s and matched employer-employee data, we find that high absorptive capacity firms increase STEM employment by approximately 46 percent relative to low absorptive capacity firms. Mean responses are positive in low-technology industries and negative in high-technology industries, consistent with a rising capability threshold. Wage effects are weak, indicating adjustment occurs primarily through quantities rather than prices. Liberalization favors the prepared firm: opening selects firms capable of converting competitive pressure into technical human capital investment, with thresholds that vary systematically with sectoral knowledge intensity.

title: Policy-induced instability and the internalisation of MNE’s low-carbon strategies
authors: Maurice Wokke* (University of Amsterdam)
abstract: Decarbonisation policy is fundamentally changing the strategic environment of Multinational Enterprises (MNEs) in carbon-intensive sectors within the European Union (EU). While International Business (IB) traditionally conceptualises formal institutions as relatively stable frameworks guiding firm behaviour, this research argues that policy environments in the context of the long-term energy (LTE) transition are unstable, and actively disrupt strategic decision-making. We discuss policy instability to explain how MNEs internalise and deploy low-carbon technologies under conditions of institutional uncertainty and complexity. Building on internalisation theory and institutional perspectives, we develop a process-oriented framework that captures how firms interpret, discount, and respond to shifting policy signals across governance levels. Drawing on qualitative data from senior executives and senior managers in the European utilities and steel sectors, as well as policymakers, the study shows that policy frameworks simultaneously enable and destabilise investments. Firms construct provisional business cases, stage investments, and position themselves across multiple technological pathways (e.g., hydrogen, electrification, Carbon Capture and Storage), reflecting a flexible strategic response to fragile and policy-contingent location advantages. The findings challenge core IB assumptions regarding the stability of institutions and extend internalisation theory by incorporating the temporal and uncertain nature of policy environments. By linking investments complexity under institutional uncertainty, this study offers a novel explanation for cross-border variation in low-carbon strategy adoption. We argue that institutions act as endogenous sources of instability in the energy transition of hard-to-abate sectors.

title: Agglomerated, Built, and Clustered: The ABCs of Infrastructure, Spillover, and Innovation
authors: Adam Koling* (University of Oxford)
abstract: Density, urbanization, and geographic co-location are implicitly or explicitly prioritized in organizational decisions, and cited in literature, as key drivers of local and regional economic productivity and innovation. Multiple proposed mechanisms may explain the outsized efficiency and performance achieved in cities, from tangible spatial connectivity to reduced friction in the flow of knowledge and ideas. It follows intuitively that physical environments and knowledge flows work together, with simultaneous movements of ideas and people as symbiotic forces in regional economies. We know relatively little, however, about which economic conditions and types of built environments are most suited to one another, and whether there are optimal combinations to activate knowledge spillovers and ensuing innovations. In this paper, we consider the role of urban built environments, in particular transport, land use, and broadband systems, and how they interact with two contrasting knowledge flow theories: Jacobs and Marshall, Arrow, Romer (MAR). We pose three research questions: first, whether industry specialization and market competition influence four outcomes (new hires, new firms, new hires in new firms, and utility patents) at the county level in the United States, evaluating evidence for the Jacobs and MAR theories across the United States. Second, we test whether Jacobs and MAR economic conditions matter more in regions characterized by one infrastructure genre over another. Finally, we deploy the same techniques to explore whether regions with higher digital connectivity tend to favor Jacobs or MAR spillovers. We find consistent differences in innovation and productivity for MAR- and Jacobs-oriented regions, and a range of interaction effects with physical and digital connectivity, with robustness to model specification but sensitivity to types of built environments, land use, and transport. Our results, while preliminary, suggest that knowledge flows may first be unlocked at the microgeographic level, and that the theorized relationships between regional infrastructure types and spillover mechanisms may not account sufficiently for much smaller-scale human connectivity. These findings deliver relevant information not only to scholars of cities, agglomeration economies, and physical infrastructure, but also to the engineering and planning professions writ large. Land use, transport, and urban development are not simply characterized by density and proximity, but also by market conditions and industry types present. Ultimately, the performance of these industries (by a variety of outcome metrics) hinges on correct measurement and interpretation of their relationships with human and built environments.

title: Communication failures surrounding Data Centers
authors: Prathyaj Mantha* (Univeristy of Virginia); (Nomad Futurist)
abstract: There is an unprecedented data center growth, with over $3 trillion in planned investment through 2030. However, over 60% of proposed projects face significant community or regulatory opposition. This paper looks to identify the systematic communication failure across the stakeholder ecosystem surrounding digital infrastructure development. Drawing on a multi-stakeholder analytical framework, this study examines twelve distinct groups — hyperscalers, AI companies, data center developers, utility providers infrastructure investors, local policymakers, regulators and permit agencies, environmental organizations, host communities, media, research institution and universities and trade associations. With each group mapped across axes of institutional power and community proximity. Each group operates with distinct information access levels, narrative frames, and communication styles, and the misalignments between them produce predictable, recurring breakdowns. This research employs a five-phase methodology: a structured literature review spanning NIMBY theory, risk communication, and stakeholder engagement; primary interviews across all stakeholder groups; systematic media and discourse analysis; synthesis into a Communications Failure Typology; and production of an actionable stakeholder engagement protocol. The study addresses four core research questions: why data center projects generate disproportionate opposition relative to their actual footprint; how different groups narratively frame the same infrastructure; what structural and institutional factors drive developer-community breakdown; and what policy and communication mechanisms can reduce friction. The research contributes original research that does not currently exist in the literature, with direct applicability to developers, regulators, community advocates, and policymakers navigating the next decade of digital infrastructure expansion.

session_name: Pharmaceutical Markets and Drug Supply Chains
category: Health Care Systems, Biotechnology, and Pharmaceuticals
title: Blockbusters, Sequels, and the Nature of Innovation
authors: Wesley M. Cohen (Duke University Fuqua School of Business and NBER); Matthew J. Higgins (Tulane University A. B. Freeman School of Business, NBER, and Max Planck Institute for Innovation and Competition); William D. Miles* (Duke University Fuqua School of Business); Yoko Shibuya (Duke University Fuqua School of Business)
abstract: Using detailed product- and invention-level data from the pharmaceutical industry, we demonstrate that firms with high-selling ``blockbuster'' products concentrate their development efforts on new products that target the same customer segments and are technologically similar to existing offerings, rather than diversifying into new approaches. We propose that this pattern can be explained by an expectation of sales stickiness, whereby firms expect current product sales to persist, making investing in R&D within that customer segment more appealing. In addition, firm's marketing and R&D capabilities reinforce this behavior, but they do not fully explain it. By shifting the focus from firm-level characteristics to product-level drivers of innovation, our findings highlight how the commercial success of individual products shapes the direction of technological change, contributing to incremental innovation in R\&D-intensive industries.

session_name: Pharmaceutical Markets and Drug Supply Chains
category: Health Care Systems, Biotechnology, and Pharmaceuticals
title: Regulatory Inspections and Supply Chain Disruption Recovery Time: Regulatory Traction and Regulatory Friction as Theoretical Explanations in the Context of Canadian Drug Shortages
authors: Saurabh Ambulkar* (University of Texas at Arlington); Johnny Rungtusanatham (University of Cincinnati); Sriram Venkatraman (University of South Carolina)
abstract: Pharmaceutical drug shortages represent a persistent public health challenge, yet limited research has examined how quickly shortages are resolved once they occur. This study investigates how regulatory inspections influence the time-to-resolution (TTR) of drug shortages, focusing on two dimensions: inspection frequency and inspection scrutiny. Using longitudinal drug-shortage level data from Health Canada, we link 10,850 resolved shortages reported between 2017 and 2023 to 6,757 regulatory inspections conducted at the associated manufacturing facilities. We analyze these relationships before and after the COVID pandemic. Our findings show that regulatory inspections do not exert a uniform or linear effect on shortage resolution. Pre-COVID, inspection frequency had no measurable effect, while inspection scrutiny was associated with faster resolution. Post-COVID, however, both inspection frequency and scrutiny display nonlinear patterns: frequency follows an U-shaped relationship with TTR, and scrutiny follows an inverted U-shape. To develop nascent theory for these effects, we conceptualize regulatory inspections as simultaneously generating value and imposing burden on regulatory targets, with their net effect lying on a value-to-burden continuum. We leverage this conceptualization to propose Regulatory Traction and Regulatory Friction, and the moderating role of exogenous disruption triggers, as theoretical explanations for when and why regulatory inspections hasten or impede drug shortage resolution.

session_name: Pharmaceutical Markets and Drug Supply Chains
category: Health Care Systems, Biotechnology, and Pharmaceuticals
title: Managing Shortages in Drug Supply Chains – A Data Analytics Approach
authors: Vincent Hargaden* (University College Dublin); Nikolaos Papakostas (University College Dublin); Sean Mcgarraghy (University College Dublin)
abstract: Drug shortages are widely recognised as a serious problem across developed and developing countries, as they directly impact the quality of healthcare outcomes for patients in hospital and primary care settings. The range of drugs regularly reported by healthcare professional bodies, regulators and the general media as being on shortage vary from basic commodities such as intravenous saline, to analgesics, antibiotics, vaccines and cancer therapeutics. The problem is highly pervasive and complex owing to the increasingly long, globalised nature of drug supply chains that operate across a wide variety of stakeholders and countries. While the issue of drug shortages is not a new phenomenon, the challenges presented during and since the COVID-19 pandemic seem to have exacerbated the problem, making the issue more topical than ever on healthcare and political agendas. A large body of academic research exists that describes the nature of the drug shortages issue. This is supported through reports from healthcare professional bodies and regulatory authorities. However, relatively few of these works develop analytical models that can assess the magnitude of the problem, suggest mechanisms to alleviate shortages, and improve the resilience of drug chains. To address this apparent gap, this research develops a preliminary machine learning model for the prediction of shortages in drug supply chains. It starts with acquiring publicly available drug shortages data from two European countries (Belgium and Italy). The machine learning approach used to develop the prediction model is Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) due to its regression and classification potential. The output from the model is a prediction when a particular drug will be unavailable. While the model is in the preliminary stage of development, the results underscore the importance of the availability of more extensive historical shortage data through harmonised reporting, larger sample sizes and diverse features for better prediction of drug shortages.

title: The Organizational Limits of AI and the Propagation of Failure
authors: Dalbert Ma* (London Business School)
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used not only to perform tasks but also to place interdependent organizational activity under unified control. This paper shows that the gains from doing so may derive in part from eliminating structural features preserved when coordination remains divided across independent decision-makers. I study a partially automated container terminal in which autonomous vehicles are centrally directed by AI and move simultaneously through two kinds of areas: areas governed predominantly by the AI alone, and areas where those same vehicles share corridors with human-driven trucks governed by independent decision-makers. Using 780,000 task-level observations over 364 days and quasi-exogenous mechanical faults as disruptions, I find that areas governed predominantly by AI remain more productive in normal periods but are less able to contain localized failures. A formal model explains this pattern. When coordination remains divided across independent actors, buffer between interdependent activities arises endogenously; under unified AI control, that buffer can be compressed more extensively, increasing productivity but also increasing the propagation of localized disruption. More broadly, the findings suggest that when AI is used to coordinate interdependent activity, its most consequential effects may appear in the organization as a whole rather than in the performance of individual tasks.

title: Governance by and of Intermediaries: Notified Bodies under the EU AI Act
authors: Michael Sierra* (Hebrew University)
abstract: As governments seek to regulate artificial intelligence while preserving innovation, they increasingly rely on intermediary institutions rather than direct state control. This paper examines the European Union’s decision to use notified bodies: third-party conformity assessment organizations, to verify compliance of certain high-risk AI systems under the EU AI Act. The paper argues that the AI Act establishes an industry governance model in which market access, innovation incentives, and regulatory credibility are delegated to specialized intermediaries positioned between regulators and firms. These actors assess technical documentation, quality-management systems, and risk controls before products enter the EU market. The EU therefore governs AI industries through intermediaries while simultaneously governing those intermediaries through designation and supervision. This raises a broader industry studies question: why do states rely on private or semi-private verification actors when regulating strategically important industries, and what are the consequences for competition, compliance costs, innovation, and accountability? Using a theory-testing process-tracing design, the paper analyzes the evolution of the EU AI regime between 2018 and 2026 through legislative materials, policy documents, and expert interviews. It evaluates three explanations: industry pressure for flexible compliance models; public-sector capacity constraints; and Europe’s market-governance tradition based on standards and conformity assessment. The findings suggest that capacity constraints were the primary driver of delegation, while industry actors influenced the scope of third-party oversight. The paper shows how regulation creates new markets, new gatekeepers, and new forms of industrial organization in the AI economy.

title: AI Insurance for Business Operations
authors: Claudio Perez De Amézaga* (IESE Business School); Mihalis G. Markakis (IESE Business School); Agni Orfanoudaki (University of Oxford); Neeraj Sarna (Munich Re)
abstract: As AI systems increasingly drive business operations, managing the financial risk arising from algorithmic errors becomes essential for sustainable deployment. In this paper, we study parametric insurance contracts for predictive AI systems, where coverage is triggered when prediction errors exceed contractually specified thresholds and ground-truth outcomes are verifiable. We develop a unified contract design that spans self-insurance (developer retains all predictive risk) and third-party coverage (external insurer assumes part of the exposure). The model identifies conditions for actuarially fair pricing and risk allocation proportional to tolerance, jointly determining tolerated deviation bounds, license fees, and premiums. Our analysis shows that the tolerated error deviation of the AI model governs local coverage intensity and depends only on model characteristics and claim costs, while the license fee serves as the aggregate adjustment variable that aligns exposure with financial capacity. Moreover, tail-risk constraints imposed through Conditional Value-at-Risk compress feasible demand and adjust equilibrium pricing without altering coverage rules. We also find that correlation and tail behavior shape contractual outcomes beyond what mean accuracy alone would predict. Finally, we propose a scalable implementation framework and validate its application through a case study in battery state-of-health prediction, combining five machine learning models with inverse conformal prediction to calibrate contracts directly from observed forecast errors. Our empirical results confirm the robustness of the proposed theoretical structure under realistic error distributions. These results establish parametric AI insurance as a mechanism for quantifying, pricing, and transferring predictive risk in AI-driven operations.

title: Contract design for AI insurance
authors: Mina Iravani* (University of Oxford); Agni Orfanoudaki (University of Oxford); Mihalis Markakis (IESE Business School)
abstract: As AI systems become increasingly embedded in business operations, managing the financial consequences of algorithmic errors is critical for safe scalable deployment. This paper studies the design of parametric insurance contracts for agentic AI systems, in which the developer commits ex ante to compensate users when the algorithm produces a confident error in binary decision settings. We study how contract design determines the insurability of AI and, in turn, the extent of operation that can be credibly guaranteed as autonomous. We compare alternative contract forms. When client value depends on the declared scope of the guarantee, profitable expansion is governed by how quickly error risk rises at the boundary. When client value instead depends on the realized share of autonomously handled cases, it is governed by the density of activity at the boundary relative to the density of errors within it. Consequently, AI systems with similar predictive performance can require very different contracts and support substantially different guaranteed autonomous regions. Our findings suggest that insurability cannot be inferred from standard global performance metrics alone. Notably, tying client value to realized autonomous activity can shrink the optimal guaranteed region rather than expand it. We further study contract scope as a design choice by allowing coverage across multiple tasks. Higher degree of generalizability increases cumulative risk exposure but can also expand the optimal guaranteed region by improving the trade-off between value creation and insured risk. However, it may decrease profit and may be undesirable even when it enlarges guaranteed autonomy.

category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
title: From Citizen Developer to AI-Augmented Innovator: Role Redistribution, Governance, and Human Capital Consequences of Generative AI Adoption in Low-Code Platforms
authors: Yazen Alsafi* (IE Business School)
abstract: The embedding of generative AI in low-code and no-code (LC/NC) platforms is reshaping the work of millions of non-technical professionals who build organizational applications without formal programming expertise. How this transformation redistributes roles, reconfigures accountability, and differentiates outcomes across workers and organizations remains empirically unresolved. We investigate these questions using a quasi-experimental interrupted time-series design applied to 96,847 behavioral observations from four independent LC/NC practitioner communities over 37 to 63 months, leveraging the staggered general availability dates of AI features as exogenous shocks. A companion comparative case study across enterprises in the energy, industrial automation, and media sectors is currently underway, with preliminary findings expected by the time of presentation. We find that AI discourse normalizes universally following adoption, that problem complexity escalates across all four communities, and that elaborative engagement deepens continuously but only in platforms characterized by high pre-adoption task generativity, a novel boundary condition that predicts outcome heterogeneity with complete ex ante accuracy. Critically, governance concern rises continuously after adoption normalizes, revealing a gap between when organizations perceive governance risk as resolved and when that risk is actually compounding. Drawing on Sociotechnical Systems Theory and Open Innovation, these findings carry direct implications for how organizations govern AI-augmented workers and for regulatory frameworks seeking to assign accountability in algorithmically mediated work.

category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
title: When Professions Legitimise but Individual Professionals Resist: A Morphogenetic Account of Loose Coupling between Analytics Expertise and Professional Work
authors: Jaejin Lee* (University of Oxford)
abstract: Professions renew their legitimacy by incorporating new expertise, yet individual practitioners often resist such expertise in everyday practice. This paradox is vividly illustrated by HR analytics (HRA): professional bodies promote analytics as a route to extend HR's jurisdiction, yet adoption within organisations remains superficial and uneven. Drawing on Archer's (1995; 2003) morphogenetic approach, we examine how institutional conditioning, situated interaction and structural elaboration jointly reproduce loose coupling between HRA and HR practice. The framework is inherently multi-level and requires data capable of capturing each phase, so we draw on two datasets each assigned a theoretically specified role. A corpus of 38 semi-structured interviews with HR professionals across diverse Korean organisations captures the field-level structural conditioning that shapes practitioners' concerns, revealing three shared orientations: HR is about people and relationships, not numbers; analytics threatens power; and analytics induces vulnerability. A two-year hybrid ethnography of a newly formed HRA team in a Korea-headquartered multinational technology firm undergoing post-acquisition restructuring captures how these orientations are enacted through social interaction and elaborated into stabilised outcomes across twelve decision episodes. The ethnography shows how episode after episode culminates in morphostasis rather than morphogenesis, hardening individual vulnerabilities into shared worlds of concern that keep analytics at arm's length. We specify the multi-level microfoundational mechanism through which macro-level legitimation and micro-level resistance are recursively reproduced, and recast capability deficits as downstream effects of this reproduction. The findings contribute to institutional theory on loose coupling and inform debates on the future of professional work amid data-driven transformations.

category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
title: Gen-AI Driven Reconfiguration of Professional Expertise in the Legal Sector
authors: Atif Sarwar* (University of Liverpool); Jingqi Zhu (University of Liverpool); Emma Forsgren (University of Leeds); Emma Gritt (University of Leeds); Shenghao Xie (University of Liverpool)
abstract: Whilst the legal sector is experiencing increased transformation through Generative AI (GenAI) enabled automation and augmentation, current scholarship has primarily articulated this phenomenon through the lens of professional resistance vs adoption. We argue that this dyadic articulation of the problem is limited in scope, overlooking the more subtle aspects of this GenAI-driven transformation of the legal sector. We highlight that with the introduction of GenAI into the legal practice, legal expertise is neither displaced nor upheld by professionals but rather fundamentally reconfigured as an epistemic expertise. Legal professionals are increasingly asked to act, what we term as ‘epistemic arbiters’. These epistemic arbiters are the expert authority determining the truth and reliability of GenAI-generated outputs and whether the legal knowledge presented is actionable, or if the outputs are hallucinated, deceptive, false and legally indefensible. Drawing on our empirical research with two law firms in the UK, we highlight that while the legal tasks such as document review, legal research, contract drafting, among others, have been automated, it still leaves legal professionals in charge of and legally responsible for substantive legal reasoning, client representation, and professional accountability. However, most importantly, legal professionals are now increasingly tasked with deploying their legal expertise to perform epistemic evaluation of GenAI-generated content, scrutinising sources, identifying fabricated case citations, and determining whether algorithmically generated arguments are contextually defensible. Whilst professionally situated and algorithmic modes of knowing are foundationally built on knowledge-validating routines, the introduction of GenAI has forced a reorientation of professional expertise from purely information-based inference towards epistemic evaluation, thus repositioning legal expertise as the core mechanism through which GenAI-generated outputs are evaluated as actionable, legally defensible or invalid.

category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
title: Rethinking work assessment: organizational tools for the future of work
authors: Fernanda Martins (Antonio Meneghetti Faculdade); Isadora Stangherlin* (Antonio Meneghetti Faculdade)
abstract: This study examines the limitations of standardized psychosocial risk assessment tools in capturing the complexity of contemporary work and discusses the implications for organizational performance and managerial practice. As work environments become increasingly dynamic and interdependent, traditional survey-based instruments often fail to detect the relational, contextual, and processual dimensions that shape how work is actually carried out. This creates a gap between formal assessments and the realities that influence coordination, decision-making, and team effectiveness. Grounded in established frameworks, including Karasek’s Job Demand–Control model, Mintzberg’s organizational structure perspective, and Edmondson’s concept of psychological safety, the study adopts a multi-level lens to analyze how work is organized and experienced across hierarchical layers. Rather than focusing on individual-level outcomes alone, the research explores how organizational conditions and interactions influence the emergence of psychosocial risks. Using an exploratory qualitative design, data were collected through focus groups with employees from operational, managerial, and strategic levels in a Brazilian company. This approach enabled the identification of patterns that standardized tools are unlikely to capture, including discrepancies between prescribed and actual work, coordination challenges across levels, and informal practices developed to manage pressure and uncertainty. The findings highlight that reliance on standardized instruments may limit organizations’ ability to diagnose and respond to critical workplace dynamics. For leaders, this suggests the need for complementary tools capable of capturing organizational nuance, enabling collective sensemaking, and improving alignment across levels. By reframing psychosocial risk management as an organizational capability, the study contributes to discussions on the future of work, emphasizing the role of managerial tools in sustaining effective, coordinated, and adaptive work systems.

category: Operations, Supply Chain, and AI-Enhanced Industry 4.0
title: Who adopts Cleantech? Evidence from 10 million truck inspections
authors: Alex Scott* (University of Tennessee)
abstract: The development and diffusion of clean technology (cleantech) is one of the primary strategies used to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. However, little is known about which firms adopt clean technology and why they do so. We study the diffusion of clean truck technology by decoding vehicle identification numbers from over 10 million trucks over an 8-year period and link these trucks to firms, geographies, local economies, and operating characteristics of the loads. We examine which firms are most likely to operate old, dirty trucks, and discuss policies that might hasten the retirement of these trucks. Finally, we develop theory explaining the adoption of cleantech.
session_chair: Miriam Wilhelm (WU Vienna University of Economics and Business)

category: Operations, Supply Chain, and AI-Enhanced Industry 4.0
title: From style-centrism to eco-design centrism? Investigating the pivotal role of the supply chain in enabling transformation in the fashion industry
authors: Paolo Barbieri* (University of Bologna); Mariachiara Colucci (University of Bologna); Eleonora Foschi (ENEA)
abstract: This study contributes to the under-researched topic of the transformative impact of industrial strategies over operations and supply chain, specifically in the domain of policies for circular economy by focusing on the recently released regulation on eco-design by the European Commission. In particular, the literature lacks a clear understanding of the impact of regulations and policies on the (re)configuration of supply chains. Amid rising social and environmental concerns, the fashion industry has become a priority on the European Union’s political agenda (European Commission, 2025). In light of the environmental impact of decisions made in the design stage (European Commission, 2018), and the strong influence of the design activities on upstream and downstream operations, this research investigates the readiness of fashion companies, as well as the pathways they envision to comply with this regulatory change. The research involved the selection of firms that play a key decision-making role (i.e., focal companies) within their respective supply chains. A total of 19 Italian companies were considered, representing 35 distinct exemplary case studies. These firms, collectively, also provide a meaningful cross-section of the national fashion system in terms of turnover, employment size, product categories, and market segments (Regione Emilia-Romagna, 2020). The research methodology combined quantitative and qualitative approaches and was structured in three phases involving companies’ key-informants: (1) a questionnaire survey, (2) semi-structured interviews, and (3) a focus group. The data collection started in 2024, right after the release of the regulation, and lasted more than 18 months. In relation to eco-design measures, the study reveals a highly heterogeneous degree of readiness: While high-end companies demonstrate a significant level of alignment with specific requirements—particularly those connected to durability, reliability, and the management of hazardous substances—the overall readiness remains partial and fragmented, showing a lack of systematic implementation of eco-design as a consolidated practice. To explicate how companies plan to address the ongoing transformation in their journey for compliance under raising regulatory pressures, an extensive framework highlighting the key dimensions, and the interrelationships among them, was developed. Specifically, the framework shows two main areas of intervention, namely: (1) the adoption of new operational logics that challenge the traditional style-centric approach, enabling a stronger integration of eco-design requirements in the design activity; (2) the rethinking of companies’ supply chains both in structural and governance dimensions, given their strong reliance on external partners.
session_chair: Miriam Wilhelm (WU Vienna University of Economics and Business)

category: Operations, Supply Chain, and AI-Enhanced Industry 4.0
title: Scaling biochar for carbon dioxide removal: a system dynamics approach to biochar in global coffee value chains
authors: Zach Rabinowitz* (Kuhne Logistics University); Johannes Meuer (Kuhne Logistics University); Maria Besiou (Kuhne Logistics University)
abstract: Climate change is intensifying pressure on policymakers and firms to reduce the environmental impact of industrial supply chains. Reducing emissions through mitigation remains the primary response, but mitigation alone is insufficient to eliminate residual emissions. To address these remaining emissions, research and industry - particularly in hard-to-abate sectors and complex global supply chains - are increasingly exploring Carbon Dioxide Removal (CDR) technologies (i.e., technologies that remove CO2 from the atmosphere and store it durably in a carbon reservoir.) Across the range of CDR technologies, biochar is emerging as a particularly promising hybrid approach because it combines durable carbon storage with potential agronomic and economic co-benefits. Yet, due to established supply chain structures and the complex interdependencies among agricultural productivity, waste management, and financial viability, the scaling potential of biochar remains poorly understood. In this study, we analyze alternative scenarios for fusing two supply chains: an emerging biochar-based carbon removal industry and an established coffee commodity chain. Using system dynamics modeling, proprietary farm-level procurement data from Honduras, and complementary archival and expert data, we jointly assess the environmental and financial outcomes of different scaling scenarios. Our inter-industry perspective highlights that scaling CDR technologies depends on how the technology is embedded in the established production, sourcing, and transport systems of the coffee industry. Specifically, we show how design choices regarding the location and placement of the technology, the end use of biochar, and the monetization of carbon savings shape scaling pathways. Our study contributes to research on industrial dynamics and supply chain management by showing how emerging and established industries can be reconfigured to support decarbonization. It also offers important insights for policymaking by identifying the incentive structures, market designs, and governance mechanisms needed to enable credible and scalable CDR deployment.

category: Operations, Supply Chain, and AI-Enhanced Industry 4.0
title: Counting Carbon, Losing Productivity: The Unintended Operational Costs of Mandatory Carbon Disclosure
authors: Sotiris Blanas (WMG, University of Warwick); Alok Choudhary* (Warwick University)
abstract: Mandatory carbon disclosure (MCD) has become a prominent policy instrument in recent years for improving environmental transparency, yet its impact on productivity-related outcomes is still not well understood. We exploit the United Kingdom’s 2013 MCD regulation as a quasi-natural experiment. Using difference-in-differences and event-study approaches on a matched sample of manufacturing firms listed on the London Stock Exchange (treated) and other European exchanges (control), we estimate its impact on productivity-related outcomes, recognising that productivity is inherently multi-dimensional and cannot be captured by a single measure. We find that MCD leads to statistically and economically significant declines across multiple dimensions of productivity, including operational productivity, labour productivity, total factor productivity, and inventory efficiency. These effects are strongest in the first two to four years following implementation and persist thereafter, particularly in the early years following implementation. Our evidence suggests that these disruptions begin at the operational level, affecting production, labour deployment, and inventory coordination, and then extend to broader firm-level productivity. Consistent with the attention-based view, carbon disclosure acts as a regulatory attention and resource allocation shock, increasing coordination and information-processing demands. We also find meaningful heterogeneity, with larger declines among firms with weaker pre-regulation capabilities and longer investment horizons. From a policy perspective, our results challenge the existing assumption that carbon disclosure-based regulation is operationally neutral. While transparency may yield long-term benefits, rapid and prescriptive implementation can impose short- to medium-run productivity costs. We discuss implications for the design and support mechanisms of disclosure policies to help mitigate some of the unintended operational tradeoffs.

title: Industrial Statecraft in the New Global Order: A Survival Guide for LMICs
authors: Max Walter* (Independent scholar)
abstract: The end of hyper-globalisation and the emergence of a fragmented, strategically contested world economy mark a historic inflection point for economic policy. Free-market globalisation is giving way to a new era of strategic competition in which major powers openly weaponise economic interdependence, using trade, finance, and technology as tools of coercion. This paper explores the return and metamorphosis of state-led industrial policy as a central tool of statecraft defining this new era. Unlike past efficiency-driven models, the new industrial statecraft prioritises technological sovereignty, secure supply chains, and national security. The paper then assesses why and how low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) must build industrial statecraft capabilities, develop industrial ecosystems, and align with strategic partners - or risk remaining stuck as raw material exporters while others capture higher-value gains. LMICs face pressure to chase quick wins - whether through transactional deals with major powers, short-term incentives to attract footloose capital, or reactive responses to global shocks. But such knee-jerk reactions jeopardize countries’ resilience and sovereignty. The paper develops an industrial statecraft ‘survival guide’ for LMICs, drawing from industrial policy, geopolitics, and government delivery insights. It posits that LMICs need a deliberate strategy that (i) leverages fit-for-purpose industrial policy tools, (ii) is geopolitically smart, and (iii) is anchored on delivery capability. Surviving and thriving in a more fragmented and competitive global order requires building robust ecosystems and leveraging national advantages, fostering strong and consistent diplomatic negotiation capabilities, and building agile state competence to execute and adapt while protecting fiscal space in the face of shocks.

title: From Picking Winners to Absorbing Winners? DeepSeek and the Adaptive Reconfiguration of Chinese Industrial Policy
authors: Xu Liu* (University of Bonn)
abstract: As industrial policy returns to the center of global political economy, China appears to be developing a more adaptive mode of state intervention in selected high-uncertainty sectors. Focusing on the rise of DeepSeek, this paper examines whether industrial policy in frontier AI is becoming less dependent on the classical logic of ex ante “picking winners” and increasingly oriented toward the ex post incorporation of market-validated actors. Rather than suggesting a wholesale replacement of earlier industrial policy, the DeepSeek case points to an emerging tendency in selected high-uncertainty sectors: instead of identifying winners ex ante, the state may increasingly move to absorb and integrate market-validated winners ex post. The paper advances this argument in three steps. First, it develops “absorbing winners” as an analytical lens for understanding a policy sequence in which market competition and technological experimentation initially identify viable firms, after which the state moves to incorporate them into broader infrastructural, regulatory, and strategic frameworks. Second, it argues that the DeepSeek case reflects such a sequence, with market breakthrough followed by incorporation into state-backed digital infrastructure and governance arrangements. Third, it contends that this tendency is sectorally differentiated: while ex post absorption may be more likely in uncertain and fast-moving domains such as AI and software, ex ante coordination remains central in more path-dependent sectors such as semiconductors. The paper thus offers a differentiated understanding of Chinese industrial policy beyond the binary of market liberalization versus state control.

title: Temporary technology and the maintenance of technological sovereignty
authors: Susanna Mansikkamäki* (Jyväskylä University); Antti Sihvonen (University of Helsinki); Mirva Peltoniemi (Tampere University); Kalle Pajunen (Tampere University)
abstract: This study investigates how technology is developed to maintain technological sovereignty when sudden societal needs arise. To study this issue, we look into the efforts of the Finnish state to overcome the shortage of mineral oil-based lubricants during the Second World War and identify tar oil as a central technology in this endeavor. It was a domestic wood-based alternative that temporarily substituted the mineral oil-based lubricants that were limitedly available because of the war. By analyzing the development and demise of the Finnish tar oil industry based on longitudinal archival data and building on the prior literature on technological sovereignty and technology evolution, we develop the concept of temporary technology, which we define as a satisficing technological solution to a short-term societal need. We further elaborate on the life cycle of temporary technology and how it is influenced by the short-term societal need that underlies it. By uncovering this form of technology evolution, we complement existing literature by showing how technologies are developed to satisfy short-term societal needs. Furthermore, we extend the technological sovereignty discussion by identifying challenges related to the maintenance of technological sovereignty with temporary technology. In doing so, our findings bring much needed evidence on how technological sovereignty is maintained in practice. The findings also have implications to the science, technology, and innovation policy as we further discuss how the limited time scale sets differing rules for developing technology- and policy-level solutions to societal needs, compared to those that characterize long-term transformative scenarios.

title: Going the extra mile: How battery, electric motor, and autonomous technologies influence the driving range of electric vehicles
authors: Antony Potter* (University of Manchester)
abstract: Over the past two decades the automotive industry has been transformed by the growing demand for electric vehicles in many countries around the world. In particular, the supply expansion of new electric vehicles is being driven by multiple advances in battery, electric motor, and autonomous driving technologies. However, one of the main limiting factors that holds back the widespread adoption of electric vehicles is consumers’ concerns surrounding vehicle driving range. Within this research paper we draw upon configuration theory to undertake one of the first empirical studies of how different powertrain, technological, and modular configurations influence the driving range of electric vehicles. To examine our research hypotheses, we use a global database of all electric vehicles in the automotive industry together with multivariate moderation analysis and endogeneity tests. Overall, we find that battery capacity, electric motor output, electric motor torque, and autonomous driving technologies are important determinants of the driving range of electric vehicles. However, to varying degrees these direct effects are influenced by the configuration of different technologies and modular architectures within electric vehicles. Our findings identify several managerial implications for different stakeholders, managers, and policymakers involved in the development of new electric vehicles in the global automotive industry.

title: Can strategic dependencies harm the acceleration towards net-zero transition? The case of the lithium-ion battery industry
authors: Nicolo Geri* (Sapienza University of Rome)
abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between technological capabilities, import dependency, and environmental policies, focusing on the lithium-ion battery supply chain (LBSC) - a critical sector for the net-zero transition. We contribute to the growing literature on the drivers and barriers to accelerating the transition in the following ways. First, we develop an original analytical framework that integrates two recent streams of literature - one focusing on the acceleration of the green transition and the other on structural dependencies and technological sovereignty - to examine potential trade-offs between these objectives. Second, we develop a strategic intelligence analysis of the LBSC allowing to quantify import dependencies and technological capacity gaps at a highly granular product/technology level. This allows to identify critical products and supply chain stages where policy action is needed to avoid the emergence of bottlenecks to the green transition. Third, we examine how technological capabilities influence import dependency, showing under what conditions technological upgrading strengthens competitive positions and mitigates dependency. Finally, we analyse how environmental policy stringency relates to import dependency, assessing whether and in which circumstances environmental goals may conflict with technological sovereignty and strategic autonomy ones. Our Ąndings suggest that technological upgrading can reduce dependencies without compromising environmental goals so that the presumed trade-off between the net-zero transition and structural dependencies does not necessarily hold. In contrast, a welldesigned policy mix, aligning environmental objectives with targeted innovation and industrial policies, can enhance both resilience and the acceleration towards the net-zero transition.

title: Time to take off? Delineating system barriers to accelerating zero-emission aircraft innovation in the UK aviation sector
authors: Qi Song* (University of Cambridge)
abstract: Aviation is widely recognised as one of the hardest-to-abate sectors in the transition to net zero. However, current policy debates largely focus on system efficiency improvements and alternative energy carriers, with comparatively limited attention to the innovation and deployment of zero-emission aircrafts. This imbalance reflects the sector’s distinctive industrial dynamics and unique market structures, also raises concerns about the future industrial leadership of incumbent economies with substantial aviation industries, such as the UK, particularly the risk of missing windows of opportunity during technological disruption. Building on the seminal work on technical change in the aircraft industry (Mowery & Rosenberg, 1981), this study takes a first step in addressing these challenges by examining the structural and functional barriers shaping both the supply of technological knowledge and the demand for innovative aircraft designs in the contemporary UK context. This project draws on primary data from over ten in-depth semi-structured interviews with senior industry representatives and sector experts, supplemented by two focus group roundtables and secondary sources including policy documents, research reports, position papers, and statistical data. The findings highlight not only inherent technological complexity, but also the co-evolution of funding structures, market valuation models, infrastructure readiness, and regulatory uncertainty in narrowing down into the current sectoral transition pathways. Furthermore, misaligned timelines between net-zero targets, sectoral innovation models, and fleet renewal cycles constrain the pace of disruptive change. Collectively, the study underscores the need to redesign innovation policy frameworks to accelerate the innovation and deployment of zero-emission aircraft.

title: PARITI: How Emerging Economies Scale Ultra-Affordable Electric Vehicles Under Geopolitical Fragmentation
authors: Vijaya Zinnoury* (University of Denver, Daniels College of Business); Ann Varghese (Transit Intelligence, LLP)
abstract: Rising geopolitical polarization, techno-nationalism, supply-chain fragmentation, and critical resource constraints are reshaping how firms innovate and scale in strategic sectors such as electric mobility. Yet existing business model innovation (BMI) frameworks provide limited insight into how macro-level geoeconomic forces shape firm-level design choices, ecosystem strategies, and inclusive market creation. This paper develops the PARITI framework — Polarisation, Alliances, Resources, Integration of Technology, and Inclusivity as a structural lens for analyzing BMI under global fragmentation. Using a comparative qualitative case study of three ultra-affordable electric vehicles in India — Yakuza Karishma (YK), Vayve Mobility EVA (VM), and MG Comet EV (MGC), we examine how firms configure localization, ecosystem partnerships, modular technology architectures, and affordability to compete in price-sensitive and infrastructure-constrained markets. The findings show that affordability-driven innovation in emerging economies leads to cost reductions, enables strategic resilience and inclusion capability, promotes scalable ventures under geopolitical risk, capital scarcity, and ecosystem dependency. While MGC exemplifies corporate-scale affordability model embedded in global supply chains, VM demonstrates a modular solar-assisted frugal architecture, and YK illustrates a localized ultra-low-cost innovation pathway. The study contributes to international business and entrepreneurship research by (1) conceptualizing BMI as a transferable ownership advantage, (2) theorizing ecosystem-orchestrated affordability as scalable and inclusive competitive pathway, and (3) demonstrating how geopolitical fragmentation, industrial policy, and resource constraints shape firm-level business model design. By re-framing emerging-economy innovation as a source of globally transferable business models rather than local adaptation, the paper offers theoretical and policy insights into building resilient inclusive ventures in a fragmented world.
