title: Breakfast
The Hare AND the Tortoise: The Stage-Contingent Effect of Vertical Integration and Technology Implementation
authors: Gregory Young* (University of Minnesota - Twin Cities)
abstract: The organizational structures that help firms commit to digital transformation also prevent them from finishing. This technology assimilation gap, between commitment and completion, indicates the organizational factors enabling firm adoption of digital technology may differ from those required for successful implementation. I show this is because the same governance structures that facilitate commitment impede execution during radical technology transitions. I develop this argument using the theoretical construct of coordination specificity, the extent to which a firm’s information protocols and coordination routines are tailored to its existing governance boundaries. Based on a stage-contingent adjustment cost logic, I distinguish between two stages of implementation: initiation, where firms commit to deployment, and deployment, where firms diffuse technology across the firm. Vertical integration reduces commitment uncertainty, lowering initiation costs, by providing better visibility into the internal restructuring requirements. However, vertical integration creates durable, firm-specific coordination structures, increasing deployment costs, that are misaligned with the standardized interfaces required by digital technologies. In contrast, inter-firm coordination provides shared digital ecosystem protocols that reduce deployment frictions but does not affect assessment. Using panel data on smart meter deployments by U.S. electric utilities, I find vertical integration increases the likelihood of initiation but slows deployment. Inter-firm coordination diminishes the execution penalty from vertical integration while exhibiting no independent effect on initiation. The results have direct implications for how established firms sequence governance investments alongside technology commitments, demonstrating that governance structures have contrasting effects across sequential stages of implementation. These findings reframe the technology assimilation gap as a governance problem, showing that the same governance properties enabling commitment generate execution frictions at scale, providing a governance-level micro-foundation for understanding organizational adaptation under radical technological change.

title: From Digital Twins to Digital Cashflows: Embedded Finance Typologies in the Industrial Metaverse
authors: Mayukh Mukhopadhyay* (IIM Indore)
abstract: The industrial metaverse is increasingly framed as a convergence of digital twins, real time data infrastructures, and AI enabled simulation for operational excellence. Yet current research largely treats value creation as an engineering or productivity outcome, leaving the financial layer under theorized. This study advances the concept of embedded finance for industrial finance by examining how financial functions are being natively integrated into industrial metaverse environments. Drawing on industry blueprints, platform architectures, and leading industrial deployments, the paper theorizes how payment settlement, asset-based financing, insurance, and working capital optimization are becoming embedded within digital twin driven production systems. We conceptualize the industrial metaverse not only as a representational space but as a transactional infrastructure where operational states directly trigger financial decisions. This shift collapses traditional boundaries between operations, finance, and strategy. The study develops a process model that links digital twin maturity to new forms of financial coordination, risk visibility, and capital efficiency across industrial ecosystems. By embedding finance into simulation, firms can move from retrospective financial control toward anticipatory and scenario based financial governance. The analysis highlights implications for firm boundaries, platform power, and competitive advantage as industrial data becomes a financial asset. The paper contributes to strategy and industry studies by reframing embedded finance as an industrial capability rather than a consumer fintech phenomenon. It offers a foundation for understanding how industrial firms, platforms, and regulators will co evolve as financial logic becomes native to the industrial metaverse.

title: How to turn mistrust into trust? A Case of Hybrid Social Symbolic Work
authors: Jadwiga Supryn* (University of Oxford)
abstract: This study examines how mistrust in digital financial systems can be transformed into trust through what I conceptualize as hybrid social-symbolic work. While digital transformation promises to expand financial inclusion, persistent exclusion—particularly in contexts marked by inequality and institutional fragility—reveals that access alone is insufficient. The central challenge lies in credibility: individuals must perceive digital systems as trustworthy, legitimate, and aligned with their values. To address this, I introduce the concept of trust narratives—shared stories and interpretive frames through which actors make sense of vulnerability and reliability. Drawing on a qualitative, process-oriented study of FinTech practitioners in Ghana, this research explores how trust is constructed, performed, and sustained in practice. Based on interviews, observations, and textual analysis, the study shows how practitioners engage in narrative work that links technological competence with moral legitimacy. Through everyday interactions, community engagement, and service encounters, they frame digital finance as a story of empowerment, inclusion, and fairness. At the same time, they navigate counter-narratives rooted in historical experiences of exclusion and institutional distrust. The findings demonstrate that trust emerges not solely from technological functionality or regulatory compliance, but from the interplay of symbolic meaning-making and relational engagement. By weaving narratives that resonate with local values and experiences, practitioners embed digital technologies within social life. This reframes digital transformation as a fundamentally social process and advances understanding of trust as a narrative accomplishment. The study contributes to research on institutional work, digital innovation, and financial inclusion by highlighting how legitimacy is built through cultural and communicative practices in the Global South.

session_name: The Past, Present, and Future of HRM Research: Theoretical and Methodological Developments
category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
title: The Past, Present, and Future of HRM Research: Theoretical and Methodological Developments
authors: Rocio Bonet (IE Business School); John Delery (University of Arkansas); John Paul MacDuffie (The Wharton School)
abstract: This panel brings together leading scholars to examine the evolution and future trajectory of research on human resource management (HRM) within the broader study of work and organizations. Spanning areas such as human capital, strategic HRM, labor, and macro-OB, the discussion will reflect on key theoretical advances that have shaped the field, assess current debates and empirical approaches, and identify promising directions for future research. Panelists will consider how HRM scholarship has evolved in response to changing industry, organizational, and labor market dynamics, as well as the growing availability of new data and methodological tools. Particular attention will be paid to the integration of micro- and macro-level perspectives and to emerging opportunities for cross-disciplinary work. By connecting insights across traditions, the panel aims to stimulate dialogue on how to advance both theory and methods in the study of work and organizations.
panelists: Rocio Bonet (IE Business School); John Delery (University of Arkansas); John Paul MacDuffie (The Wharton School)

category: Operations, Supply Chain, and AI-Enhanced Industry 4.0
title: Cyber-Physical Systems Beyond the Hype: Empirical Industrial Evidence for a Lifecycle Framework
authors: Michael Gfoellner* (Graz University of Technology); Franz Haas (Graz University of Technology)
abstract: Cyber-physical systems (CPS) have long been regarded as key enablers of Industry 4.0, yet industrial adoption has remained limited despite significant research activity. Existing standards and architectural models offer conceptual clarity but provide little operational guidance for translating CPS concepts into deployable solutions. This work addresses this gap through an empirical investigation of two patented implementations in high-volume automotive body-in-white operations: a cyber-physical inspection system in serial production and a cyber-physical assembly system validated in prototype. These systems reveal practical constraints and enabling mechanisms of CPS deployment, demonstrating proven quality improvements and cost reductions in automotive production. They serve as the empirical foundation for deriving four technology-independent building blocks: integrated data capture, automated analytics, automated decision-making, and autonomous process intervention. Cross-case analysis confirmed their applicability and associated deliverables across inspection and assembly domains and project phases. Together, they form the foundation of the CADI (Capture-Analyze-Decide-Intervene) model. The systematic integration of CPS lifecycle phases enhances CADI into a structured lifecycle framework. This results in an implementation-ready roadmap that goes beyond architectural or axiomatic-design frameworks. Ongoing work operationalizes this framework through a multi-agent tool supporting readiness assessment, lifecycle entry-point selection, and next-action recommendations via an AI-powered chatbot. Next steps focus on validating CADI in discrete-manufacturing contexts toward cross-industry application and applying it in learning-factory environments using a CPS demonstrator. The vision is to contribute to moving CPS toward the Plateau of Productivity in the Gartner Hype Cycle by enabling mature, scalable applications and opening pathways into domains such as mobility, healthcare, and energy.

category: Operations, Supply Chain, and AI-Enhanced Industry 4.0
title: Assessing AI Readiness in Small- and Medium-Sized Manufacturers: Insights for Operations and Supply Chain Transformation
authors: Sadan Kulturel-Konak* (Penn State Berks); Abdullah Konak (Penn State Berks)
abstract: While Artificial Intelligence (AI) is central to Industry 4.0 transformation, small- and medium-sized manufacturers (SMMs) face persistent barriers to adopting AI-enabled Industry 4.0 technologies, including limited resources, workforce capabilities, leadership readiness, and digital infrastructure. Despite these challenges, there is limited empirical evidence on how SMMs assess and navigate AI adoption in operational and supply chain contexts. This paper presents preliminary findings from a study that develops and validates the Survey of Manufacturing AI Readiness and Transformation (SMART-AI). The research applies participatory methods, including focus groups with manufacturers, policymakers, and technology providers, to inform survey design. The SMART-AI instrument captures key dimensions of AI readiness, including adoption decision-making, implementation processes, organizational capabilities, ecosystem support, and leadership strategy. Pilot results reveal critical gaps in workforce preparedness, data infrastructure, and strategic alignment that constrain AI integration into production systems and supply chain operations. Early evidence suggests that SMMs are more likely to adopt AI in discrete operational functions (e.g., quality control, predictive maintenance) rather than across integrated supply chain systems, reflecting both capability limitations and risk considerations. The study advances research on AI-enabled Industry 4.0 by operationalizing firm-level AI readiness and linking organizational capabilities to operational and supply chain integration outcomes. The findings provide actionable insights for manufacturers, technology providers, and policymakers seeking to accelerate Industry 4.0 adoption among SMMs. More broadly, the work informs strategies to strengthen supply chain resilience, workforce development, and regional manufacturing competitiveness.

category: Operations, Supply Chain, and AI-Enhanced Industry 4.0
title: Bridging the Deployment Gap: Organizational Variance-Processing and the Drift Compatibility Model
authors: Melissa Appleyard* (Portland State University); Meena Al-Azzawe (Kinaxis); Kristi Yuthas (Portland State University)
abstract: Industry and policy analyses report a regional gradient in AI deployment, with organizations in Asia-Pacific and Europe consistently operationalizing AI systems more rapidly than those in North America (Eurostat, 2024; OECD/BCG/INSEAD, 2025). These differences persist despite the U.S.’s global dominance in model development and cannot be fully explained by infrastructure, regulation, digital maturity, or access to talent. We propose this gradient reflects a deeper sociotechnical variable: cultural drift compatibility—the degree to which national and organizational cultures can operate smoothly in the presence of probabilistic variance fields—distributions of plausible outputs and action pathways generated by stochastic AI systems. Instead of deterministic workflows, they produce non-repeatable, context-dependent outputs, introducing epistemic, operational, and interpretive variance. This differs from exogenous uncertainty or social equivocality, and instead is an intrinsic, technical property of the computational core. We introduce the “Drift Compass” framework for the metabolization of such variance. We posit that many Asian organizational cultures demonstrate variance-smoothing tendencies that harmonize with drift, an expected variation inherent in the system rather than model error. In contrast, Western organizations—particularly those in the U.S.—exhibit variance-exposing and escalation-oriented tendencies that produce structural friction as AI processes depart from deterministic systems. We resolve the paradox of North American innovation yet operational lag by distinguishing between variance-producing “Experimental Mavericks” and variance-suppressing “Deterministic Guardians.” Finally, we develop a “Drift Compatibility Model” that seeks to predict regional differences in AI adoption velocity and offers a culturally attuned framework for the governance, integration, and risk management of probabilistic AI systems.

category: Operations, Supply Chain, and AI-Enhanced Industry 4.0
title: AI and the value of the "human-in-the-loop"
authors: Francisco Brahm* (London Business School); Dalbert Ma (London Business School); Shengwu Sun (London Business School)
abstract: Across industries, AI is slowly taking over processes that used to be executed by humans, such as image analysis in radiology, fraud detection in banking, and document drafting and review in legal services. However, frequently a human is kept “in-the-loop”, to validate, complement and/or supersede AI when needed. In this paper we provide an empirical case study of autonomous trucks in the largest port in China in which human takeover of the autonomous truck is executed in the eventuality that a truck is stuck for more than 2 minutes. Given that the number of stuck trucks exceeds human takeover capacity, we use this as a quasi-natural experiment. Under the assumption of random arrival to becoming stuck, we compare trucks that are taken over with those that became stuck while no human was available for the take-over. We complement this with a matching approach to make the comparison tighter. We find that the human improves productivity—measured by the time to complete a task—by roughly 7%. However, this average impact mask heterogeneous treatment effects: we find that the impact is concentrated in the case in which the autonomous truck has difficulties sorting the problem out independently and the human is not overwhelmed by attention demands and the complexity of the problem. Our results fit well with Luis Garicano’s “management by exception” model. We also document a behavioural response: after a take-over, humans tend to take over trucks in the vicinity but without any real impact. Currently we are working with the company to optimize the rules that govern the “human-in-the-loop” in our setting.

title: Public Performative Linkage and Energy Industry Resilience: Strategic Narratives in the 2026 Strait of Hormuz Crisis
authors: Mariyam Manik* (Hong Kong Baptist University)
abstract: This article reconceptualises coercive linkage from a traditionally private bargaining mechanism into public performative linkage. Using the 2026 Strait of Hormuz crisis as a paradigmatic case, it examines how U.S. public performative linkage, Iranian selective accommodation, Chinese and allied sovereignty-centred counter-narratives, and multilateral diplomatic framing have produced energy supply-chain resilience alongside successful resistance to coercive pressure. Drawing on Schelling’s (1966) linkage theory and Miskimmon, O’Loughlin and Roselle’s (2013) strategic narrative framework, the article introduces public performative linkage as a publicly contested practice. It argues that public performative linkage must shift from raising sender audience costs to being resisted through consistent sovereignty-centred narratives stressing UN Charter principles, multilateral de-escalation and energy security, combined with selective accommodation. Practical pathways for the energy industry include coordinated narrative strategies, strengthened multilateral chokepoint governance, and scenario-based resilience planning. By reframing linkage as public performative practice rather than private bargaining, the article contributes both to the critical study of strategic narratives in international bargaining and to the practical evolution of public policy for energy supply-chain resilience and global competitiveness. The Hormuz case highlights how energy supply-chain resilience and operational continuity in critical chokepoints depend not on coercive power alone, but on the capacity of states and industry actors to craft coherent counter-narratives, enable selective accommodation, and sustain effective multilateral governance. Keywords energy industry, supply chain resilience, strategic narratives, public performative linkage, coercive diplomacy, public policy, Strait of Hormuz, comparative industry studies

title: Geopolitical Tensions and Sourcing Reconfiguration: An Abductive Study of Localization in the U.S. Electric Vehicle Industry
authors: Nan Jia (University of South California (USC)); Carl Shen (Macquarie University); Yifan Wei* (Simon Fraser University); Clara Zhou (Macquarie University)
abstract: Amid rising geopolitical tensions, governments increasingly promote local sourcing through industrial policy, forcing firms to navigate trade-offs between political compliance and global supply-chain efficiency. Using granular component-level data on electric vehicle (EV) models produced worldwide from 2012–2023, we adopt an abductive approach to examine how firms respond to U.S. localization policies. We document four empirical regularities that were unexpected previously: U.S. EV makers localized both core and non-core components; localization disproportionately displaced European rather than Chinese suppliers; non-U.S. firms maintained high levels of domestic sourcing and further increased them; and increased localization was associated with lower production volume only for U.S. firms. Examining plausible explanations, we show that firms’ localization responses reflect contextual and structural conditions, rather than a binary of compliance versus noncompliance.

title: The impacts of Brexit on UK international trade with EU and non-EU countries: A firm-level analysis
authors: Rekha Rao-Nicholson* (University of Essex); Israa Kishk (University of Northampton)
abstract: Following Brexit, a substantial body of literature has emerged examining its potential economic and trade-related consequences. Building on this work, our study provides a detailed firm-level analysis of how Brexit has affected the United Kingdom’s international trade patterns with both European Union (EU) and non-EU countries. In contrast to earlier studies that primarily relied on simulation methods or aggregate trade data, this research utilises a rich panel dataset of UK-based firms engaged in international trade over the period 2008 to 2024. This approach allows us to capture heterogeneity in firm behaviour and observe actual post-Brexit adjustments. The study addresses two central research questions. First, how has Brexit influenced UK firms’ trade with EU markets? Second, what has been the corresponding effect on UK firms’ trade with the rest of the world? By comparing pre- and post-Brexit trends, we identify significant shifts in both trade flows and firm-level investment patterns. Our findings indicate that, following Brexit, UK firms’ sales to the EU declined relative to their sales to non-EU markets, suggesting a reorientation of export activity away from the EU. At the same time, we observe an increase in UK firms’ asset holdings within the EU relative to those in the rest of the world, potentially reflecting strategic adjustments such as establishing a physical presence to mitigate new trade barriers. Overall, this study contributes to the empirical literature by providing evidence based on realised firm behaviour rather than projected outcomes. These insights help reduce post-Brexit uncertainty for businesses and offer policymakers valuable guidance in designing targeted trade and investment policies.

session_name: Assessing Green Industrial Policy Design and Outcomes
title: Institutional design models of green industrial policies supporting clean technology commercialisation in the EU, US, UK and Germany
authors: Sergey Kolesnikov* (Centre for Environment, Energy and Natural Resource Governance, Department of Land Economy, University of Cambridge); Kashina Perlinger (Centre for Environment, Energy and Natural Resource Governance, Department of Land Economy, University of Cambridge); (TUM Campus Straubing for Biotechnology and Sustainability, Technical University of Munich); D. Cale Reeves (Centre for Environment, Energy and Natural Resource Governance, Department of Land Economy, University of Cambridge); August Rud Jacobsen (Department of Environmental Science, Policy and Management, University of California, Berkeley); Em Finkelstine (Department of Environmental Science, Policy and Management, University of California, Berkeley); Jonas Meckling (Department of Environmental Science, Policy and Management, University of California, Berkeley); (Harvard Business School); Laura Diaz Anadon (Centre for Environment, Energy and Natural Resource Governance, Department of Land Economy, University of Cambridge); (Belfer Center for Science and International Affairs, Harvard Kennedy School)
abstract: Green industrial policies have expanded rapidly in recent years, as governments seek to align industrial development with climate and sustainability objectives, alongside other concerns including energy security and economic competitiveness. To achieve these goals, countries combine different approaches ranging from funding packages and deployment incentives to infrastructure provision and networking support, applied at different stages of technological development and sometimes attached to conditionalities. A systematic understanding of the range of policy design options, policy outcomes, and the relationships between them is of paramount importance to guide policy decision-making in this space. This four-paper panel establishes patterns in green industrial policy design and connects them to several policy outcomes across different sectors and jurisdictions. The first paper, Institutional design models of green industrial policies supporting clean technology commercialisation in the EU, US, UK and Germany, introduces a framework for analysing institutional design models in green industrial policy. The second paper, The impact of demand-side incentives for electric vehicles on innovation, connects subsidy policy as an input to patenting outcomes in the transportation sector. The third paper, More than Derisking: Bundles of Functions and their Effectiveness in Cleantech Industrial Policy, expands to seven combinations of three policy inputs – including both subsidies and conditionalities – and estimates impacts on patenting and funding outcomes in the U.S. context. The fourth paper, Can Green Subsidies Build Green Industries? Analyzing IPCEI subsidy effects on firm collaborations, picks up the thread of conditionalities and connects it to a further outcome, firm-level collaboration, in the European context.

session_name: Assessing Green Industrial Policy Design and Outcomes
title: More than Derisking: Bundles of Functions and their Effectiveness in Cleantech Industrial Policy
authors: D. Cale Reeves* (Centre for Environment, Energy and Natural Resource Governance, Department of Land Economy, University of Cambridge); Em Finkelstine (Department of Environmental Science, Policy, and Management, University of California, Berkeley); Jonas Meckling (Department of Environmental Science, Policy, and Management, University of California, Berkeley); (Harvard Business School); Laura Diaz Anadon (Centre for Environment, Energy and Natural Resource Governance, Department of Land Economy, University of Cambridge); (Belfer Center for Science and International Affairs, Harvard Kennedy School)
abstract: Green industrial policies have expanded rapidly in recent years, as governments seek to align industrial development with climate and sustainability objectives, alongside other concerns including energy security and economic competitiveness. To achieve these goals, countries combine different approaches ranging from funding packages and deployment incentives to infrastructure provision and networking support, applied at different stages of technological development and sometimes attached to conditionalities. A systematic understanding of the range of policy design options, policy outcomes, and the relationships between them is of paramount importance to guide policy decision-making in this space. This four-paper panel establishes patterns in green industrial policy design and connects them to several policy outcomes across different sectors and jurisdictions. The first paper, Institutional design models of green industrial policies supporting clean technology commercialisation in the EU, US, UK and Germany, introduces a framework for analysing institutional design models in green industrial policy. The second paper, The impact of demand-side incentives for electric vehicles on innovation, connects subsidy policy as an input to patenting outcomes in the transportation sector. The third paper, More than Derisking: Bundles of Functions and their Effectiveness in Cleantech Industrial Policy, expands to seven combinations of three policy inputs – including both subsidies and conditionalities – and estimates impacts on patenting and funding outcomes in the U.S. context. The fourth paper, Can Green Subsidies Build Green Industries? Analyzing IPCEI subsidy effects on firm collaborations, picks up the thread of conditionalities and connects it to a further outcome, firm-level collaboration, in the European context.

session_name: Semiconductor Sovereignty and Supply Chain Resilience
title: A Big Data-Driven Hybrid Simulation Framework for Assessing Critical Mineral Vulnerabilities in Semiconductor Supply Chains
authors: Naoum Tsolakis (University of Cambridge); Wei Nie* (University of Cambridge); Zhong Guan (University of Cambridge); Fangrui Li (University of Cambridge); Mariel Alem-Fonseca (University of Cambridge); Deepesh Jayasekara (University of Cambridge); Garry Clawson (University of Cambridge); Gavin Harper (University of Birmingham); Yongxu Zhao (University of Cambridge); Mukesh Kumar (University of Cambridge)
abstract: Critical mineral supply chains (SC) underpinning semiconductor manufacturing are vulnerable to geopolitical disruption, export restrictions, and structural capacity constraints. Existing SC stress testing methods are limited by two compounding weaknesses: single-paradigm simulation models that cannot capture cross-layer failure dynamics, and poorly parameterised models that rely on stylised rather than empirically grounded inputs. This paper addresses both gaps through a big data-driven hybrid simulation framework demonstrated on the cerium oxide SC for semiconductor chemical-mechanical planarisation. The framework comprises two integrated components. First, a structured big data pipeline ingests and harmonises heterogeneous open-source data such as UN Comtrade bilateral trade flows, USGS and BGS mineral production statistics, and news data to generate reproducible, empirically grounded simulation parameters. Second, a hybrid simulation architecture integrates System Dynamics, Agent-Based Modelling, and Discrete-Event Simulation across strategic, tactical, and operational decision layers respectively, synchronised through a coordinated time-stepping protocol. Three stress scenarios are examined: upstream capacity restriction, trade-related export constraints, and a compound multi-echelon shock. Results demonstrate that SC failure under stress is non-linear and abrupt, driven by simultaneous binding of structural capacity limits, tactical ordering failures, and operational bottlenecks that are only jointly observable through multi-layer modelling. The framework provides end-to-end diagnostic traceability, identifying where constraints emerge, when service collapse occurs, and why failure arises. Contributions include a transferable big data pipeline for simulation parameterisation, a replicable hybrid simulation architecture for failure-oriented stress testing, and empirically grounded vulnerability insights directly relevant to semiconductor SC policy.

session_name: Semiconductor Sovereignty and Supply Chain Resilience
title: The Localization Paradox: Ecosystem Inertia and Socio-Technical Anchors in the Semiconductor Supply Chain
authors: Shardul Phadnis* (Asia School of Business)
abstract: Prompted by the U.S. CHIPS and Science Act and parallel global initiatives, semiconductor firms have announced multi-billion-dollar investments in localized fabrication (“fab”) capacity to secure sovereign supply chains. Yet the feasibility of localizing highly specialized upstream tiers remains underexplored. Leveraging the recent industry shift as a qualitative natural experiment, this study conducts a longitudinal ecosystem analysis (2022–2024) to examine the determinants of supplier location choices. Drawing on 15 global driving forces and detailed factsheets for nine front-end fabrication processes, we identify key barriers to reshoring. We uncover a Localization Paradox: while capital and policy are mobile, “work culture” and global talent availability act as persistent anchors. In particular, Eastern manufacturing norms (e.g., intensive work hours) create structural friction for Western re-shoring efforts. We also identify a material–regulatory bottleneck driven by extreme concentration in legacy inputs (e.g., near-monopoly supply of organic substrates), creating dependencies that are largely insensitive to financial incentives. Finally, we show that supply chain resilience is less about geographic replication than technological leapfrogging, particularly transitions to emerging alternatives such as glass substrates. These findings challenge “deglobalization” narratives and contribute to OSCM by highlighting how socio-technical and regulatory interdependencies sustain global integration despite intensifying geopolitical decoupling.

session_name: Semiconductor Sovereignty and Supply Chain Resilience
title: Geopolitical Shocks and Firms’ Technological Exploration: Evidence from the Semiconductor Industry
authors: Menghe Zhu* (University of Bristol); Minhao Zhang (University of Bristol); Phil Davies-Walker (University of Bristol); Palie Smart (University of Bristol)
abstract: Why do some firms continue to explore new technological fields while others deepen within existing ones when geopolitical shocks disrupt the global innovation system? The semiconductor industry provides a revealing setting for this question because innovation depends on specialised suppliers across national borders, while governments increasingly intervene in technology access, trade, and cross-border coordination. This paper asks how geopolitical shocks shape firms’ technological search behaviour. Existing research has examined how uncertainty affects innovation intensity and performance, but we know much less about how geopolitical shocks shape the direction and boundary of technological exploration. The paper examines how geopolitical shocks affect semiconductor firms’ technological exploration radius, defined as the distance between newly generated inventions and a firm’s historical knowledge base. It argues that geopolitical shocks compress this radius by restricting access to external knowledge, destabilising supply arrangements, and increasing the cost of technologically distant search. Under these conditions, firms become less likely to pursue distant recombination and more likely to search close to existing capabilities. The paper further argues that this effect depends on supply chain structure. Supplier technological breadth expands the range of external knowledge available to the focal firm, while supply chain embeddedness stabilises coordination under uncertainty. Empirically, the study builds a firm-level panel of semiconductor companies by linking patent data, technology classifications, and inter-firm supply chain relationships around the escalation of the U.S.–China trade conflict. This study contributes by showing how geopolitical shocks narrow firms’ technological search within a highly interdependent industry and reshape firms’ technological trajectories through public intervention.

session_name: Semiconductor Sovereignty and Supply Chain Resilience
title: Innovation Intermediaries and Regional Structural Change: The Adaptive Role of Fraunhofer Institutes in East Germany.
authors: Steffen Redeker* (University of Oxford); Keno Haverkamp (University of Cambridge)
abstract: In times of geoeconomic disruption governments increasingly seek to develop high-tech innovation capacity. While these strategies are often formulated at the supranational or national level, their success is ultimately determined regionally. It is at this level, where ecosystems either adapt or stagnate, and where the high-tech race produces winners and losers. Yet, we lack a clear understanding of the institutional mechanisms through which regions, particularly those embedded in national institutional frameworks not typically associated with the development of new high-tech innovation, respond to these pressures and reorganise their innovation systems accordingly. This paper focuses on innovation intermediaries, particularly research and technology organisations (RTOs), as key actors shaping regional adaptive capacity. RTOs support the commercialisation, scaling, and diffusion of technologies and, due to their embeddedness in local innovation systems, can coordinate knowledge flows, facilitate collaboration, and respond to regional constraints. However, their role within regional growth coalitions shaping those ecosystems and responding to strategic change remains insufficiently understood. Empirically, the study analyses Fraunhofer-Society in Eastern Germany after reunification, focusing on Saxony’s emergence as a leading European semiconductor hub despite Eastern Germany’s weak economic performance, deindustrialisation and a national institutional model associated with incremental innovation within established industries rather than the development of new high-tech industries. Using process tracing, we show how Fraunhofer developed distinct organisational configurations, acquired developmental capacities, and leveraged regional specialisation to mediate national constraints and support regional capability-building. This demonstrates how innovation intermediaries can enable regionally differentiated growth trajectories and contribute to the reconfiguration of regional growth coalitions.

session_name: Plenary: Value Chains and Industrial Innovation Policy
title: Plenary: Value Chains and Industrial Innovation Policy
authors: Julia Sutcliffe; Eoin O’Sullivan
abstract: Industrial innovation policy has returned as a major priority for national and regional governments around the world. While reservations about the wisdom and effectiveness of industrial policy continue in some quarters, it is now widely accepted that governments must have a considered position on their relationship with their industries. There are many challenges, however, to the development and delivery of effective industrial policies. This panel opens by exploring patterns of industrial innovation policy internationally, highlighting emerging trends and priorities. The UK Government’s Chief Scientific Advisor will then introduce the UK's approach, drawing on the most recent national policies and early observations from their delivery. Finally, we draw together perspectives from different systems of industrial policy and explore ways in which these might usefully be integrated to provide more comprehensive and robust theoretical foundations for industrial innovation policy going forward.
moderator: Professor Sir Mike Gregory CBE, FREng

session_name: Space: Can the Final Frontier Become a Market?
title: Space: Can the Final Frontier Become a Market?
authors: Dr Paul Bate; Nigel Chandler; Raja Roy
abstract: Space has become one of the most strategically significant industries of this century. Once the preserve of government agencies pursuing scientific, military and exploratory missions, it now underpins communications, Earth observation, climate monitoring, and national security. Yet a central question remains open: can space become a genuine market, or will its structure, demand and economics remain largely shaped by the state? What makes space unusual is that markets here often have to be built before demand is visible. Governments, investors, and firms must make long-term commitments under extreme uncertainty, and the commercial landscape is shaped as much by public procurement, industrial policy, and venture capital as by ordinary consumer demand. Bringing together speakers from venture capital, the space and defence industry, the UK Space Agency, and academia, this panel asks how space markets are created, financed, and governed. In doing so, we address a broader question of how markets are constructed when demand, technology, and industry boundaries are all still being formed?
panelists: Dr Paul Bate; Nigel Chandler; Raja Roy

session_name: Drug Shortages: Drivers, Consequences, and Solutions
title: Drug Shortages: Drivers, Consequences, and Solutions
authors: Dr. Markus Felgenhauer; Damien Holly; Mujaheed Shaikh
abstract: Drug shortages have hit record highs worldwide. In addition to causes common to all global industries (e.g., national disasters and geopolitical disruptions), in the pharmaceutical industry there is also a mix of manufacturing fragility, market economics, regulatory friction, and supply chain opacity. The consequences of drug shortages ripple from clinical care to public trust. This panel brings together research, policy, and industry perspectives to unpack the drivers of shortages, public policy responses, and private sector solutions. Discussion will draw on firsthand experience managing drug supply, covering the underlying economics, such as rewarding manufacturers for staying in markets with razor-thin margins, a tendency for single sources of supply, and environmental regulation continuing to push production toward Asia. Expect insights from work with data and decision-makers across several countries, and a live demo of predictive tools that flag shortage risk before it hits the shelf.
panelists: Dr. Markus Felgenhauer; Damien Holly; Mujaheed Shaikh

title: Lunch
Industry Leadership in the Global Paper and Pulp Industry 1906—2026: Unchanging Complexity, Lost Opportunities, and Surprising Plasticity
authors: Juha-Antti Lamberg* (University of Jyväskylä); Christa Könönen (University of Jyväskylä); Jari Ojala (University of Jyväskylä)
abstract: Industry leadership — a combination of market position and technological and managerial capabilities — is examined across the global paper and pulp industry from 1906 to the present. Drawing on a unique multi-source dataset covering 120 years of firm-level production data, the study identifies three theoretically significant patterns: the persistent dominance of firms from the United States, Germany, and Scandinavia; the unrealized potential of resource-rich nations such as Russia; and the remarkable plasticity of select incumbents successfully navigating multiple waves of technological discontinuity. The findings complement existing theoretical accounts of industry evolution and underscore the explanatory role of contingency.

title: The Feel Of Time: Emotional Regimes of Industrial Decline
authors: Roosa Oinasmaa (Tampere University of Applied Sciences); Jarmo Taskinen* (University of Jyvaskyla); Antti Sihvonen (University of Helsinki)
abstract: When an industry sector grapples with global trade shifts, increasing competition, and technological disruption leading to long-term decline, its actors face a profound emotional and cognitive dilemma regarding how to move forward. While existing research highlights how shared narratives bridge past experiences with threatened futures, we know relatively little about the affective dimensions that shape collective strategic outlooks on an industry-wide scale. We address this by asking: How do emotions shape the formation of strategic narrative outlooks during long-term industrial decline? Drawing on 101 open-ended interviews with elite members of the Finnish pulp and paper industry, ranging from CEOs to research institution leaders, we employ inductive narrative analysis to explore the interplay between affective histories and strategic envisioning. Our findings offer three primary contributions. First, we introduce the concept of emotional regimes: shared, enduring affective patterns (fear, anger, and sadness) that connect an industry’s past with its expected future. Unlike fleeting responses to acute crises, these regimes function as durable cognitive-affective schemas that shape the industry’s self-understanding and perceived scope for action. Second, we demonstrate a recursive relationship where affective narrativization causes perceived futures to feed back into the interpretation of the past. Third, we show that subgroups among industry elite can be under distinct emotional regimes, which then upkeeps highly distinct understandings of the industry’s situation. Ultimately, our study suggests that emotional resonance often outweighs pure rationalization in determining which past trajectories and narrative anchors become a basis for strategic outlooks.

title: The Organizational Logics of Charity Retailing.
authors: Steve New* (University of Oxford)
abstract: Charity Retailing is important but neglected. In the UK, over 10,000 outlets provide 23,500 full-time equivalent jobs, and benefit from the efforts of more than 200,000 volunteers. In 2024/5, they are estimated to generate more than £300m for parent charities (CRA 2026). Nevertheless, public sentiment about the sector is mixed; the growth of the sector is seen to be synonymous with urban collapse. As charity shops receive significant tax advantages over conventional retailers, it is argued that they crowd out opportunities for genuine entrepreneurs, perpetuating a cycle of civic decay (Roberts and Ellison 2019). Conversely, they can be seen as ‘hubs of innovation’ for the fashion industry (Britten 2025), The charity retail sector raises interesting questions about purpose. What are the shops for? Here, we demonstrate the ways in which the conflicts between these objectives are illuminated by consideration of the question: “how much inventory should be held”? Using a model developed for a chain of charity stores in southern England, the paper shows the limited applicability of conventional retailing theory, and points to a new approach which has wide implications for the management and regulation of the sector. category: Health Care Systems, Biotechnology, and Pharmaceuticals
title: Coordination under constraints in a pro-social supply chain – The case of deceased donation program in India
authors: Satyajit Roy* (Masters Union School of Business); Haritha Saranga (IIM Bangalore)
abstract: Prosocial supply chains often lack effective coordination due to multi-stakeholder involvement and constraints at different levels, especially in developing countries. Ineffective coordination leads to sub-optimal utilisation and decreasing social welfare, especially when the demand greatly exceeds supply. We study the case of deceased organ donation in Indian states to investigate (i) how coordination is affected in a pro-social supply chain and (ii) how to improve coordination to maximise utility, respecting the constraints. Our findings suggest that a shared vision across the value chain is the first step in ensuring coordination. The input constraints can be managed by creating an idiosyncratic resource environment, such as the “factory-within-factory” approach, and through opportunistic collaboration, such as public-private partnerships. The process constraints can be bypassed with the help of social capital, where a “nexus-of-contracts” perspective is transformed into a “team” perspective for the greater good. We also find that enforcing output constraints through accountability and rewards helps ensure coordination.

category: Health Care Systems, Biotechnology, and Pharmaceuticals
title: Developing A Web-Based Decision Support Tool for Healthcare Services to Reduce Waiting Times
authors: Usame Yakutcan* (University of Hertfordshire); Eren Demir (University of Hertfordshire); Zichong Lyu (University of Hertfordshire)
abstract: The National Health Service (NHS) faces critical operational challenges, including constrained budgets, limited capacity and workforce shortages. Elective care waiting lists have reached about 7.25 million cases, with nearly 40% of patients waiting more than 18 weeks. Similar pressures are evident in the Hertfordshire region, which the services support 1.6 million people across three hospital trusts. To address these challenges, we developed a web-based decision support tool (DST) for cardiology services to reduce waiting times and improve capacity planning. The tool integrates a discrete event simulation model with a workforce optimisation model, implemented in JavaScript. Through qualitative mapping and extensive stakeholder engagement, including clinicians, nurses, service managers, data specialists, and senior leadership, we conceptualised seven distinct cardiology pathways. The pathways cover the complexity of care from referral through outpatient and inpatient services. The DST captures the system’s complexity while remaining user-friendly and visually accessible. It enables users to test a range of intervention scenarios, with over 100 parameters per pathway. The tool has undergone rigorous testing and validation. It generates 23 interactive dashboard pages presenting key outputs across pathways, services, and workforce settings. The DST has enhanced the capacity planning for the Cardiology departments in Hertfordshire by providing actionable and evidence-based solutions with zero software licensing cost and an intuitive interface. The research advances operations management by integrating patient pathway modelling with dynamic workforce optimisation. This innovation supports tackling operational challenges in complex multi-level services.

category: Health Care Systems, Biotechnology, and Pharmaceuticals
title: Balancing Planned and Spontaneous Births: Congestion Effects on Emergency Caesarean Interventions
authors: Pinelopi Stamou* (University of Oxford); Harshita Kajaria-Montag (Kühne Logistics University); Agni Orfanoudaki (University of Oxford); Yueyang Zhong (London Business School)
abstract: Maternity units operate under constrained capacity, creating a fundamental scheduling tension: planned caesarean sections and inductions compete with unplanned spontaneous births for limited resources. Using detailed national pregnancy data from the NHS England Maternity Services Data Set (MSDS), we examine how different demand flows interact and how congestion due to planned birth appointments affects the risk of emergency caesarean sections. We use statistical modelling to estimate the effect of congestion due to elective caesareans and inductions on the risk of emergency caesarean section interventions for spontaneous arrivals. To address endogeneity, we follow an instrumental variables approach that exploits exogenous variation in congestion at neighbouring hospitals outside a mother’s catchment area. We find that higher load from planned appointments increases the likelihood of emergency caesarean sections for spontaneous arrivals, with an effect size comparable to established clinical risk factors such as age or BMI. In addition, imbalance between planned and spontaneous births further increases emergency caesarean risk. These findings highlight the importance of better balancing planned and unplanned demand to manage congestion and maintain control over delivery timing under capacity constraints. In light of this, we discuss operational and managerial implications for healthcare managers and clinical practitioners.

category: Health Care Systems, Biotechnology, and Pharmaceuticals
title: Supervised Autonomy in the Age of AI: How Algorithmic Oversight Reorganizes Professional Judgment
authors: Alfred Marcus* (University of Minnesota); Greg Silverman (University of Minnesota); Mani Subramani (University of Minnesota); Ella Glickson (Bar Ilan)
abstract: Professional decision making has long been conceptualized as a balance between autonomy and control. In contemporary hospitals, however, that dichotomy is increasingly inadequate. We develop a theory of supervised autonomy in which expert judgment is preserved formally but embedded within distributed, data-mediated, and increasingly algorithmic systems of oversight. Focusing on antibiotic prescribing in large U.S. hospitals, we conceptualize antibiotic stewardship programs as second-order judgment systems that evaluate how clinicians exercise discretion rather than replacing that discretion outright. We argue that artificial intelligence is unlikely to enter these settings primarily as a substitute for physicians. More plausibly, it becomes enmeshed in existing stewardship architectures, intensifying evaluative visibility, shifting accountability forward in time, amplifying ethical tension between patient-centered and population-centered logics, and transforming the nature of professional expertise. The paper contributes to management theory by extending work on professional autonomy, institutional logics, evaluation, audit, and algorithms at work. It also contributes to the growing literature on AI in organizations by showing that the main organizational effect of AI in high-stakes settings may be less direct substitution than the institutional augmentation of distributed oversight. We develop propositions and conclude with an empirical agenda that includes designs closely aligned with comparative work on clinician and AI prescribing decisions in antibiotic contexts.

title: Who Stayed, Who Joined, Who Climbed: How did startups reconfigure their human capital after AlexNet?
authors: Shinjinee Chattopadhyay* (University of Illinois at Urbana Champaign); Mingtao Xu (Tsinghua University); Natarajan Balasubramanium (Syracuse University)
abstract: Hiring and retaining key employees is one of the central challenges of startups particularly in times of uncertainty following a technological shift. While it is established that technological discontinuities drive innovation and firm growth, little is known on how startups adjust their human capital composition after major technological changes. The introduction of deep learning in 2012 — marked by the success of AlexNet — represents a significant technological change that led to the foundation of AI-based technologies. AlexNet rendered AI expertise central to IT incumbent startups’ competitive advantage potentially reshaping the human capital composition of startups, and the vertical structures through which that knowledge is coordinated and orchestrated. In this paper we examine how firms altered their hiring, promotions and retention of their scientists, engineers and managers over different hierarchical levels following AlexNet. We further investigate how these choices differed by firms’ pre-existing technological capabilities, based on whether they were engaged in computational innovation prior to the shock or not. We find that relative to a control group of firms that would be unaffected by AlexNet, IT firms grew in size, but controlling for overall firm growth, most of the growth was driven by new hiring and retention in middle management, with no significant expansion in junior-level new hires. Firms engaged in computational innovation prior to AlexNet tended to hire mid-level and junior engineers and promoted their senior managers internally but showed no increase in hiring or promotion of scientists.

title: Coupling and Decoupling Founder and Firm Innovation: Evidence from the Genetics Industry
authors: Jennifer Woolley* (Santa Clara University)
abstract: Innovation is a critical activity for nascent technology firms. However, how founders shape innovative outcomes is not well understood. While work has emphasized the role of founder experience in driving firm performance, less attention has been paid to whether a founder’s personal technical prowess serves as a catalyst for organizational R&D or remains tethered to the individual. This study examines the relationship between a founder’s prior pre-founding innovation experience and subsequent innovative activity—both at the individual and firm levels. Using a unique dataset of genetics firms founded after 1980, we consider the impact of a founder’s pre-founding patenting experience and human capital on both their personal post-founding patenting and their firm’s overall patenting output. We find that a founder’s pre-founding patenting is a strong predictor of their continued personal involvement in innovation. Also, founders with a high level of technical expertise, such as professors or having doctoral or medical degrees, continue patenting after starting a firm, but this does not correlate with an increase in the firm’s total patent output. In contrast, founders with MBAs typically patent less after starting a company, yet their firms demonstrate higher patenting productivity, suggesting that these founders value innovation even if they are not involved individually. Together, these results highlight a potential decoupling between founder-driven and firm-driven innovation. If a founder’s expertise does not translate into firm-level productivity, the "human capital" advantage of technical founders may be more fragile than previously assumed.

title: Nice to Meat You, But What’s Your Name? Theorizing Category Inception and Signification
authors: Alberto Nucciarelli* (University of Trento)
abstract: This study advances the understanding of category labels as linguistic constructs that capture the endowments, identities, and inducements of heterogeneous actors in a nascent industry. I analyze the development of the cellular meat industry, focusing on the sequence of labels that actors have created and abandoned from the early 2010s to the mid-2020s to encode and signal meanings they aimed to communicate to customers and regulators. Borrowing terms and methods from semiotics to study how words convey meaning in social contexts, my nascent industry semantics framework – a process of language construction – shows how heterogeneous actors interact to support the positioning of a new product in the market (i.e., industry semantics construens), oppose it to hinder its path to market (i.e., industry semantics destruens), and formalize its existence (i.e., industry semantics institutionalization). These observations motivated me to theorize the category inception and category signification, two notions that expand our understanding of category formation. Category inception refers to when a label moves from its original domain (i.e., technological discovery) into an industry setting with actors interested in assigning it meanings that can attract potential customers. Category signification is about the process of generating meanings through the association between a signifier (i.e., words used for a label) and the signified (i.e., specific concepts of meat). This study contributes to the category innovation literature by examining how actors contribute to nascent industries through language choices, as expressed through new labels, and expands the study of categorical evolution by proposing new linguistic mechanisms.

title: Beyond the Generalist Penalty: Identity Misalignment and New Entrants in Category-Based Evaluation
authors: Samira Dias Reis* (Universidad Carlos III de Madrid); Alicia Barroso (UCM); Marco Giarratana (IE)
abstract: Research on categories has shown that actors spanning multiple categories often face penalties because their identities are harder for evaluators to interpret. This literature has established identity ambiguity as a central mechanism shaping evaluation, as audiences rely on clear category associations to form expectations about candidates’ capabilities and relevance. Yet prior research has often treated different relationships to categories - spanning across categories, being anchored in the “wrong” category, and lacking category experience - as manifestations of a broader form of interpretive uncertainty. In particular, candidates without prior category experience - new entrants - have received less systematic attention, despite representing a common and theoretically distinct position in evaluation settings. Candidates, however, may occupy different positions relative to the focal category, raising an important question: how are these positions evaluated relative to one another? We extend categorization research by disentangling three analytically distinct forms of category-based identity: identity ambiguity, identity misalignment, and the absence of prior category identity. Identity ambiguity reflects spanning across categories, identity misalignment reflects anchoring in categories that differ from the focal category, and the absence of identity reflects the lack of prior category experience altogether—a position characteristic of new entrants. We argue that these positions generate different evaluative consequences because they convey different signals about capability relevance and uncertainty. In particular, identity misalignment may generate stronger penalties than both identity ambiguity and the absence of prior category identity, as it signals expertise that is clearly defined but potentially inappropriate for the focal category, whereas new entrants may be evaluated with greater flexibility due to the absence of contradictory signals. We further argue that these penalties intensify when categorical expectations are strong, such as when evaluators have stronger membership in the category and enforce category boundaries more strictly. We test our hypotheses using longitudinal data on producer–director collaborations in the Brazilian film industry, a setting characterized by project-based production, high uncertainty, and heterogeneous candidate backgrounds. Our findings clarify how distinct relationships to categories - including the often-overlooked position of new entrants - shape partner selection and contribute to research on categorization, evaluation, and collaboration under uncertainty.
