category: Operations, Supply Chain, and AI-Enhanced Industry 4.0
title: Understanding resistance to inter-organizational digital transformation over time: Evidence from a multi-site digital control room in UK capital projects
authors: Jas Kalra* (University of Manchester); Kell Jones (Bartlett School of Sustainable Construction, University College London); Grant Mills (Bartlett School of Sustainable Construction, University College London); Kieran Conboy (University of Galway)
abstract: Digital transformation is central to improving productivity, transparency, and coordination in fragmented industries such as construction and infrastructure. However, many industry-level initiatives struggle to deliver value beyond pilots and demonstrations. This paper examines why digital transformation becomes difficult to sustain when it depends on organizations that are legally independent but operationally connected. Drawing on a longitudinal qualitative case of a multi-site digital control room initiative in the UK construction and infrastructure sectors, we study sector-level transformation in a project-based industry where value depends on coordination across firms. The study draws on 38 interviews, 102.5 hours of observation, and artefacts across a contractor/professional service firm, three project clients, three technology firms, and a research organization. We show that resistance to digital transformation is not simply user reluctance or poor technology adoption. Instead, it develops through inter-organizational governance issues around data ownership, quality, metrics, and decision rights. Our process model identifies four mechanisms: vision–resource gaps that legitimate temporary exceptions; symbolic adoption that presents legacy reporting as digital progress; operational decoupling that creates dual baselines and parallel regimes; and business-case evaporation as reconciliation work outweighs visible benefits. Uneven timing across sites amplifies these dynamics: while no single organization appears non-compliant, the network fails to (digitally) transform. The study contributes to industry studies by explaining how sectoral digital transformation can stall despite formal commitment, apparent compliance, and policy pressure productivity and transparency. It offers practical insight for industry bodies, clients, and policymakers seeking to improve digital platform adoption in fragmented project-based sectors.

category: Operations, Supply Chain, and AI-Enhanced Industry 4.0
title: Financial non-disclosure of private suppliers and dependability in times of geopolitical disruption
authors: Dean Sammanthan (ETH Zurich); Oliver von Dzengelevski* (ETH Zurich); Benn Lawson (University of Oxford); Torbjørn Netland (ETH Zurich)
abstract: Firms may face increased supplier risk in times of geopolitical turmoil if they rely on suppliers with insufficient resilience to external shocks. In assessing resilience, buying firms rely on the information available about their suppliers. However, when dealing with private suppliers the lack of public financial disclosure limits traditional methods of risk assessment and requires buyers to negotiate for the disclosure of such information to them. Drawing on company data from the medical devices industry, this paper explores whether and to what extent non-disclosure of financial data by private suppliers serves as a signal of elevated supplier risk when faced with an exogenous shock in the geopolitical arena. In our empirical setting, the focal firm requests disclosure of financial information from its private suppliers and informs them that a risk penalty is applied in the firm's supplier risk management system if disclosure is withheld. Suppliers anticipating that disclosure would lead to risk judgements higher than the threatened risk penalty on the side of the firm, may strategically choose non-disclosure. We investigate whether non-disclosure is associated with lower supplier dependability and greater probability of adverse events following the implementation of U.S. tariffs announced in April 2025, including late and incomplete deliveries as well as price hikes. We expect this relationship to be moderated by suppliers' negotiation power, with non-disclosure from those with less negotiation leverage vis-à-vis the focal firm carrying more informational weight about their riskiness.

category: Operations, Supply Chain, and AI-Enhanced Industry 4.0
title: Observatories for critical mineral supply chains: building industrial resilience in an age of contested supply
authors: Mukesh Kumar* (University of Cambridge); Naoum Tsolakis (University of Cambridge); Wei Nie (University of Cambridge); Deepesh Jayasekara (University of Cambridge); Anandarup Mukherjee (University of Cambridge); Mariel Alem Fonseca (University of Cambridge); Garry Clawson (University of Cambridge); Edison Li (University of Cambridge); Paul Beecher (University of Cambridge); Zhong Guan (University of Cambridge); Aukrit Unahalekhaka (University of Cambridge); Ben Macdonald (University of Cambridge); Gavin Harper (University of Cambridge); Nidhi Pathak (University of Cambridge); Rana Hajirasouli (University of Cambridge); Yongxu Zhao (University of Cambridge); Sunil Tiwari (University of Bristol); Manoj Dora (Anglia Ruskin University)
abstract: The twin green and digital transitions have made a narrow set of critical minerals indispensable to industrial activity, yet the supply chains that carry them remain among the least visible systems in the global economy. Extraction and especially midstream processing are geographically concentrated, while classification frameworks designed in the 1980s no longer adequately track the materials upon which contemporary industry depends. In this paper, we argue that closing this information deficit requires dedicated, public good digital infrastructure: a supply chain observatory organised around three mutually dependent goals: visibility, traceability and transparency. Methodologically, the observatory combines multi source data ingestion, data cleaning and harmonisation pipelines, entity resolution, relational and geospatial database design, supply chain data models, network analytics, satellite enabled monitoring, and scenario based stress testing to generate actionable intelligence from fragmented public, commercial and primary data. Drawing on the Global Supply Chain Observatory, a research initiative at the University of Cambridge developed with Google Cloud and now deployed through the UK India Critical Minerals Supply Chain Observatory, we set out what an observatory can observe that conventional data cannot, how it connects to emerging instruments such as the UN Transparency Protocol for Critical Raw Materials and EU Digital Product Passports, and why observatories should be understood not as enterprise tools but as national and international digital infrastructure: the twenty first century equivalent of the roads and ports that enabled the last wave of industrial development.

title: Data Regulation, Platform Encroachment, and the Matthew Effect
authors: Shiva Shekhar* (Tilburg University)
abstract: Marketplace platforms are central players in online retail and are in an advantageous position to leverage data generated by third-party sellers. This paper analyzes how a platform's encroachment decision--whether to enter its marketplace as a direct competitor--is shaped by regulations that restrict its use of seller data. We show that the platform's encroachment decision follows a non-monotonic pattern: it enters against sellers with either relatively low or sufficiently high brand value, but remains a pure intermediary for intermediate brand values. The data ban regulation alters this strategy by making the platform more likely to exclude low brand-value sellers and more likely to accommodate high brand-value sellers. This creates a Matthew Effect in platform ecosystems: the regulation favors high-value sellers and harms low-value sellers. These results underscore the need for more nuanced regulatory approaches that promote data sharing in emerging markets and targeted bans in mature, established markets to better balance welfare and competition.

title: Industrial Transformation in the Rocket Launch Sector: SpaceX, State Support, and Competitive Dynamics
authors: Oguz Karasu* (University of Oxford); Marc Ventresca (University of Oxford)
abstract: The rocket launch sector has undergone a major industrial transformation over the past two decades, shifting from a state-dominated procurement model toward a more competitive system centred on private firms. Before the rise of SpaceX, launch services for NASA and other public agencies were largely organized through cost-plus contracting, limited competition, and dependence on established space players. This model prioritized reliability and mission assurance but often generated high costs and slow innovation cycles. This paper examines how NASA’s procurement reforms helped create a viable market for private launch companies. NASA shifted toward milestone-based, fixed-price contracting that transferred greater technical and financial responsibility to firms while preserving public demand through long-term contracts. These policy changes reduced entry barriers and enabled new actors to scale rapidly. Using SpaceX as the primary case study, the paper analyses how state support, procurement design, and competitive pressure reshaped market structure in the global launch industry. The firm’s extraordinary private valuation and persistent IPO speculation which is approximately $1.75 trillion underscore how state-created markets may culminate in concentrated private rewards. The paper argues that SpaceX’s emergence was not simply the result of entrepreneurial innovation, but of a public-policy framework combining risk sharing, demand guarantees, and performance-based competition. The study contributes to comparative industry research by showing how procurement institutions can transform technologically complex strategic sectors. It also raises broader policy questions concerning public dependence on dominant private suppliers, market concentration, and the governance of strategic industries in an era of renewed state involvement in markets.

title: The Transition from Oil to Electricity: Reshaping the Global Automotive Industry and Energy System
authors: Martin Kenney (University of California, Davis); Jun Sun* (East China University of Science and Technology)
abstract: The ongoing transition from internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles to electric vehicles (EVs) represents more than a technological substitution; it constitutes a fundamental restructuring of the global energy landscape and the geopolitical configuration of the automotive industry. This paper frames this shift through the lens of Carlota Perez’s techno-economic paradigm theory, arguing that the world is moving from a long-dominant Fossil Fuel Triad (oil extraction, refining, and ICE vehicles) to an emerging Cleantech Triad (solar photovoltaics, batteries, and EVs). The Cleantech Triad, wherein renewable assets enable the manufacturing of energy rather than the continuous importation of combustible fuels, offers a systemic alternative for nations seeking to reduce long-term energy import dependence. China has emerged to lead global technology diffusion during this paradigm shift, as evidenced by its “New Trio” of photovoltaics, batteries, and EVs becoming a central pillar of the export economy. Through an integrated analysis of global trade and investment data, semi-structured interviews, and supply chain projects, this paper examines the global transition from ICE vehicles to EVs. Empirically, we show how China, as the world's largest producer, market, and—since 2024—exporter of automobiles, is driving this transition. This transition is unfolding unevenly across space. We map how the diffusion of the Cleantech Triad, led by Chinese firms like BYD and CATL, is actively redrawing the global map of automobile manufacturing, instigating a new industrial spatial fix. This includes the pivotal shift to Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) battery chemistry and the movement from exports to foreign direct investment by Chinese manufacturers. Simultaneously, this spatial shift is reconfiguring the global automotive order at its core—away from oil and toward electricity—directly challenging established petroleum usage patterns and industry incumbents and fueling new geopolitical tensions and trade resistance.

title: Navigating Circular Economy Transitions in the Automotive Sector: A Comparative Study of Social Value Integration Across Organisational Maturity Stages
authors: Vinayak Sharma* (University of Exeter)
abstract: The automotive industry faces unprecedented pressure to transition from linear to circular business models, yet the social dimensions of this transformation remain poorly understood. While environmental and economic aspects of circular economy (CE) transitions receive substantial attention, organisations frequently discover that social factors, workforce reskilling, community adaptation, stakeholder alignment, determine implementation success or failure. This paper addresses this critical gap through qualitative multiple case study research examining how organisations within the UK automotive and related sectors develop dynamic capabilities to integrate social value within CE business model transitions. Drawing on 36 semi-structured interviews, over 100 documents, and observational data across three multinational enterprises at nascent, emergent, and mature CE maturity stages, the study employs Gioia methodology within a critical realist framework. The comparative cross-maturity design reveals how capability development trajectories differ across organisational contexts while identifying consistent mechanisms underpinning transformation. Three interconnected theoretical contributions emerge. First, a multi-level social value integration framework demonstrates how organisations progressively embed social considerations through operational, strategic, and ecosystem dimensions. Second, a nested stakeholder development model reveals cumulative relationship-building from workforce through value chain to broader society. Third, an extended dynamic capabilities framework identifies “reactive responsiveness” as a fourth capability alongside sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring, explaining how organisations manage temporal tensions between immediate stakeholder pressures and long-term transformation. The findings offer comparative insights across maturity stages and industry positions, with implications for public policy design supporting just transitions, capability development programmes, and regulatory frameworks that balance environmental ambition with social equity in the automotive sector’s ongoing transformation.

title: Moving towards circularity: How corporate diversification affects circular economy transition
authors: Corina Fehlner (BI Norwegian Business School); Gabriel R.G. Benito* (BI Norwegian Business School)
abstract: Transitioning to a circular economy (CE) is a compelling way forward to increase sustainability, but little is known about the development of more sustainable business systems, which we argue can be contingent on corporate factors. In many industries, multinational enterprises play an influential role in shaping the design and implementation of CE by determining key product features and technology selections, and by orchestrating global value chains. Taking a diversification perspective, we study the extent to which corporate strategies about businesses (focused-related-unrelated) and locations (geographical scope) facilitate or impede circularness, i.e., the development and implementation of circular solutions and business systems. We use a rich longitudinal dataset (2012 to 2021) from the global automotive industry (comprising in total 101 key brands), and apply a variety of indicators that cover key aspects of circularity in the automotive industry; i.a., waste generated, composition of product portfolio (small vs. large cars), pre-owned certification schemes, waste recycling ratio, and EV in product portfolio. We find that diversified companies are more likely to have a higher degree of circularness than focused brands. Regarding geographical diversification, exclusively domestic brands display the lowest CE levels; the degree of circularness first increases and then tapers off with geographical scope. Zooming in on one of the most important industries globally, and a main contributor to pollution and emissions, this study shows that moving towards circularity hinges on corporate strategies regarding diversification. The findings also inform current debates regarding international business by suggesting that multinationality is not counterproductive to increasing sustainability.

title: Vertical Integration and Decarbonization Outcomes
authors: Navya Pandit* (University of Cologne); Qiang Xiong (Nova School of Business and Economics)
abstract: Firms are facing increasing scrutiny to curb emissions in compliance with regulations and stakeholder pressures, forcing firms to transition away from fossil fuels and towards more efficient and cleaner modes of production. Given this, how firms coordinate decarbonization initiatives across their value chain partners and stakeholders and manage associated risks has become increasingly critical and presents a core strategic challenge. Research has shown the relationship between firm structure and sustainability outcomes to be complex, highlighting the need to empirically investigate whether and how variations in a firm’s corporate strategy influence its ability to coordinate and reduce carbon emissions and other environmental costs across a firm’s value chain. As a result, in this work we explore the effect of vertical integration on decarbonization outcomes. Using a longitudinal panel dataset for US public firms from 2005-2021, we examine how the degree of vertical integration relates to firms’ emissions intensity. We find an inverted U-shaped relationship: moving from low to moderate integration is associated with higher carbon emissions, while further integration is associated with lower emissions. Interestingly, this effect is only true for firms in the manufacturing sector highlighting financially material incentives for emissions reduction. The findings highlight the non-linear environmental consequences of firm boundaries and underscore when greater integration may enhance firms’ ability to coordinate, monitor, and implement decarbonization initiatives across their value chains.

session_name: Conducting Field Research with Organizations: Opportunities, Challenges, and Best Practices
title: Conducting Field Research with Organizations: Opportunities, Challenges, and Best Practices
authors: Matthew Amengual (University of Oxford); Francisco Brahm (London Business School); Florian Englmaier (LMU Munich)
abstract: This panel brings together scholars to discuss the opportunities and challenges of conducting field research in organizational settings. As field-based approaches gain prominence across areas such as human resource management, organizational behavior, strategy, and labor, researchers must navigate practical and methodological complexities when working with organizations. The discussion will draw on panelists’ experience with field experiments, quasi-experiments, and other applied designs to reflect on key stages of the research process, including building partnerships, designing credible and feasible studies, and addressing data access and ethical considerations. Panelists will also consider trade-offs between internal and external validity, as well as emerging opportunities linked to new data sources and digital environments. By sharing lessons learned and best practices, the panel aims to provide guidance to scholars seeking to conduct rigorous and impactful field research on work and organizations.
panelists: Matthew Amengual (University of Oxford); Francisco Brahm (London Business School); Florian Englmaier (LMU Munich)

session_name: When the Chips are Down: Europe's Stake in the Global Chip War
title: When the Chips are Down: Europe's Stake in the Global Chip War
authors: Dr Monica Gorman; Dr Katie Hore; Sebastian Weiske
abstract: The global semiconductor industry is in the midst of a historic transition, driven by geo-strategic rivalry, growing demands for supply chain resiliency, and China's rapidly expanding role in mature-node manufacturing. While public attention gravitates toward the most advanced chips, the sharpest competitive pressures are emerging in the power and foundational semiconductors that underpin Europe's automotive, industrial, and energy sectors. As products across nearly every industry come to depend on an increasingly complex and growing array of chips, semiconductor competition is no longer a story confined to the chip industry itself. This panel draws together corporate strategy, industrial policy, and technology commercialization to examine what is actually at stake and assesses where the industry is heading, what it means for Europe's downstream industries, and which policy responses can meet the moment.
panelists: Dr Monica Gorman; Dr Katie Hore; Sebastian Weiske

session_name: Infrastructure—From Concrete to Cloud: A Laggard Leviathan or a Leading Light?
title: Infrastructure—From Concrete to Cloud: A Laggard Leviathan or a Leading Light?
authors: Alison Baptiste; Julia Pyke; Chetan Kotur
abstract: Delivering large-scale infrastructure is fundamental towards realizing our future societal ambitions and meeting our global grand challenges. On the one hand, age-old challenges still exist - uneven skilled labour availability, operational complexity, and time-cost-quality pressures amidst ever increasing geopolitical turmoil and economic turbulence. On the other hand, we see remarkable advancements in machine learning, robotics & physical AI, nuclear fission & fusion, renewables, to name only a few, that are allowing us to reimagine the possible. In this panel, we will explore what this duality spells for the future of infrastructure. Will we continue to genuflect to age-old problems that continue to seemingly spring anew or will these novel breakthroughs allow us to inflect to a new reality? The answers do not just have implications for those leading, studying, or enacting large-scale projects and policy around infrastructure but also for those seeking to use these assets as springboards for new imaginative futures.
panelists: Alison Baptiste; Julia Pyke; Chetan Kotur

session_name: Rules and Governance in Digital Markets
title: Secrecy, Spectrum, and Certification: Evidence from Wireless Electronic Devices
authors: Ruby Zhang (Harvard University); Roberto Fontana* (University of Pavia); Shane Greenstein (Harvard Business School); Do Yoon Kim (Boston College)
abstract: This paper examines the strategic decisions of firms to withhold information in innovation intensive markets, highlighting that secrecy contains distinct temporal dimensions. The study illustrates the thesis using wireless products, the majority of which innovate by utilizing unlicensed spectrum. Using all FCC equipment filings from 2001 to 2021, we analyze firms’ choices between long-term confidentiality (LTC), which permanently conceals technical information such as block diagrams, and short-term confidentiality (STC), which temporarily delays the public release of marketing information, including user manuals. We argue that the former acts to preserve “trade secrets,” the traditional role of IPR. In contrast, the latter acts as “commercialization insurance,” a previously unrecognized role for secrecy to ensure against launch and coordination risks in the commercialization process. We examine evidence consistent with this view. We find that the determinants for LTC and STC differ sharply. LTC use reflects appropriability concerns and institutional complexities - technically complex products and competitive markets are 12 to 35% more likely to adopt it. Traditional forms of IPR, such as patenting, are a substitute for LTC, especially in the case of WiFi. By contrast, STC is driven by the commercialization timing of branded products by large firms. Large, domestic, patent-owning firms with regulatorily complex products are more likely to use STC. Technical aspects of the product do not predict STC usage. Usage is consistently higher among incumbents for STC, while it quickly converges for LTC, even after controlling for all other variables. An exposure-based event study further shows that firms with a high ex-ante propensity to use STC bring products to market faster after the policy becomes available, with no corresponding changes in product complexity or volume. Together, these results show that permanent and temporary confidentiality serve distinct strategic purposes.

session_name: Rules and Governance in Digital Markets
title: When the Apolitical Cannot Hold: Technical Discipline and Political Pressure in Critical Infrastructure Governance
authors: Pedram Pourasgari* (University of Victoria)
abstract: Across industries, critical infrastructures are increasingly governed through communities, consortia or standard bodies whose legitimacy is founded on technical discipline and apolitical norms. International financial transactions, water and energy management, fishing allocations, and scholarly publishing are among those relying on conventions that bracket the political dimensions of the work, directing attention instead toward bounded technical issues. These governance mechanisms have proven their efficiency, yet the same apolitical disposition makes them fragile. Professional communities, particularly the ones with influence over critical infrastructure, are increasingly being forced to acknowledge political dimensions that they had been disciplined to ignore. The pressure comes either from external shocks that render political contestation unavoidable, or from communities' own pragmatic accommodations of outside actors. This paper draws on the history of one such community, dedicated to maintenance and development of the Linux kernel, which is arguably one of the most critical technical infrastructures operating across industries today. The study benefits from the community's commitment to radical transparency, which offers rare analytical access to the dynamics of tension emergence and resolution. I systematically analyzed three episodes of adoption and abrupt abandonment of a proprietary version control system (2002-2005), absorption of Android's kernel fork (2008-2012), and compliance-driven removal of sanctioned Russian maintainers (2024). Read together, these episodes reveal two dimensions of the apolitical governance problem. Pragmatic accommodations generate structural dependencies to an extent that the community's procedural repertoire was not designed to absorb, while external pressures force political acknowledgements, for which the community's legitimizing rhetoric had no provisions.

session_name: Rules and Governance in Digital Markets
title: From Data Assets to Institutional Intermediaries: The Role of Bricolage Approaches
authors: Xiangfeng Chen (Fudan University); Shenghao Xie (University of Liverpool); Ning Su* (Western University)
abstract: The past decade has witnessed digitalization across a wide range of industries, fueling the emergence of industrial digital platforms. However, the development of these platforms has been hindered by the absence or ineffectiveness of supporting institutions such as industry standards and regulations, commonly known as institutional voids. While prior research has identified data as a strategic asset that can drive firms’ digital transformation in general, how data assets can enable firms to address these voids remain underexplored. In this study, we investigate the evolution of an industrial digital platform in the manufacturing industry. Drawing on the concept of bricolage lens, we unpack three processes by which the platform leverages the data it had accumulated to address institutional voids: institutional bricolage, platform bricolage, and data bricolage. These processes enable the platform to build digital infrastructure, expand digital resources, and develop scalable data asset products. This process also marks the platform’s evolution into an institutional intermediary. Our findings contribute to the understanding of how digital platforms can leverage institutional voids to address industry challenges and promote digital industrialization. Furthermore, this study advances the literature on data asset, demonstrating that the data-based bricolage is not merely a second-best coping mechanism but a generative force that drives the emergence of institutional intermediation. These insights offer actionable guidance for the development of nascent digital platforms seeking to harness institutional voids to accelerate digital transformation.

title: Inventive novelty
authors: Holmer Kok (Stockholm School of Economics); Kristina Dahlin* (Copenhagen Business School); Xu Li (London School of Economics)
abstract: Inventive novelty is central to management, economics, and entrepreneurship research. Highly novel inventions are often seen as key to firm performance, market disruption, and addressing grand challenges such as climate change. Building on Schumpeter’s distinction between radical and incremental innovation, scholars widely accept that inventions differ in their degree of novelty. Yet, despite its importance, novelty itself is rarely clearly defined—likely because it is so commonly used that it is taken for granted. In contrast, the measurement of novelty has expanded rapidly with the digitization of patent data. Large databases have enabled researchers to develop numerous patent-based indicators. We identify more than 50 such measures across 447 studies. While these measures often appear valid, they frequently produce inconsistent results: correlations between them are low, and they often fail to identify the same inventions as novel. This suggests that measurement choices substantially influence findings, raising concerns about comparability and cumulative knowledge. We reviewed empirical studies where novelty was either a dependent or independent variable and applied their measures to a dataset of 589,400 patents. The results show there is no single “best” measure. Some perform better than others, but many are misaligned with their theoretical assumptions, and guidance on matching theory with measurement remains limited. We examine how novelty is conceptualized across literatures and assess strengths and limitations of patent-based measures. We identify key assumptions embedded in patent data providing a taxonomy of measures and concepts to align theory and measurement, improving validity, and enhancing comparability across studies.

title: Tracing the Arc of Innovation: Patterns and Drivers of Technology Evolution
authors: Anubha Shokhand (Masters' Union); Nilam Kaushik (IIM Bangalore); Sai Yayavaram* (IIM Bangalore)
abstract: A central question in innovation research is how technologies evolve over time. While the technology life cycle framework predicts an S-curve trajectory of emergence, growth, maturity, and decline, empirical evidence reveals considerable variation. This study examines the temporal evolution of cumulative inventive effort and technological performance across 574 technologies. We identify three distinct archetypes of technological evolution: (1) a classic S-curve, (2) sustained exponential growth, and (3) a hybrid pattern in which an initial S-curve transitions into exponential growth. Using two parameters---the time to exponential growth and the exponential growth rate---we develop a parsimonious classification of these trajectories. Because technology evolution patterns are widely used as a basis for prediction, we ask whether early technology-level characteristics can predict its long-term evolutionary patterns---focusing on the roles of initial generality and initial coupling. We find that high initial coupling delays the onset of exponential growth but is associated with higher growth rates, while high initial generality accelerates the transition to exponential growth and boosts growth rates only in highly coupled domains, highlighting the contingent value of broadly applicable knowledge. These findings extend technology life-cycle theory by identifying boundary conditions, showing that some technologies escape maturity altogether, and demonstrating how early knowledge structures shape the pace and trajectory of technological progress. Methodologically, our two-parameter framework offers a tractable approach to classifying evolutionary patterns.

title: Where do firms search? Macroeconomic conditions and the direction of technological exploration
authors: Amit Kumar* (Warwick Business School)
abstract: This paper distinguishes between two forms of distant search: niche exploration—entry into new technological domains—and science-based exploration—innovation grounded in epistemically and institutionally distant scientific knowledge. These forms rely on distinct resource logics and serve different strategic objectives. I examine how macroeconomic conditions shape the direction of firms’ distant search. I argue that economic contractions encourage niche exploration, as firms pursue low-cost growth options in peripheral, emerging, and nascent domains, whereas economic expansions favor science-based exploration, which requires sustained, resource-intensive investment under conditions of abundant capital and strong demand. Using a panel of leading U.S. innovator firms across industries from 1995 to 2022, I find robust support for these predictions. The findings contribute to the distant search literature by disaggregating exploration and to research on business cycles by showing that macroeconomic conditions (business cycles) influence not only the intensity but also the direction of firms’ exploratory search.

title: The Effects of Voluntary Performance Standards on the Diffusion of Innovation
authors: Almantas Palubinskas* (emlyon Business School)
abstract: Innovation ecosystems play an important role in the development, performance, and emergence of innovation. However, scholars have largely overlooked the role of voluntary standards within an ecosystem and their effect on the diffusion of innovation. Research examining the effects of standards on innovation has typically focused on their effect on innovation rates and their ability to diffuse cutting-edge knowledge within an industry. While industry-level standards set by regulators and standard-setting bodies introduce limitations on the manufacturer, manufacturers often impose their own standards on consumers adopting new technologies. This issue is particularly salient within high-tech industries where users must have a complementary element that surpasses a minimum performance threshold to use a new technology. It is not unusual for companies to recommend additional performance thresholds that may be significantly higher than the minimum requirements for optimal use. This paper frames these higher requirements as voluntary standards. Voluntary standards are particularly prevalent in the video game industry, and act as signals to consumers indicating that they may need to upgrade their hardware to achieve optimal performance when playing their new game. We test our hypotheses using an original dataset that incorporates existing user hardware and video game requirements (minimum and voluntary) to examine how voluntary standards influence the diffusion of graphics cards from 2010 to 2026. This paper contributes to the literatures on innovation ecosystems, performance standards, and the diffusion of innovation by providing insights into how voluntary standards within an innovation’s ecosystem influence the diffusion of innovation.

session_name: Uneven Ground: How Context Shapes Who Builds, Who Stays, and Who Thrives
category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
title: Exceptional but Exhausted: Women Founders and Higher Rates of Venture Closure in Male-Dominated Industries
authors: Lena Lizunova (BYU Marriott School of Business); Jennifer Merluzzi* (George Washington School of Business)
abstract: This panel brings together four empirical studies united by a persistently troubling observation, that organizational rewards are not evenly (fairly) distributed. Together, the papers encompass studies across private sector entrepreneurship and public sector management, across multiple national contexts, and large-scale administrative and longitudinal data, triangulated where possible with qualitative evidence and natural or quasi-natural experiments. Yet, all four papers are united in a common theoretical concern with how context, such as industrial, organizational, and biographical, generates enduring disparities in organizational and individual performance. Three papers converge on the same central puzzle, why do women-led ventures systematically underperform relative to men-led ventures even when founders are equally qualified, work harder, and follow the rules more faithfully? Together, they offer three complementary and mutually reinforcing answers: women founders in male-dominated industries are exhausted into failure by the relentless pressure to overperform (Lizunova & Merluzzi); women founders lose employees at higher rates because gendered legitimacy doubts weaken employee attachment regardless of actual performance (Yoon & Leung); and women founders who comply with workplace regulations are penalized because their ethical behavior is a disadvantage in markets where violations correlate with survival (Alsanousi & Kacperczyk). The fourth paper extends this structural logic from private enterprise to public administration, showing that the contextual conditions of early career assignments, and not individual talent alone, determine which public managers can most effectively deliver welfare programs to vulnerable populations (Bhatt, Bonet & Jandhyala). These papers highlight the fact that persistent inequality in organizational outcomes is not primarily a story of individual deficits but of structural environments. The panel is directly relevant to the Industry Studies tradition of grounding organizational analysis in the specific conditions of industries and institutional environments and will be of broad interest to scholars working in entrepreneurship, organizational inequality, human capital, and public sector management. Below we detail the title, authors and affiliations, and the abstracts for each paper in the session.

abstract: This panel brings together four empirical studies united by a persistently troubling observation, that organizational rewards are not evenly (fairly) distributed. Together, the papers encompass studies across private sector entrepreneurship and public sector management, across multiple national contexts, and large-scale administrative and longitudinal data, triangulated where possible with qualitative evidence and natural or quasi-natural experiments. Yet, all four papers are united in a common theoretical concern with how context, such as industrial, organizational, and biographical, generates enduring disparities in organizational and individual performance. Three papers converge on the same central puzzle, why do women-led ventures systematically underperform relative to men-led ventures even when founders are equally qualified, work harder, and follow the rules more faithfully? Together, they offer three complementary and mutually reinforcing answers: women founders in male-dominated industries are exhausted into failure by the relentless pressure to overperform (Lizunova & Merluzzi); women founders lose employees at higher rates because gendered legitimacy doubts weaken employee attachment regardless of actual performance (Yoon & Leung); and women founders who comply with workplace regulations are penalized because their ethical behavior is a disadvantage in markets where violations correlate with survival (Alsanousi & Kacperczyk). The fourth paper extends this structural logic from private enterprise to public administration, showing that the contextual conditions of early career assignments, and not individual talent alone, determine which public managers can most effectively deliver welfare programs to vulnerable populations (Bhatt, Bonet & Jandhyala). These papers highlight the fact that persistent inequality in organizational outcomes is not primarily a story of individual deficits but of structural environments. The panel is directly relevant to the Industry Studies tradition of grounding organizational analysis in the specific conditions of industries and institutional environments and will be of broad interest to scholars working in entrepreneurship, organizational inequality, human capital, and public sector management. Below we detail the title, authors and affiliations, and the abstracts for each paper in the session.

session_name: Supply Chain Discovery - Emergence, Evolution and Growth
category: Operations, Supply Chain, and AI-Enhanced Industry 4.0
title: Supply Chain Discovery - Emergence, Evolution and Growth
authors: Guven Demirel (Queen Mary University London); Francois Lafond (Institute for New Economic Thinking, University of Oxford); James Hall (Environmental Change Institute, University of Oxford); Alexandra Brintrup (University of Cambridge)
abstract: Society’s critical reliance on the performance of globally dispersed supply chains and networks is now evident. However, the challenges in discovering, estimating and mapping multilayered supply networks are less well appreciated. More fundamentally, how supply chains and networks emerge, evolve and grow over time has received very limited attention. Supply networks do not appear fully formed – they are evolving industrial systems shaped by technology, economics, competition, regulation and policy decisions. Technological breakthroughs in areas such as quantum computing, bioengineering or small modular reactors are insufficient alone to ensure an industry grows and becomes profitable in a particular location or region. Supply chains and networks are needed to support the critical value-adding stages that enable successful production at scale. Today’s industrial era is characterised by geopolitical tensions and uncertainties, coupled with a strong emphasis on protectionism, regionalism and security of supply, affecting many supply networks, including semiconductors, batteries, energy technologies and pharmaceuticals. How much do we understand about the lifecycle of supply chains and networks, their fundamental structures, how they emerge and develop, and how they respond to industrial and international trade policies? How can global supply networks be estimated when links are unobserved or incomplete? Can a new science develop combining insights from industry studies, complex systems modelling, economic geography, industrial policy and supply chain management to explain how supply networks grow, become resilient (or fragile), and survive over the long term? The panel aims for multidisciplinary understanding and debate on supply network discovery, structure, emergence, evolution and growth.
moderator: Bart L. MacCarthy (Nottingham University Business School)
panelists: Guven Demirel (Queen Mary University London); Francois Lafond (Institute for New Economic Thinking, University of Oxford); James Hall (Environmental Change Institute, University of Oxford); Alexandra Brintrup (University of Cambridge)

title: Contested Transitions and the Reproduction of Inequality: A Three-Dimensional Justice Framework
authors: Muhammad Umar Boodoo* (Warwick Business School); Miguel Macías (Warwick Business School)
abstract: Governments and firms are committing trillions of dollars to industrial transitions under the banner of equity and sustainability. Yet across green energy, global supply chains, carbon markets, and agricultural certification, a consistent pattern emerges: transitions invoking equity rhetoric concentrate benefits among powerful incumbents while externalizing costs to marginalized communities, particularly in the Global South. With clean-energy investment projected at $4.5 trillion annually by 2030, understanding why this pattern persists and what governance conditions can interrupt it is among the most consequential questions facing industry scholars and policymakers. We develop a three-dimensional justice framework of inequality reproduction and transformation in contested transitions, defined as field-level changes marked by significant power asymmetries and irreconcilable conflicts over redistribution, representation, and recognition. Drawing on comparative evidence across energy, supply chain, and carbon market industries, we theorize three position-dependent forms of coordinated action. Appropriative work by incumbents entrenches advantage through cost shifting, rule-arena shaping, and epistemic dominance. Legitimation work by intermediaries stabilizes contradictions between equity rhetoric and exclusionary practice. Resistance work by challengers contests exclusion through allocation challenges, demands for meaningful participation, and assertion of marginalized knowledge. These forms interact through escalation cycles and legitimation crises to generate innovation opportunity windows. Whether these windows yield genuine transformation or green inequality, which we define as symbolic institutional change that preserves material power asymmetries, depends on the capacity of Internal Governance Units across authority, autonomy, resources, and accountability. The framework offers directly applicable lessons for industrial policy design: effective governance of just transitions requires embedding enforceable safeguards.

title: The Limits of Infrastructure-Led Green Transition: Feedback Failures and Policy Contestation in Serbia
authors: Sonja Avlijas* (University of Belgrade - Faculty of Economics)
abstract: Contemporary green transition strategies in the European periphery increasingly rely on large-scale infrastructure investment, public–private partnerships, and de-risking instruments to accelerate decarbonisation. While effective in mobilising capital, less attention has been paid to the institutional conditions required to coordinate complex infrastructure systems in practice. This paper examines the case of Serbia to show how infrastructure-led transition policies can generate systemic risks and political contestation in contexts marked by clientelism, fragmented governance and weak societal feedback and accountability mechanisms. The analysis is based on a qualitative case study combining policy analysis, sectoral data on transport infrastructure, and evidence from recent infrastructure failures and protest dynamics. The paper conceptualises “infrastructural risk” as a product of top-down, project-based investment models operating through clientelist and weakly embedded institutional arrangements. Because the system lacks effective channels through which risks can be detected, communicated, and corrected, signals from workers, users, and professionals do not translate into institutional response. As a result, risks accumulate until they materialise as technical failure or public crisis. The paper argues that student mobilisation following the November 2024 railway canopy collapse represents a response to this deficit, functioning as an informal societal mechanism for aggregating dispersed concerns and restoring feedback into an informationally blind and captured system. More broadly, it highlights a critical dimension of green industrial policy: the need to sustain effective feedback loops between infrastructure systems and the societies that depend on them. Without this, infrastructure-led transitions risk both material failure and political backlash.

title: Green Industrial Policy and the Diffusion of Low-Carbon Cement: Evidence from a Cross-National QCA
authors: Malek Al Jebaie* (Erasmus University Rotterdam); Beatriz Calzada Olvera (Erasmus University Rotterdam); Lasse Gerrits (Erasmus University Rotterdam)
abstract: The cement industry accounts for approximately eight per cent of global CO₂ emissions, yet the diffusion of proven low-carbon alternatives remains slow and geographically uneven. This study examines why Limestone Calcined Clay Cement (LC3), a technically mature and cost-competitive clinker substitution technology, has not achieved widespread adoption. Rather than treating adoption as a purely technical or cost-driven process, we investigate how country preconditions, sector preconditions, and industrial policy conditions together form the configurations necessary or sufficient for LC3 diffusion. Adapting the green windows of opportunity framework of Lema et al. (2025) to the low-carbon cement context and integrating innovation systems, institutional, and diffusion theories, we apply a two-step crisp-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (csQCA) to 17 countries. The analysis identifies sectoral institutions and networks as a necessary but not sufficient condition for adoption, and reveals two equifinal pathways: a policy-enabled pathway, in which normative demand pressure and technology policy complexity trigger adoption in structurally ready contexts, and an autonomous pathway, in which adoption proceeds without formal policy compulsion. These findings challenge incumbent-led voluntary decarbonisation frameworks and point toward mission-oriented, directional industrial policy as the necessary architecture for accelerating LC3 diffusion at the pace that climate mitigation targets demand.

title: Exit Foreclosed: Structural Non-Exit from Coopetition
authors: Alfred Marcus* (University of Minnesota)
abstract: Sustainable innovation increasingly shapes firm strategy by enhancing reputation, opening new markets, and enabling long term value creation. Achieving large scale impact, however, requires engagement across multi stakeholder ecosystems involving startups, incumbents, regulators, and complementary partners. Prior research has focused largely on single firms or bilateral partnerships, leaving ecosystem level dynamics underexplored. This paper develops a conceptual framework explaining how collaboration, competition, and coopetition evolve across innovation stages and market contexts. Drawing on evidence from precision agriculture, alternative proteins, electric vehicle batteries, and micro mobility, it shows that patterns differ systematically between business to business (B2B) and business to consumer (B2C) markets. In business-to-business settings, collaboration remains central due to technical complexity and infrastructure needs, transitioning into coopetition as markets mature. In business to consumer contexts, competition emerges earlier, driven by branding and customer engagement. The paper contributes a pathway model that clarifies how ecosystem dynamics shape adoption and diffusion of sustainable innovation. The framework in the paper highlights the central role of startup incumbent relations and shows how firms balance shared development with rivalry for market leadership.

title: Constructing Embeddedness on Digital Platforms: The Case of Virtual Food Banking Platforms
authors: Fuaad Coovadia* (University of Oxford)
abstract: Digital platforms are increasingly deployed to address sustainability challenges by coordinating resource flows across organisations. An emerging example growing rapidly in adoption is virtual food banking: non-profit digital platforms that connect food businesses (e.g. retailers, restaurants, manufacturers) with frontline charities to donate surplus food. These platforms operate under dual constraints: limited and specialised user populations, and a social mission that can make indiscriminate scaling up the user-base counterproductive. This raises a problem that existing platform strategy, which focuses on user growth to generate network effects, struggles to address: how can platform owners generate network value when user growth is constrained? This paper examines this question through an inductive, multi-country study of four virtual food banking platforms in the UK, Ireland, the USA, and South Africa. The analysis draws on 38 semi-structured interviews with platform managers and users, organisational documents, and platform event-log data capturing over 10 million donation exchanges. Drawing on structural embeddedness, the findings show that platform owners enhance value for users by shaping relationships among existing participants. Specifically, they cultivate value for both food donors and charities through four strategies: nurturing persistent donor-charity dyads, structuring neighbourhood-level arm’s-length backup ties, leveraging off-platform relationships, and developing users’ relational capabilities. By foregrounding a non-profit, surplus-redistribution platform, the paper contributes to research on sustainable innovation by showing how digital platforms can reduce waste through relational coordination rather than scale. It also extends platform theory by demonstrating how network value can be constructed through the deliberate orchestration of embeddedness.

title: Mapping Net-Zero Technologies through web scraping: Evidence from Italian corporate websites
authors: Marco Cucculelli* (Università Politecnica Delle Marche); Noemi Giampaoli (Università Politecnica Delle Marche); Matteo Renghini (Università Politecnica Delle Marche)
abstract: The Net-Zero Industry Act (NZIA) is a key initiative of the European Union aimed at accelerating the green transition and strengthening the EU’s clean-tech industrial base. However, the adoption of net-zero technologies across firms, sectors and regions remains largely undocumented, mainly due to the limitations of conventional innovation metrics. This paper addresses this gap by operationalising the NZIA technology framework at the firm level and combining structured firm-level data with unstructured information extracted from corporate websites via large-scale web scraping. Focusing on Italian companies, we map the adoption of net-zero technologies by company and, within adopters, identify firms that are also engaged in their technological development by integrating web-based signals with patent data. We document the geographical and sectoral distribution of adopters and developers and analyse the firm-level drivers associated with technology adoption and development. Our results show that web-based data are effective in identifying the adoption of net-zero technologies, but they need to be complemented with patent information to accurately capture technological development. These findings have important implications for the design of targeted, place-based industrial policies under the NZIA framework.

title: A Critical Integrative Assessment of the GenAI/LLM Industry Dynamics and Its Socio-Environmental Consequences in a Resource-Constrained World
authors: Jeroen Struben* (emlyon Business School)
abstract: Innovation is central to societal renewal. But are our current ways suited for doing this within a resource-constrained world? The GenAI/LLM industry, promising drastic innovation across sectors, is also growing, attracting, and using resources; and altering human attention and practices at an unprecedented rate, and with deep societal consequences—some of which themselves also interact with these growth dynamics. Using archival analysis this paper performs an integrative analysis to examine the main mechanisms underlying the extraordinary growth path of the GenAI/LLM industry and the various social-environmental impacts of the present GenAI/LLM pathway—in realms ranging from resource extraction and consumption to greenhouse gas emissions, to labor exploitation and displacement, inequality, education systems, mis- and disinformation, to global security. With the aid of causal loop diagramming, the analysis reveals not only domains and, where possible, extent of impacts but also the underlying dynamics driving these including through mechanisms of self-perpetuating dependence on growth, and of crowding out of other industry and GenAI developments. Together these dynamics demonstrate the risk of an industry locking into a perverse pathway with near- and longer-term irreversibilities. The paper concludes considering feasible ways of re-aligning this industry with desirable directions in ways—drastically improving positive and decreasing negative consequences. It considers collective governance models, promotion and protection of responsible AI, and education. Across these notions is the critical need and high-leverage for mindset changes towards responsible innovation in a way that is consistent with societal thriving in a resource-constrained world.

title: From Nascency to Commercial Viability: How the Construction of Financing Mechanisms Shaped the Emergence of the Commercial Space Industry
authors: Utkarsh Amitabh* (University of Oxford)
abstract: Why do some nascent industries fail to achieve commercial viability despite the presence of enabling technology and latent demand? Drawing on the industry emergence framework of Moeen et al. (2020) and Agarwal et al. (2025), I show that the commercial space industry entered the period 2000 to 2010 with technological and demand uncertainties substantially reduced through decades of state-led development, yet remained commercially non-viable because ecosystem and institutional uncertainties remained unresolved. I trace how six coexisting financing mechanisms were constructed, selected, and institutionalised over this period, showing that financing arrangements functioned as the primary instrument through which these uncertainties were reduced. Drawing on a longitudinal archival analysis of NASA programme documents, government records, and private financing data, I make three contributions. First, I extend the ecosystem construction literature by showing that public agencies, rather than entrepreneurs, performed the alliance and boundary work through which ecosystem uncertainty was reduced, using financing contracts rather than alliance portfolios as the primary instrument. Second, I extend the institutional voids framework beyond its geographic origins, showing that voids arise within mature economies wherever structural misalignment between existing intermediaries and novel exchange requirements renders private participation infeasible. Third, I apply a variation, selection, and retention logic to a population of financing arrangements rather than firms, showing that industry stabilisation proceeded through the institutional selection of a financing architecture rather than the survival of the fittest firms.

title: Market Formation in Commercial Space Stations: Ecosystems, Legitimacy, and Optionality
authors: Mehdi Montakhabi* (University of Oxford); Benn Lawson (University of Oxford); Jens Roehrich (University of Bath); Brian Squire (University of Bristol)
abstract: How is the emerging commercial low-Earth-orbit (LEO) space industry being made commercially viable under conditions of long investment horizons, high capital intensity, and deep state involvement? We examine this question through an abductive qualitative case study of a venture developing a commercial LEO station while generating bridge revenues through private astronaut missions and adjacent microgravity research services. Drawing on ongoing fieldwork, including interviews with senior executives, board members, and operations-level managers, triangulated with sector convenings and external practitioner insight, we develop a mechanism-based model of commercialization. We identify four interlocking mechanisms. First, firms engineer commercial viability under long horizons by combining bridge revenues with disciplined attention to unit economics, investment pacing, and contracting constraints. Second, they orchestrate ecosystems by building missing supply chains, stabilizing interfaces, and aligning policy-operational dependencies that condition partner commitment. Third, they perform legitimacy and meaning-making through narratives, boundary work, convening, and evidence-based claims that make public support and procurement more defensible. Fourth, they learn through campaigns while preserving strategic optionality through modular architecture, portfolio diversification, and cross-functional integration. The paper contributes to industry studies by showing how the emerging LEO space industry becomes commercially viable when market formation depends on the joint evolution of firm strategy, ecosystem capacity, and public policy.

title: Supply Network Evolution in High Tech Industries
authors: Elcio Mendonça Tachizawa (Universidad Politécnica de Madrid); Tim Schlaich* (Copenhagen Business School)
abstract: This study examines how supply networks evolve in high-tech industries when technological change, market formation, and public policy transformation occur simultaneously. While supply chain research increasingly recognizes networks as dynamic, existing studies have largely focused on mature industries or early-stage commercialization, offering limited insight into how governance structures and network configurations change as sectors scale. We address this gap through a qualitative case study of the Spanish space sector, which is undergoing a transition from “Old Space” dominated by public procurement, centralized coordination, and hierarchical relationships toward “New Space” characterized by commercialization, modular technologies, private investment, and entrepreneurial entry. Drawing on interviews with private firms and public institutions, the study shows that supply network evolution is not a linear shift from hierarchy to market. Instead, the Spanish New Space sector is developing hybrid governance structures in which relational, captive, modular, and market mechanisms coexist. Institutional customers continue to require control, reliability, security, and long-term supplier relationships, while private customers emphasize cost, speed, performance, and scalability. These divergent demands create dual supply structures and persistent governance tensions. The findings also show that increased product modularity, commercial off-the-shelf components, and specialized new entrants reshape network complexity. Horizontal and spatial complexity increase as more geographically dispersed suppliers enter the network, while vertical complexity declines in some standardized components but remains important where control and mission-specific capabilities are required. The study contributes to supply chain theory by showing how supply networks co-evolve with technological architectures, policy instruments, and market logics in emerging high-tech industries.

title: Beyond the Kármán Line: Governing Scarcity and Competitive Advantage in Space
authors: Mayukh Mukhopadhyay* (IIM Indore)
abstract: Low Earth Orbit (LEO) has emerged as a strategically scarce industrial domain where public policy, financial architecture, and competitive strategy intersect. Crossing the Kármán Line marks not only a physical boundary but also a shift in the institutional logic governing value-creation, rivalry, and control. This study conceptualizes LEO as industrial real estate whose scarcity is actively constituted through regulatory discourse, valuation practices, and coordinated state and firm action rather than arising solely from technological constraint. We argue that scarcity in this domain functions as a strategic resource, enabling competitive advantage for actors that shape the rules, timing, and legitimacy of access. Methodologically, the study adopts a multimodal semiotic approach informed by institutional meaning-making. From a corpus of over 120 satellite launch videos, investor briefings, and industry communications, and 180 policy and regulatory documents issued by space agencies and telecommunications authorities, the analysis examines 18 videos and 42 policy documents selected for engagement with orbital congestion, access prioritization, and valuation. Tracing recurring narratives and regulatory framings shows how scarcity is normalized and operationalized as a governing mechanism collectively. Building on the concept of the space value of money (Papazian, 2020) our work explains why conventional valuation frameworks fail under conditions of irreversible environmental risk and interdependent rivalry. By reframing Low Earth Orbit as a governed scarce resource rather than neutral infrastructure, the paper contributes to industry studies and strategic management by explaining how competitive advantage is co-produced through institutional design beyond the planet.
