title: Breakfast
System Integration Capability in the Smartphone SoC Industry: Combining In-House Technologies, External Technologies, and Alliances
authors: Junichiro Tanabe* (Keio University)
abstract: Previous research has emphasized the importance of the use of external technologies and inter-firm alliances. For instance, architecture theory suggests that modular products benefit from openness. Similarly, research on inter-firm relations argues that alliances with competitors can contribute to competitive advantage. However, in the semiconductor industry, which this study focuses on, even firms that have exited the market utilized external technologies and formed alliances. This suggests that the key lies not in in-house technologies, external technologies, or alliances themselves, but in how they are combined. Accordingly, this study addresses the following research question: How have semiconductor companies decided on the combination of in-house technology, external technology procurement, and inter-company collaboration? It compares the technology strategies of successful firms and those that exited the market, focusing on system integration capabilities. Specifically, the study examines smartphone SoC firms, such as Qualcomm and Texas Instruments, from the 2000s to the 2010s. It analyzes how these firms combined IC components (e.g., CPUs and GPUs) within their SoCs. The data sources will be a combination of interviews with semiconductor companies, specialized magazines, and data obtained by actually disassembling smartphones. This study is expected to show that, in the 2000s, core components were often based on modularized external technologies, while peripheral components relied more on in-house technologies. Over time, selective alliances emerged among firms specializing in different peripheral components. However, firms differed in their ability to catch up with their partners’ technologies, leading to differentiation. Thus, both the scope of alliances and catch-up ability are critical.

title: From Making to Designing: A Neo-Schumpeterian Perspective on Learning by Supplying in Global Sourcing
authors: Ning Su* (Western University)
abstract: Offshore outsourcing has reshaped global value chains by shifting production to emerging economies, enabling some suppliers to upgrade from low-cost manufacturing to innovation-a process termed “learning by supplying”, although only a small group of suppliers succeeded in this transformation. This study examines this capability-building process through a multi-case study in China’s technology sector, including an in-depth longitudinal study of HealthTech—evolving from a 1990s service provider to a leading medical technology firm—complemented by a study of three major technology firms in the software, electronics, and electric vehicle industries, with varying degrees of success in learning by supplying. Drawing on a neo-Schumpeterian lens, which views production as combining resources and innovation as recombining them, three findings emerge. First, suppliers’ capability-building is shaped by client firms’ institutional logics, which define required “capability profiles.” Suppliers acquire capabilities through imitation and integrate them through recombination, generating product and process innovations. Second, capability development follows a recursive cycle of imitation, integration, and innovation, where experimentation during imitation produces innovation that enables further capability upgrading. Third, suppliers face a “capability trap”: advancement depends on clients offering higher-value tasks, yet client logics are often stable. Only firms committed to investing beyond immediate client demand can escape this capability trap, explaining why few successfully move up the global value chain.

title: CEO Industry Embeddedness: Industry-Association Board Service and Firm Performance
authors: Arun Datta (University of Texas); Bukky Oyedeji* (London Business School)
abstract: While research on CEO embeddedness has shown that executives’ external ties shape firm outcomes, it has focused overwhelmingly on corporate-board interlocks and other board-based networks, paying far less attention to competitor-dense industry settings. At the same time, research on trade associations has largely examined them as vehicles for collective action, nonmarket strategy, and institutional change, rather than as arenas of CEO embeddedness. We examine one such form of embeddedness: CEO service on industry-association boards. By participating in these collective industry bodies, CEOs are embedded in recurring forums for interaction, shared sensemaking, and governance around common industry issues. Drawing on upper echelons theory, we argue that this form of industry embeddedness enhances firm performance by improving CEOs’ ability to interpret industry conditions and anticipate shifts, particularly in high-growth industries. Using hand-collected data on CEO industry-association board memberships and a matched panel of 18,548 CEO-years, we find that such memberships are positively associated with firm performance, with stronger effects in high-growth industries. Supplementary analyses suggest that these benefits are more consistent with improved interpretation of industry conditions than with direct influence over industry rules or outcomes. Our findings contribute by extending CEO embeddedness research beyond corporate-board networks and by showing how participation in collective industry structures can generate strategic advantage.

title: Overcoming Fit-Induced Rigidity: The Role of Acquisitions in Activity System Renewal
authors: Panos Desyllas* (University of Bath); Tomi Laamanen (University of St. Gallen)
abstract: Organizations that continuously optimize their activity systems to enhance performance often develop rigidities that constrain renewal. While acquisitions can, in principle, help organizations overcome this tension, their relationship to long-term renewal remains unclear because acquisitions also give rise to major integration challenges and internal inconsistencies. Drawing on a longitudinal comparative analysis of Amazon and Alphabet, which made over 370 acquisitions from their founding to 2020, we traced how the two companies used sequences of acquisitions to continuously renew their activity systems, a process we term "acquisitive morphing." We classified acquisitions into four types according to whether they reinforced the companies’ existing activity system elements ("thickening") or introduced new ones ("patching"), and whether their impact was major ("enabling") or minor ("supporting"). While both companies employed all four types, they followed distinct pathways. Alphabet pursued an "expansion-oriented" pathway, initially emphasizing acquisition-enabled patching before shifting toward acquisition-supported thickening. In contrast, Amazon followed a "coherence-oriented" pathway, beginning with acquisition-enabled thickening, followed by selective expansion through acquisition-supported and enabled patching. Counterintuitively, Amazon's ostensibly less ambitious approach led to greater renewal and higher coherence of the activity system than Alphabet’s approach, because its acquisitions better complemented one another within the evolving activity system context. The sequencing of acquisitions enabled Amazon to better balance between renewal and coherence over time. Our study extends activity systems theory by highlighting the important role of acquisition sequences and intertemporal complementarities in the renewal of activity systems.

session_name: Politics, Institutions, and Strategy in Health Markets
category: Health Care Systems, Biotechnology, and Pharmaceuticals
title: Pharmaceutical Pricing Dynamics Under Price Control Regulation
authors: Ujjal Mukherjee* (University of Illinois - Urbana Champaign); Gopesh Anand (University of Illinois - Urbana Champaign); Alok Raj (XLRI, India); Priyatam Anurag (Indian Institute of Management - Lucknow)
abstract: This study examines pharmaceutical industry pricing dynamics in response to governmental price control regulations, particularly for essential drugs. The context of the study is India's price control regulation adoption to manage the escalation of prices for pharmaceutical drugs. We evaluate the effectiveness of India's Drug Price Control Order 2013 (DPCO 13) using difference-in-differences analysis on pharmaceutical pricing data from January 2010 through March 2021. We analyze three regulatory phases: initial announcement (June 2013), mandatory price information submission (June 2015), and establishment of state-level vigilance infrastructure (June 2019). Using coarsened exact matching and multiple robustness checks including Lewbel IV estimation, Arellano-Bond dynamic panel models, and regression discontinuity design, we find that regulatory effectiveness follows a non-linear pattern. The announcement phase produced minimal price reductions. However, the information mandate phase generated significant price decreases of approximately 6% for treated drugs, representing the most substantial impact relative to prior periods. The enforcement infrastructure phase showed further reductions (15% overall) but with diminishing marginal effects. Exploring the mechanisms of the price control through competition, firm characteristics, and drug characteristics. We find that the effectiveness of price control varies significantly across different drug types categorized by the broad-level ICD codes they are approved for. We find that the price dampening effect of price control regulation is the highest for cardiovascular drugs, followed by pain medication and cancer drugs. We find that the effect of regulation is higher when industry concentration is low, and the presence of large firms with high industry concentration negates the affect of regulation to a large extent. Price elasticity of a drug is an important predictor of industry reaction to price regulations. Foreign MNCs as compared to domestic corporations are more conforming to the price regulation mandates. Finally, the number of drug options within a therapeutic class moderates the effect of price regulation on pricing of drugs. Critically, we identify two spillover mechanisms. Competition-driven spillover reduced prices of untreated drugs within the same therapeutic class by 3-5%, with effects strongest in fragmented markets (low HHI) and among high-volume products. Product commonality spillover reduced combination drug prices by 7-8%. Market concentration, firm origin (MNC vs. Indian), and therapeutic category significantly moderate treatment effects. Analysis of likelihood of violation of price ceilings for specific drugs reveals that while violations decreased over time, market leaders in concentrated markets remain more prone to non-compliance. Penalty analysis using Hawkes process modeling demonstrates that regulatory sanctions significantly dampen future violations, though effects decay rapidly. These findings suggest information-based interventions may yield higher marginal impact than enforcement expansion in pharmaceutical price regulation. Finally, we conduct consumer welfare analysis and show that such regulations improve consumer welfare significantly. The study has significant implications for pharmaceutical drug industry in India and globally. The evidence supports that price cap regulation not only directly lowers prices of controlled drugs but also indirectly reduces prices of untreated substitutes through competitive pressure. The effect is stronger in competitive markets, grows over time, and is reinforced by credible penalties. Regulators should design enforcement strategies that are swift, targeted, and risk‑based, while also addressing market concentration where spillovers are weak.

session_name: Politics, Institutions, and Strategy in Health Markets
category: Health Care Systems, Biotechnology, and Pharmaceuticals
title: Political Geography and Market Entry: Evidence from the U.S. Blood Plasma Industry
authors: Yu Li* (SKEMA Business School)
abstract: The U.S. blood plasma industry is dominated by four foreign multinationals (CSL, Grifols, Takeda, and KEDPLASMA) that collectively control over 85% of more than 1,000 collection centers. Unlike most healthcare markets, growth is constrained not by demand but by regulatory access to plasma donors, making the political environment a first-order determinant of where firms can profitably operate. We ask whether nonmarket strategy (NMS) capabilities shape not only policy outcomes, but firms' prior identification of politically viable market opportunities. Specifically, we examine whether plasma collection centers are systematically more likely to open in areas represented by legislators with relevant committee assignments (Health, Appropriations) even after controlling for market-level demand characteristics. If firms with stronger NMS capabilities can read the political landscape ahead of entry decisions, center locations should cluster on the politically safer side of legislative district boundaries, where otherwise similar communities differ primarily in their political representation. We exploit legislative district boundary discontinuities as a source of quasi-random variation in political representation, comparing census tracts on opposite sides of district boundaries that are similar in demographic and economic characteristics but differ in their political exposure. Using FDA establishment data on more than 1,000 U.S. plasma center locations (2014 to 2021), we present preliminary evidence consistent with politically informed location choice. These findings illuminate how political factors shape firm expansion decisions and the geographic distribution of capacity in highly regulated, supply-constrained industries, extending NMS theory to the ex ante stage of market entry.

session_name: Politics, Institutions, and Strategy in Health Markets
category: Health Care Systems, Biotechnology, and Pharmaceuticals
title: Publicly Elected Leaders and Contraceptive Uptake in the Public Sector: Evidence from India
authors: Amir Karimi (University of Texas San Antonio); Dwaipayan Roy* (University of Virginia Darden Graduate School of Business)
abstract: Problem Definition. In many developing economies, the public sector bears primary responsibility for ensuring access to essential health commodities and services such as contraceptives. However, despite extensive government-led initiatives, contraceptive uptake remains persistently low in such settings, leaving over 160 million women with an unmet need. We investigate the impact of an oft-overlooked yet potentially consequential driver of contraceptive uptake: female vs. male publicly elected leaders. Methodology/results. Using a quasi-experimental design based on close elections across 653 districts in India over a decade (2010–2019), we examine the impact of publicly elected female legislators on contraceptive uptake. We find method-specific effects: female legislators increase uptake of intrauterine devices (IUDs)—a long-acting, reversible contraceptive—while having no meaningful effect on short-acting reversible (i.e., oral pills) or permanent non-reversible methods (i.e., tubal ligation). Interestingly, this increase in IUD uptake is concentrated among younger women, for whom the distinct features of IUDs—minimal client adherence, preserving future childbearing potential and easier concealability—are particularly valuable. We also find that, in districts with higher representation of female legislators, frontline health workers engage more with younger women on reproductive health—likely raising awareness of IUD-specific benefits and driving its uptake among this client segment. Managerial Implications. Our findings demonstrate the importance of aligning contraceptive method features with the needs of specific client segments, particularly younger women, to enhance uptake. Meaningful engagement by frontline health workers with younger women on reproductive health facilitates this alignment, serving as a scalable pathway to improve awareness and informed decision-making on uptake. More broadly, our study strengthens the case for institutional reforms—such as quotas for female political leaders—to improve reproductive health outcomes.

session_name: Navigating Uncertainty: IP, Commercialization, and AI-Driven Changes in Biotech
title: Biopharmaceutical Contracting Dynamics
authors: Carolin Häussler* (University of Passau)
abstract: New ventures and incumbents in high-technology sectors operate under conditions of deep uncertainty: technological trajectories shift, intellectual property regimes evolve, and institutional environments remain in flux. Recent developments are compounding these pressures. Artificial intelligence is disrupting established innovation pathways, geopolitical tensions are redrawing the boundaries of global knowledge production, and evolving IP regimes are unsettling the foundations on which firms build and sustain competitive advantage. Critically, these shifts do not operate in isolation; they interact in ways that fundamentally reshape how firms organize, contract, collaborate, and capture value from innovation. How new ventures and incumbents navigate this compounding uncertainty represents one of the central challenges facing innovation and entrepreneurship research today. This panel examines these questions in the context of the biopharmaceutical industry, where institutional complexity is acute, and the consequences of uncertainty are particularly consequential. This panel brings together scholars whose work addresses these challenges from complementary angles. The paper presentations examine how contracts shape alliance outcomes, how IP uncertainty and geopolitical tensions affect value capture and the locus of pharmaceutical innovation, and how AI is reconfiguring established models of biotech commercialization. Together, they advance our understanding of the institutional and strategic conditions under which new ventures and incumbents navigate uncertainty. The panel speaks directly to core themes of the ISA conference related to innovation, entrepreneurship, and AI-driven transformation. It is designed to generate substantive cross-paper discussion on the mechanisms linking uncertainty in the biopharmaceutical industry to firm behavior and outcomes.

category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
title: Boundaryless for Whom? Career Mobility and Intrapreneurship in Technology Firms
authors: Weiyi Ng* (National University of Singapore); Eliot Sherman (Georgetown University)
abstract: An extensive literature documents how firms benefit from employee mobility in the technology sector. External hires introduce new ideas that enable knowledge recombination, while being less beholden to the local priorities and routines that inhibit it. One valuable consequence is a positive association between external mobility and intrapreneurship—that is, entrepreneurship within existing organizations. However, the evidence that supports this association derives from samples that are predominantly male. This invites our research question: Does external mobility facilitate intrapreneurship for women in the same way as it does for men? We addressed this question by analyzing the career histories of 154,859 gender-matched employees at 51 established technology firms in the U.S. Among female technology workers, internal hires were more intrapreneurial than observably equivalent external hires, and accumulated internal moves were positively associated with intrapreneurship. As a result, the intrapreneurial gender gap was larger in firms that filled more positions through external hiring. Supplementary analysis using regional variation in firm density to instrument for career mobility provided corroborating evidence. While intrapreneurship accelerated promotion for all, the effect was twice as large for men. Our findings reinforce a general principle: As workforces diversify, conclusions drawn from studies of majority populations require systematic re-examination.

category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
title: Gendered Effects of Remote Work on Knowledge Workers: Evidence from Inventors
authors: Su Jung Jee* (University of Leeds and University of Oxford); Jangho Yang (University of Oxford and University of Waterloo); Torsten Heinrich (University of Oxford and Chemnitz University of Technology); Kejia Zhu (University of Waterloo)
abstract: Can the post-pandemic equilibrium of increased remote work benefit both men and women knowledge workers equally? How does this question apply across societies with different gender systems? This study investigates the gender-specific effects of remote work on the relative participation of women inventors in R&D and examines how these effects vary across societies with different gender systems. We employ a quasi-experimental design that leverages the pandemic lockdown period during which both men and women inventors in the same field were required to work remotely to a similar extent. Using a novel text-based index capturing the feasibility of remote inventive work, we find an aggregate pattern that the relative proportion of women inventors declines more in fields with high feasibility of remote work during the lockdown. However, disaggregation of this result reveals significant variation across societies characterized by different gender systems. The pattern is more pronounced in societies with high gender inequality, whereas in low-inequality societies, such as the Nordic countries, the pattern even reverses. Within a country, this pattern is more pronounced in teams of senior inventors, where traditional gender norms tend to persist. We discuss implications for the importance of considering society-specific gender systems in remote work policy design, the reinscription of existing gender inequality, and the direction of technological evolution in the long run.

category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
title: So Close, No Matter How Far: How Do Companies Compete for Talent Amidst Competitor Scandals?
authors: Damir Turkmanovic* (IE Business School); Marco Minervini (IE Business School)
abstract: Organizational scandals can impose legitimacy penalties and create talent attraction opportunities for competitors in labor markets, yet we know little about whether and how competitors strategically respond to such events. Drawing on optimal distinctiveness theory, we argue that scandals reshape the socio-competitive labor market environment through two channels. First, scandals reweigh the relative importance of different hiring dimensions for labor market audiences, prompting competitors to emphasize scandal-relevant dimensions in their hiring content. Second, scandals differentially shift legitimacy and competitive payoffs on scandal-relevant and scandal-irrelevant dimensions, incentivizing competitors to differentiate from the perpetrator on scandal-relevant dimensions but to assimilate to it on scandal-irrelevant ones. We test these claims using staggered DiD estimates on a sample of 27,865 job postings from U.S. public firms whose competitors underwent major ESG-related enforcement actions (i.e., ESG scandals) between 2018 and 2023. We measure ESG emphasis in job-posting content using ESG dictionary counts and capture similarity to the perpetrator using cosine similarity of semantic embeddings. We find that, following an ESG scandal, competitors (i) increase the share of ESG-related content in their postings, (ii) become less similar to the perpetrator on ESG-related dimensions, and (iii) become more similar on non-ESG dimensions. The findings suggest that competitor firms actively reposition hiring strategies in response to scandals to navigate heterogeneous spillovers. We contribute to research on labor market competition, optimal distinctiveness, and misconduct spillovers, elucidating how competitor events such as scandals shape the response strategies organizations use and the positions they occupy when competing for talent.

category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
title: Managers' Social Media Activism and Organizational Human Capital Losses: Evidence from US Corporate Law Firms, 2015 to 2022
authors: Forrest Briscoe* (Cornell University); Hye Joon Park (Bowling Green State University); Paul Merritt (Cornell University)
abstract: Research on corporate sociopolitical activism has focused on CEOs taking public stances on controversial social issues. Yet over the past decade, large numbers of managers at all organizational levels of organizations have engaged in sociopolitical activism via social media, often in ways that are more partisan, frequent, and unfiltered than the CEO statements previously studied. This unofficial managerial activism is a consequential but understudied organizational phenomenon. Here, we consider how managers’ social activism influences other organizational members. Focusing on partisan managers—those strongly aligned with a political party—we propose that their social media activism will spark subsequent turnover among coworkers, implying a loss of organizational human capital. To investigate this phenomenon, we link social media, job spell, and political data on the partners and other employees of large U.S. corporate law firms from 2015 to 2022. We find that partisan managerial activism is followed by elevated employee departures that are disproportionately concentrated among employees whose political views conflict with those of the activist managers. Departing employees sort into organizations with weaker activist signals and, for liberals, greater ideological fit. Correspondingly, liberal managerial activism is associated with a leftward shift in firms’ aggregate ideological composition, driven by the selective loss of conservative employees. These findings extend research on stakeholder strategy and human capital, and suggest practical implications for professional service firms in an era of political polarization.

title: The Effects of Corporate Investment and Public Grants on Climate and Energy Startup Outcomes
authors: Kathleen Kennedy (University of Maryland College Park); Morgan Edwards (University of Wisconsin-Madison); Claudia Doblinger (TU Munich); Zachary Thomas (University of Wisconsin-Madison); Maria Borrero (University of Maryland College Park); Kavita Surana* (WU Vienna)
abstract: Climate-tech startups are central to innovation policy for accelerating clean energy transitions, yet face persistent challenges: low investment, high failure rates, and a historically underinvested private sector. While public policies have focused on grants and demand-pull mechanisms, scaling startups from R&D to widespread adoption requires private capital. Corporate investors have emerged as a growing but poorly understood force in this setting — distinct from venture capital and other private investors in their strategic motivations, risk appetites, and return expectations — yet their effects on startup outcomes remain underexplored. We analyze how corporate investment, in combination with public grants and other private investment, shapes commercialization trajectories of climate-tech startups. Using a Cox Proportional Hazards model applied to 2,910 US climate-tech startups founded between 2005 and 2020, we examine associations between investor type and two outcomes: successful exits (IPOs and mergers/acquisitions) and failures (bankruptcy or closure). Corporate and other private investments are both significantly associated with exits and failures, while public grants alone show no significant association with either outcome. However, grants fill critical funding gaps in high-risk sectors and catalyze subsequent private investment: publicly funded startups that later receive corporate investment exit at a 155% higher rate, compared to 78% for other private investment. Findings are robust across sectors, timelines, and public funding types. These results reveal the complementary and differentiated roles of public and private investors in directing climate innovation and scaling technologies toward climate goals, with direct implications for how public policy can better incentivize strategic corporate investment.
session_chair: Kavita Surana (WU Vienna University of Economics and Business)

title: Sustainable Operations in Hospitality Industry: Energy, Water and Carbon Usage Trends Across the Globe
authors: Diep Pham (University of South Carolina); Rohit Verma* (University of South Carolina); Kejia Hu (University of Oxford); Eric Ricaurte (Greenview)
abstract: This study examines global hotel sustainability performance across energy, carbon, and water consumption for multiple countries for approximately a decade. By comparing resource use per occupied room, it reveals that sustainability outcomes are shaped more by structural and contextual factors than by operational efficiency alone. Across all three resources, country trajectories show uneven progress, with consistent leaders such as France, Spain, and the UK. Improvements in carbon intensity are strongly linked to national grid decarbonization, particularly in Europe, rather than hotel-level actions. The COVID-19 shock in 2021 exposed a critical limitation in performance metrics: per-room and per–square meter indicators often moved in opposite directions, with over 40% of country-level changes showing conflicting signals. Regional patterns highlight divergence rather than convergence. Europe demonstrates declining energy and carbon intensity, while the Middle East remains the highest across all resources. Climate is a dominant determinant, with hotels in tropical zones consuming up to three to four times more energy and water than those in temperate regions due to structural HVAC and resource demands. While GDP correlates with carbon and water reductions, it poorly explains energy use. Instead, cultural factors, especially uncertainty avoidance significantly influence energy intensity, as risk-averse societies tend to over-provision services. Finally, industry shows little evidence of convergence, with persistent disparities and increasing dispersion. Structural characteristics, particularly service level, further reinforce these differences, as full-service hotels consistently consume approximately 2.5 times more resources than limited-service properties.
session_chair: Kavita Surana (WU Vienna University of Economics and Business)

title: Delivering reliable reserve commitments from intermittent electricity resources
authors: Anil Kaya (KIT); Yashar Ghiassi-Farrokhfal* (Erasmus University Rotterdam); Derek Bunn (London Business School)
abstract: Renewable Energy Producers (REPs) in electricity supply are increasing the need for flexible reserve facilities to manage their short-term intermittencies. Thus, reserve markets have become increasingly profitable. REPs may be attracted by this profitability but reserve markets require reliable commitments. It is an open question whether reliability is aligned with the profitable operations of REPs who use storage assets and/or financial hedging to manage their output reliability risks. Analyzing this question at an operational level requires a detailed analysis of the market microstructure and trading arrangements. We find that the outcomes depend on intraday market arrangements, either discrete (D-ID) auctions or continuous (C-ID) trading. We model a profit-maximizing REP's operation, with and without storage, providing reserve services via a multi-stage stochastic mixed-integer program with decision-dependent probabilities, supported by DID or C-ID trading. Using Benders decomposition and stochastic-dual-dynamic programming (SDDP), we analyze German data, which includes both C-ID and DID trading opportunities. Our findings indicate REPs could most effectively use C-ID trading for profitable and reliable reserve market participation, wherein batteries neither enhance participation nor improve system reliability. Conversely, in DID trading, REPS mostly rely on batteries for reliable, profitable participation. Accordingly, we also provide some regulatory recommendations.

session_name: Autonomy Without Abdication: Ethics, Control, & Responsibility in Agentic AI
title: Autonomy Without Abdication: Ethics, Control, and Responsibility in Agentic AI
authors: Nitin Joglekar (Villanova); Meena Al-Azzawe (Kinaxis); Caryn Lusinchi (Nemko Digital); Oliver Cronk (Cronk Advisory); Mimi Bulfin (IBM); Phaedra Boinodiris (Author of AI for the Rest of US)
abstract: As organizations move beyond generative AI toward increasingly autonomous, agentic AI systems—capable of planning, decision-making, and acting across complex workflows—the ethical, organizational, and governance challenges intensify dramatically. Unlike traditional automation, agentic AI introduces new forms of distributed agency, opaque decision rights, and emergent behavior that strain existing corporate controls, regulatory frameworks, and professional norms. This panel comprises academic and industry leaders to examine how organizations can responsibly design, deploy, and govern agentic AI at scale. The panel will explore three interrelated questions: (1) How do agentic systems reshape accountability, risk ownership, and human-in-the-loop governance? (2) What organizational capabilities—skills, structures, and decision processes—are required to prevent ethical drift as autonomy increases? (3) How can firms align innovation incentives with integrity, transparency, and societal trust? Through real-world enterprise cases and conceptual frameworks, the panel will propose practical governance mechanisms, including auditability for autonomous agents, ethical “control planes,” and new roles for AI stewardship within firms. The session will bridge theory and practice, offering industry studies scholars and practitioners a shared language for analyzing agentic AI not merely as a technical frontier, but as a fundamental transformation in how organizations exercise power, responsibility, and strategic choice.
moderator: Melissa M. Appleyard (Portland State University); Kristi Yuthas (Portland State University)
panelists: Nitin Joglekar (Villanova); Meena Al-Azzawe (Kinaxis); Caryn Lusinchi (Nemko Digital); Oliver Cronk (Cronk Advisory); Mimi Bulfin (IBM); Phaedra Boinodiris (Author of AI for the Rest of US)

title: Coffee Break
What is Industry Studies Research?
authors: Saurabh Bansal; Laura Dupin; Juliane Reinecke
abstract: Industry studies draws on perspectives from strategy, organization theory, operations, innovation, and public policy, yet its distinctive contribution remains a subject of ongoing discussion. At its core, industry studies seeks to understand how industry-specific characteristics shape organizational, firm, and industry outcomes through attention to the technologies, institutions, competitive dynamics, and historical trajectories that define particular sectors. This panel brings together leading scholars to explore what defines industry studies research, the questions it is uniquely positioned to answer, and its relevance for addressing contemporary challenges. Panellists will discuss industries as a critical level of analysis, the balance between industry-specific insight and broader theory development, and the opportunities and challenges of conducting and publishing industry-focused research. Reflecting on the field's evolution, current boundaries, and future directions, the discussion will offer perspectives on how industry studies can contribute to understanding industries as complex systems of competition, collaboration, innovation, and change, while providing practical guidance for scholars interested in advancing this distinctive area of research.
panelists: Saurabh Bansal; Laura Dupin; Juliane Reinecke

session_name: Resilience and Reconfiguration of Global Supply Chains
title: Resilience and Reconfiguration of Global Supply Chains
authors: Edward Anderson; Nitin Joglekar
abstract: As geopolitical tensions, technological disruption, and systemic vulnerabilities reshape global supply chains, new approaches to resilience are emerging. This panel examines four critical themes: (1) managing cascade risks in increasingly interconnected supply networks; (2) the growing use of supply chains as instruments of statecraft through export controls, technology restrictions, and resource access; (3) industrial resilience and supply chain reconfiguration driven by breakthrough technologies and new organisational models; and (4) the opportunities and risks created by agentic AI systems, including new approaches to visibility, coordination, and risk management. Together, the discussion explores how firms, industries, and governments can adapt to an increasingly uncertain global environment.

session_name: Digital Transformation, Data Governance and Policy
title: Exploring the Dutch and Danish Port Digital Transition: A Strategic Narratives-Ontological Security Framework and Toolkit
authors: Maitrayee Mullick (Aalborg University); Carolijn Van Noort* (Aalborg University)
abstract: Contemporary European Ports transitioning towards digitalisation and AI adoption are reeling under discursive and organisational challenges that threaten their ontological security, i.e., the port stakeholders’ sense of agency, workflows, and routines. Although literature suggests that organisational narratives can promote meaningful adoption, limited research highlights the intertwined roles of stakeholders’ ontological securities and organisational narratives in the digital transition and AI adoption in smart ports across Europe. We confront this gap by investigating the digital trajectories of European Smart Ports at different scales to understand the roles of strategic narratives and ontological security in digitalisation and AI adoption. The research uses an empirical, sequential mixed-methods design, developing a Diagnostic framework (Strategic Narratives Alignment for Ontological Security) to analyse the influence of strategic narrative on ontological security. Semi-structured interviews and a deductive quantitative survey grounded in the framework were conducted with Port Authority Management at selected Core and Comprehensive Dutch ports (Rotterdam, Amsterdam) and Danish Ports (Fredericia, Aalborg, Vordingborg, and Kalundborg). The results highlight strategic narratives as essential macro-political tools for future-making, while also working to bridge the gap between digital and AI technologies and the workforce’s need for security, stability and agency. While larger ports leverage these accounts for structural integration, smaller and medium hubs use them to navigate resource restrictions and secure local buy-in. The study also provides an Operational-Decision-Toolkit for secure AI adoption as a guide for practitioners and policy-makers to formulate narratives that mitigate anxiety and support the sustainable transition of maritime infrastructure into the AI era. Keywords: Smart Ports, AI adoption, Digitalisation, Ontological Security, Strategic Narratives

session_name: Digital Transformation, Data Governance and Policy
title: Rhetorical Nationalism as a State-Alignment Signal: Implications for Firm Digital Transformation
authors: Kaixian Mao (Renmin University of China); Baoting Peng (Renmin University of China); Yao Lu (Renmin University of China); Huidi Lu* (University of Oxford)
abstract: This paper examines how rhetorical nationalism shapes firm digital transformation in China. We argue that rhetorical nationalism functions as a state-alignment signal by publicly linking the firm to national priorities such as technological self-reliance and digital upgrading, firms strengthen their legitimacy with politically relevant audiences and improve access to complementary external resources, including government support or subsidies. These resources, in turn, facilitate digital transformation by reducing uncertainty and easing resource constraints around costly technological change. Using panel data on 31,998 firm-year observations of Chinese A-share listed firms from 2007 to 2023, we test whether stronger nationalist rhetoric predicts greater digital transformation. The results show a positive and robust relationship between rhetorical nationalism and digital transformation. The effect is stronger for non-state-owned firms and firms located in regions with stronger intellectual property rights protection, but weaker for firms facing high supplier concentration. These findings suggest that rhetorical nationalism is most consequential where the state-alignment signal is more informative and where externally accessed resources can be more effectively converted into organizational change. The paper contributes to comparative industry studies by showing how ideological signaling interacts with ownership structure, supply-chain dependence, and regional policy environments to shape firm strategy. More broadly, it demonstrates how public-policy priorities influence industrial transformation not only through formal regulation and incentives, but also through the symbolic channels by which firms signal alignment and secure transformation-relevant resources.

session_name: Digital Transformation, Data Governance and Policy
title: Data Assetization as National Policy: A Dialectical Perspective on Firms’ Strategic Responses
authors: Ning Su* (Western University); Chen Wang (Tsinghua University)
abstract: Data constitutes a valuable resource for both organizations and nations in today’s global economy. In 2024, China became the first country to allow firms to recognize and disclose data on balance sheets as an intangible asset and a factor of production, alongside capital, labor, and technology. This policy experiment in institutionalizing data as an asset foregrounds its value, while policy advisors in other jurisdictions, such as the United States, have increasingly advocated for, or debated, national policies on data assetization. This study explores firms’ responses to such emerging policies, which remain uncertain yet consequential for both firms’ strategic decision-making and nations’ policy design and implementation. Based on an interview-based qualitative study of two firms, and drawing on management theories—particularly the lenses of dialectics and real options—the findings conceptualize firms’ responses as a dialectic between firms’ epistemic bounds in data valuation and the institutional options embedded in data policies. Specifically, the value of data cannot be determined ex ante by firms due to a set of unique attributes, including relationality, context specificity, and combinatoriality, coupled with firms’ limited—albeit growing—organizational capabilities in data governance. Simultaneously, national data policy affords firms a repertoire of options in selecting, partitioning, estimating, or withholding data during valuation. By navigating the tension between their changing epistemic bounds and the enactment of a portfolio of institutional options, firms achieve, and leverage, legitimacy in response to an emerging national data policy.

session_name: Digital Transformation, Data Governance and Policy
title: Regulating Product Innovation: Certification Reform and Market Entry in U.S. Wireless Communications
authors: Haiyang Zhang (Harvard Business School); Shane Greenstein (Harvard Business School); Roberto Fontana* (University of Pavia); Do Yoon Kim (Boston College)
abstract: Between 2000 and 2010, active U.S. wireless-equipment firms rose fivefold following the Federal Communications Commission's 1997–2001 reforms, which privatized device certification through Telecommunications Certification Bodies and expanded unlicensed (Part 15) spectrum. Yet the entrants who drove this expansion faced elevated exit hazards, while incumbents retained the complex, standards-bound corners of the market. This pattern fits neither canonical account of deregulation: creative destruction would predict entrants displacing incumbents, while regulatory capture would predict entry and exit favoring the pre-reform establishment. To adjudicate these alternatives, we exploit a near-census of 195,000 equipment authorization applications (1990–2020) and a bottom-up 275-category product taxonomy built to track fast-moving wireless technologies that NAICS cannot. Comparing entrants and incumbents across regulatory domains around the reform window, we find entrants introduced products at 12 to 31 percentage points above incumbents, concentrated in Part 15. Decomposing firm heterogeneity into four capability pillars—engineering sophistication, innovation breadth, technical-standards participation, and prior regulatory experience—we find the first three predict survival, while the fourth, the capture-aligned pillar, does not. Firms that persisted did so on the strength of engineering, innovation, and standards—not regulatory access. Reform decoupled access from advantage: reduced friction broadened entry at the periphery; capability-based sorting preserved incumbent dominance at the core. The market converged on neither homogeneous competition nor incumbent displacement, but on a stratified equilibrium in which capability—not regulation—determined position. The framework speaks to contemporary debates on privatized certification and commons governance for frontier technologies including autonomous systems and artificial intelligence.

title: The Aging Consumer: Demand Inertia and the Direction of Innovation under Population Aging
authors: Maria Zhu* (Duke University); Yoko Shibuya (Duke University)
abstract: This paper studies how population aging shapes firms’ innovation strategies through a demand-side channel. Using U.S. household scanner data from the consumer goods industry, we first document evidence of demand inertia across age groups: while older consumers are less likely to switch across firms within a product module, they are more likely to switch across new products offered by firms they have previously purchased from within that same product module. Moreover, we find that older consumers are more likely to transition to healthier products within the same firm and product module. Motivated by these findings, we examine how consumer aging influences firms’ product development decisions. We show that firms with greater exposure to aging are less likely to introduce products in new product modules and instead rely more on introducing new products within product modules where they already operate. In addition, newly introduced products are more likely to be healthier, consistent with firms adapting their innovation strategies to cater to the preferences of older consumers. Overall, our results suggest that population aging moves innovation away from expansion into new product modules toward incremental improvements within existing product lines.

title: A Lab-Grown Diamond is Forever...Too: Disruption from a Sustainability-Focused Substitute Ecosystem (SSE)
authors: Melissa Appleyard* (Portland State University); Kristi Yuthas (Portland State University); Turanay Caner (NC State University)
abstract: Laboratory-grown diamonds (LGDs) grew from 12% to over 50% of U.S. engagement ring purchases between 2019 and 2024 (BriteCo, 2024), disrupting a century-old industry built on monopoly power, manufactured scarcity, and marketing might, where the “A Diamond is Forever” advertising campaign was deemed the top slogan of the 20th century by Advertising Age (Advertising Age, 1999). How did a sustainability-positioned entrant overcome an entrenched incumbent with deep resources, cultural embeddedness, and world-class marketing? Through in-depth case analysis of this transformation, we find that no single factor—not price, technology, ethics, nor generational values—explains the disruption alone. Rather, rapid substitution resulted from the alignment and mutual reinforcement of three interdependent forces: supply chain reconfiguration that created structural sustainability advantages difficult for incumbents to match; institutional changes (regulations, standards, verification) that conferred legitimacy on the substitute; and consumer demand evolution that aligned ethical values with economic incentives in a women-focused industry (WFI). These forces interacted through reinforcing feedback loops that, once aligned, produced tipping point dynamics and accelerated transformation. We formalize these findings as the Sustainability-Focused Substitute Ecosystem (SSE) framework, which extends innovation ecosystem theory (Adner & Kapoor, 2016) and the multi-level perspective on sustainability transitions (Geels, 2011; Geels & Schot, 2007) by specifying how sustainability-driven substitution requires coordinated evolution across production, institutions, and demand, where technological change alone provides insufficient for the market shift and institutional legitimation and demand-side value alignment are required.

title: Purpose or Payout: Competing Logics of Being Deep Technology Acquisitions
authors: Jennifer Woolley* (Santa Clara University)
abstract: Acquisitions are considered a preferred exit strategy for startups. Research on acquisitions has largely taken an acquirer-centric perspective, focusing on how buyers assess risk, strategic fit, and growth potential. Work has shown how acquirers time their purchases based on a target’s maturity, technological quality and intellectual property portfolio, as well as information asymmetry and competition. Other work has emphasized the value of an acquisition for firm investors who seek a liquidity event to obtain financial returns from their investment. Less work has taken the perspective of other stakeholders, especially that of the firm founders who contribute the initial knowledge and skills essential for the development and success of the firms. Indeed, founders of deep technology firms are often the inventors of scientific intellectual property (IP) on which the firm was based — IP that was designed with pro-social objectives. Thus, the decision to be acquired is complicated by the uncertainty regarding the potential for ownership changes to jeopardize the mission or advancement of their scientific work. This study examines the tension between pursuing an acquisition and maintaining independent operations from the perspective of deep technology firm founders. Based on interviews with genetics firm founders, we find that founders forgo acquisitions when they fear that an exit will get in the way of scientific advancement. These findings have important implications for theory and practice regarding technology transfer, science commercialization, and the strategic dilemmas inherent in founding teams.

title: The Global Leadership Acumen Continuum Model for CEOs Leading Small Multinational Enterprises
authors: John LeCounte* (St John Fisher University)
abstract: A systematic literature review has identified gaps in understanding the role of CEOs in Small Multinational Enterprises, underscoring the need for a comprehensive understanding of the cultural, political, and economic environments. The Global Leadership Acumen Continuum Model offers a structured framework to enhance CEO power and leadership competencies required to address complex challenges across multiple environments. This model comprises several key components: (a) CEO’s Global Mindset, (b) CEO Organizational Identification, (c) Strategic Leadership, (d) Normalization of Strategic Errors, (e) Performance Management, and (f) Behavioral Integration. By incorporating these elements, CEOs are better positioned to make informed decisions, demonstrate ethical leadership, and cultivate enduring relationships with diverse stakeholders to promote organizational success. The importance of this approach is particularly evident in sectors such as defense and petroleum, where the convergence of business and politics necessitates strategic foresight and adaptability (Buckley, 2022; Giolito & Golsorkhi, 2023; Hamid, 2023). CEOs of Small Multinational Enterprises (SMEs) operate within an increasingly complex and interconnected environment that demands a broad range of leadership competencies. They must be perceived as powerful and capable of exercising various forms of power, such as influence, expertise, and legitimate authority, in an ethical manner to achieve positive outcomes across diverse contexts. Globalization heightens competition and introduces multifaceted challenges that require a sophisticated understanding of geopolitical, economic, and sociocultural dynamics. Therefore, a comprehensive framework is necessary to encapsulate the essential skills and knowledge for managing the micro-foundations of leadership and trust.

category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
title: Peer Information in Team Incentivization
authors: Matylda Trocinska* (LMU Munich)
abstract: As organizations increasingly rely on team-based work, cooperation among employees becomes essential yet difficult to incentivize. Traditional evaluation systems focus on individual outcomes, often neglecting the helping behavior among peers that sustains collective performance. This study examines whether and how peer information about helping can improve cooperation in team-based incentive structures. We conduct a preregistered online experiment with 492 participants performing real-effort tasks in teams consisting of three workers and one manager. Workers decide whether to contribute to their own or others’ projects under three evaluation schemes: Manager Evaluation (manager decides rewards without peer input), Peer Feedback (workers provide helping information to the manager), and Peer Evaluation (workers allocate part of the reward themselves). Results show that incorporating peer information meaningfully improves cooperation. The Peer Evaluation condition substantially increases total output, through greater helping behavior. It also leads to higher allocation efficiency. These effects appear to operate through shifts in moral norms. Our findings contribute to theories of incentives and organizational design by demonstrating that evaluation systems not only reward effort but also organize cooperation. We offer practical guidance on how peer information can be leveraged to promote fairness, efficiency, and sustained collaboration in modern organizations.

category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
title: Training investments and firm performance: The role of collective employee representation
authors: Federica De Stefano (University of Oxford); Roxana Barbulescu* (HEC Paris); Shinjinee Chattopadhyay (University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign)
abstract: In labor markets characterized by rapidly evolving skill demands, firms increasingly rely on employee training to build human capital. Yet training creates a fundamental tension: it enhances productivity while increasing employees’ outside options, making it difficult for firms to capture returns. Whether organizational arrangements can mitigate this tension remains an open question. This study examines how collective employee representation in training decisions—through institutions such as works councils—shapes firms’ ability to realize returns from training investments. We argue that employee representation enhances firm returns from training via two simultaneous mechanisms: a relational one, that signals organizational commitment to employee development, fostering reciprocity and reducing turnover, and an informational one, that improves the flow of information between employees and the firm, enabling better alignment between evolving skill needs and internal opportunities. Together, these mechanisms improve how training investments translate into firm performance. Using longitudinal data on French firms and a regulatory reform mandating employee consultation in training decisions, we find support for our hypothesis. Exploratory analyses suggest that the effect operates not through more training but through the ways that returns are realized: via lower turnover, greater internal mobility, and a shift away from firm-specific training without wage increases. These effects are strongest in firms with weaker prior training investments and in settings with higher information frictions, such as volatile markets and dispersed workforces. These patterns highlight when employee voice is most valuable and how firms can better retain, redeploy, and capture value from human capital in changing labor markets.

category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
title: Human Capital Investments and Complementary Assets: Evidence from the Hotel Sector
authors: Alex Fitz (IE University); Charo Silva (IE University); Maria Del Rocio Bonet* (IE University); Damir Turkmanovi (IE University)
abstract: In the service sector, particularly in hospitality, human capital is central to organizational performance and customer experience. Unlike manufacturing, where outcomes depend largely on technology and standardized processes, service quality relies heavily on employees’ skills, behaviors, and interactions with customers. As a result, investing in human capital is a key strategic priority. Training plays a crucial role by enhancing employee competencies, aligning behaviors with service standards, and promoting continuous improvement. A growing body of research has examined how training affects firm performance, with recent work emphasizing complementarities between training and other organizational assets. For instance, studies show that the benefits of training are amplified when combined with certain intangible assets, such as marketing or brand investments, but may be weaker when paired with heavy physical capital. This aligns with broader research in strategic human capital, which highlights how the value of workforce investments depends on their interaction with other firm practices. This study extends this literature by examining how complementary assets influence both the adoption of training and its performance effects within firms. Using data from a global hotel chain operating across the Caribbean and Latin America between 2020 and 2024, we analyze a staggered training rollout across 539 hotels in 36 countries. Preliminary results indicate that training adoption is more likely among higher-revenue and managed hotels, as well as those investing more in intangible assets. However, we find limited evidence of sustained performance gains, with only short-term revenue increases and indications of selection bias into training adoption.

category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
title: Developing the Manufacturing Innovation Workforce for Crossing ‘Valley of Death’: Understanding Fraunhofer-Gesellschaft’s Dynamic Role
authors: Athar Mansoor* (University of Cambridge); Eoin O'Sullivan (University of Cambridge)
abstract: Fraunhofer-Gesellschaft — one of the world’s largest organisations for applied research — develops and deploys a skilled innovation workforce across technology readiness levels (TRLs) 3-4 and 7-8. It represents a pre-eminent model of a Research and Technology Organisation (RTO) that systematically operates various stages of technology maturation. We are particularly interested in understanding the institutional mechanisms, career pathways, and knowledge-transfer dynamics that enable Fraunhofer to engage in upstream (basic) and downstream (applied) research and development and how it develops the skilled innovation workforce for crossing the ‘Valley of Death’. Our focus is to explore the movement of the innovation workforce between TRLs 3-4 and TRLs 7-8 and how this impacts the workforce requirements for emerging technologies. Through in-depth semi structured interviews, we seek to investigate the following research questions: 1. Does the movement of researchers between Fraunhofer institutes, universities, and industry create feedback and feedforward loops across TRLs, and what institutional mechanisms facilitate this mobility? 2. To what extent is the turnover of scientific staff into industry a deliberate feature of the Fraunhofer model, and how do institutes manage the balance between retaining expertise and fulfilling the technology-transfer mission? 3. How does Fraunhofer-trained human capital enhance the absorptive capacity of receiving firms? 4. What role do concurrent appointments (professors holding both university and Fraunhofer positions), contractual research and industry collaboration play in sustaining the bidirectional flow of knowledge between basic research and applied development?

category: Operations, Supply Chain, and AI-Enhanced Industry 4.0
title: How Product Variety Impacts Food Waste in a University Dining Environment
authors: Aydin Alptekinoglu* (Penn State); Suvrat Dhanorkar (Georgia Tech); Fan Zou (Penn State)
abstract: The received wisdom in the field of operations management on product variety is that it is detrimental to efficiency. But there is not much evidence that supports this, and nowhere near enough is known on why or how product variety is linked to various notions of inefficiency, including waste. To contribute to the field's understanding of how product variety influences waste in supply chains, we explore the link between food product variety and food waste at the consumer level, where a great majority of food waste occurs in economic terms. Our empirical context is the all-you-can-eat buffets of a university dining system at a large U.S. public university. We collected granular post-consumer food waste data and daily menus over a full academic year for multiple dining halls. Besides establishing the first-order effect – that higher product variety (increased choice on the dining menu) is associated with higher food waste – and estimating the magnitude of this effect, we explore several contextual factors that moderate it by managing the diners’ choice architecture. We find that, on average, an additional main dish in the menu results in a 6.72% increase in post-consumer food waste. We also discover that factors imposing greater time pressure on the diners (classes and final exams), menu design accounting for historical popularity of main dishes, and removal of trays significantly reduce and sometimes altogether eliminate this positive link between variety and waste. We recently presented our findings to the university’s dining executives, who have found our insights valuable and actionable.

category: Operations, Supply Chain, and AI-Enhanced Industry 4.0
title: Resilience in Grocery Supply Chains: National Brands vs Private Label Food Products
authors: Tonya Boone* (Mason School of Business, College of William & Mary); Ram Ganeshan (Mason School of Business, College of William & Mary); Robert L. Hicks (Department of Economics, College of William & Mary); Amy Xia (Mason School of Business, College of William & Mary)
abstract: Recent surveys highlight the increasing growth of private label (PL) products in sales volume, number of SKUs (PLMA 2026) and customer purchase intentions (Nielsen 2024). Retailers offer National Brands (NB) along with PLs in order increase market coverage through both product and price differentiation. NB supply chains are governed by branded producers who offer products to multiple retail outlets. We compare NB vs PL resilience using distribution center fill rates for a mid-size regional grocery chain (481 store locations) through the 2020 demand-driven disruption and the 2021–2022 supply-driven disruption. We find that PL case fill rates exceed NB fill rates in every disruption phase, by 4.7 percentage points during the 2020 demand surge and 7.0 points during the 2021-2022 supply-chain-tightening peak. The PL advantage is larger in product categories with lower market concentration and thus more competing brands.PL supply chains are typically unique to retailers. Production may be in-house or outsourced to branded producers or other third-party manufacturers. Economic disruptions typically see increased price competition between PLs and NBs. Volpe (2011) found that PL prices increased faster than NBs during the 2008 recession.

category: Operations, Supply Chain, and AI-Enhanced Industry 4.0
title: Supply Chain Complexity and the Governance–Biodiversity Disconnect: Evidence from Ocean Warming and Fishery Improvement Projects
authors: Zhimin Chen (Nanyang Technological University); Guangzhi Ye (Nanyang Technological University); Sangho Chae* (University of Warwick); Alok Choudhary (University of Warwick)
abstract: This study examines whether greater supply chain complexity strengthens or weakens the effectiveness of multi-tier sustainability governance under climate stress. Focusing on Fishery Improvement Projects (FIPs), the dominant private-governance mechanism in global seafood supply chains, we investigate how the number of supply chain tiers represented in a FIP shapes fishery responses to ocean warming. We link annual data on 1,190 fishery-FIP pairs from 2018 to 2024 with FishSource sustainability scores, NOAA sea-surface-temperature anomalies, FIP participant rosters, and independent FIP progress ratings. We develop a two-channel framework. On the one hand, broader multi-tier participation should enhance visibility, distributed monitoring, and cross-tier leverage, producing stronger governance responses to environmental stress. On the other hand, commercially interdependent tiers may face coordination failure, adaptation costs, and institutional decoupling, limiting substantive ecological improvement. Using a fixed-effects interaction design, we find that supply chain complexity positively moderates the effect of ocean warming on governance-related outcomes, particularly harvest strategy and compliance scores. However, complexity does not improve biodiversity outcomes on average and is associated with weaker independent progress ratings under warming stress, consistent with a governance-biodiversity disconnect. Further heterogeneity analysis shows that this disconnect becomes sharper in thermally vulnerable fisheries, where biological limits are more likely to bind. The findings contribute to operations and industry studies by identifying a novel form of decoupling in multi-tier sustainability institutions: structurally complex supply chains generate stronger visible governance responses to climate disruption, but these gains do not reliably translate into verified biological protection.

title: Do Carbon Taxes Work for All Firms? Causal Evidence on Carbon Pricing and ESG-Moderated Abatement in the Global Cement Sector
authors: Malek Al Jebaie (Erasmus University Rotterdam); Beatriz Calzada* (Erasmus University Rotterdam); Jolanda Hessels (Erasmus University Rotterdam)
abstract: The cement sector accounts for 7–8% of global CO₂ emissions, with a substantial share arising from calcination — a process-level source resistant to conventional abatement. While carbon taxes are the primary market-based instrument to incentivise structural investments in decarbonisation, evidence on their effectiveness in cement remains thin, and the mechanisms through which abatement occurs are poorly understood. This paper develops a two-layer identification framework using plant-level process emission data from 2,034 cement plants across 1990–2022. The first layer estimates whether carbon tax introduction causally reduces plant- and country-level emission intensity, exploiting staggered adoption across eight treated countries via Callaway & Sant'Anna (2021) cohort-specific difference-in-differences. The second layer asks who responds more strongly: linking 266 plants to 117 listed firms through a plant–firm matching procedure, we estimate whether plants owned by higher-ESG firms reduce emissions more following carbon tax introduction — identified through the interaction coefficient β on (Tax × ESG) — and through which organisational and financial mechanisms this differential operates. We hypothesise that high-ESG firms exhibit stronger abatement at prevailing tax rates, that the governance gap narrows at higher prices, and that anticipatory abatement during the announcement window reveals governance-dependent absorptive capacity. Given the small treated sample, robustness checks include wild cluster bootstrap standard errors and causal random forests to recover heterogeneous treatment effects. Findings inform carbon pricing design and establish country-specific price thresholds under real-world political economy constraints.

title: The Climate-Industrial Policy Gap and Stranded Asset Risks in Europe's Low-Carbon Industry
authors: Christian Rumpelnik* (WU Vienna); Morgan E. Edwards (University of Wisconsin); Gregor Semieniuk (University of Massachusetts Amherst); Kavita Surana (WU Vienna)
abstract: European Union (EU) climate and industrial policy are increasingly converging, yet remain heavily reliant on supply-side measures that assume stable industrial demand. We show that this assumption is fragile and may generate substantial stranded-asset risks, mirroring those observed in the fossil sector. Using a dataset of 4,500 industrial installations, we find that under current trajectories (based on legislated policies in the European Commission’s Energy and Climate Outlook) industrial energy demand could decline by up to 35% between 2025 and 2050. Sectors (steel, non-metallic minerals, refining) and regions (Central and South-Eastern Europe), where poor emissions performance, high local renewable energy costs, and older asset vintages increase exposure to relocation and decline could experience even steeper declines. This misalignment may generate significant stranded asset risks for both low-carbon production and infrastructure. Announced low-carbon production capacity exceeds modeled demand by 33% in steel, 18% in cement, and 40% in nitrogen-based chemicals, implying potential stranded capital expenditures of EUR 20-40 bn, EUR 3-6bn, and EUR 30-50 bn, respectively. At the same time, declining industrial activity reduces country-level renewable energy deficits by around 15% (310 TWh), weakening the utilization and cost-recovery prospects of large-scale infrastructure projects such as the German hydrogen core grid, where the grid tariff would need to increase by up to 13% to remain revenue-neutral. Our results point to a systematic risk of stranded assets in the low-carbon transition and highlight the need to better integrate demand-side considerations into climate and industrial policy design.

title: The Emergence of Industrial Decarbonisation in the UK
authors: David Reiner* (University of Cambridge)
abstract: Following failed efforts in both 2010 and 2015 to deploy carbon capture and storage (CCS) at UK power plants through £1bn competitions, the government fundamentally reoriented its approach. We trace that shift and identify three keys to the successful relaunch: moving away from a focus on power generation to heavy industry, from standalone projects to industrial clusters, and from commercial exclusivity to knowledge sharing. The five-year Industrial Decarbonisation Challenge (IDC), which launched in 2019, combined £210 million in public funding with almost £1 billion in industry investment, nearly four times more than originally anticipated. The funds were used to support cluster plans in six regions of the UK and front-end engineering design (FEED) studies for nine projects, which could then underpin developers' ability to reach final investment decision on several projects. Unlike previous efforts, a winner-take-all approach was not adopted -- the government did identify frontrunners at both the cluster and project levels, but still actively engaged slower-progressing clusters and projects, whether as 'track-2' clusters or 'standby' projects. Building in this flexibility has proven valuable given the challenges of successfully developing projects in the face of competitiveness pressures, rising energy prices, and shifting corporate commitments.

title: Episodes of Substitution: Institutional Conditions and the Recurrent Emergence of Meat Alternatives in Finland
authors: Kata Isenring* (University of Jyväskylä); Juha-Antti Lamberg (University of Jyväskylä)
abstract: While contemporary debates often frame plant-based alternatives as a recent sustainability-driven innovation, historical evidence suggests that meat reduction has emerged repeatedly under very different institutional conditions. This study examines how distinct institutional settings have shaped the meaning and diffusion of meat substitution practices in Finland over more than a century. Finland provides a particularly revealing setting. As a late-industrializing economy marked by periods of acute wartime scarcity, strong civic associations, and more recently high-profile plant-based innovation, it offers substantial institutional variation within a single national context, enabling structured comparison across episodes while holding broader cultural and political conditions relatively constant. The study traces four historically distinct episodes. In the late nineteenth century (1865–1910), voluntary vegetarianism emerged as an ideological reform movement mediated by newspapers, urban networks, and restaurants. During the Finnish Civil War (1918), vegetarianism expanded through supply breakdown, with civil society organizations translating scarcity into household substitution practices. In World War II, industrially produced substitutes emerged within a state-regulated wartime economy where resource allocation and product legitimacy were centrally controlled. Finally, in the mid-2010s, plant-based products expanded within a hype-driven consumer market, with legitimacy negotiated through entrepreneurial framing and retail categorization. Across these episodes, meat substitution emerges under fundamentally different conditions — reformist persuasion, structural crisis, centralized regulation, and market-driven entrepreneurship. Each moment reflects a distinct institutional configuration shaping how meat substitution was evaluated, organized, and stabilized — with direct implications for how contemporary sustainability transitions are understood and governed.

title: Recursive innovation and the non‑linear evolution of technology: The rise, fall, and re-emergence of an alternative protein source
authors: Susanna Mansikkamäki* (Jyväskylä University School of Business and Economics); Kata Isenring (Jyväskylä University School of Business and Economics); Mirva Peltoniemi (Tampere University); Antti Sihvonen (University of Helsinki)
abstract: In this study, we theorize the non-linear dynamics of technology evolution. We extend the literature by elucidating how technologies can recursively oscillate between innovation process, commercialization, and alternative life cycles. In doing so, we join recent studies in technology and innovation management that have begun to question linear models of technology development in which product development leads to commercialization and sets of a technology life cycle where a more efficient technology replaces an old one. We build on the idea of transient, incomplete, and plural nature of innovation and the notion that the technology replacement process is not unidirectional as old technologies can re-emerge. While informed by prior literature, our theorization stems from an analysis of the development of Pekilo single-cell protein technology, a nutritional protein derived from fungi. Our longitudinal archival data cover several decades, and we complement the archival data with published sources. Originally developed in the 1960s and 1970s to address an anticipated global protein shortage, the protein was produced as animal feed in Finland until the early 1990s. It then disappeared for almost three decades, only to be revived by a start-up in 2020. The case is interesting not only because of the long gap between the disappearance and re-emergence of the technology, but also because of its multiple purposes: the protein product was initially envisioned for human nutrition but reached production as animal feed, whereas the cultivation process also helped purify the pulp mill effluent that was used as the culture medium.

category: Operations, Supply Chain, and AI-Enhanced Industry 4.0
title: Managing Trade-offs Between Resilience and Cost in Emerging Food Supply Chains
authors: Mariel Alem-Fonseca* (University of Cambridge); Helen Rogers (Technische Hochschule Nürnberg); Naoum Tsolakis (University of Cambridge); Mukesh Kumar (University of Cambridge)
abstract: Existing scientific research has made significant contributions to the field of supply chain (SC) resilience; however, without considering cost, resilience remains a myopic concept, detached from practical implementation. The purpose of this research is to study the concepts of SC resilience and cost within the context of emerging food SCs, particularly alternative proteins (AP). These SCs, continuously evolving, face increasing pressure to bring down costs and develop resilience for success amid competition and disruptions. However, the perception that resilience is costly has led companies to doubt their ability to afford it. Adopting a qualitative multiple case-study approach, this research presents empirical observations from the AP industry, considering plant-based and fermented-based protein technologies. Specifically, this study examines four stages of the SCs: (i) breeding, (ii) farming, (iii) processing, and (iv) production, to gain an in-depth understanding of emerging food SC configurations and the cost-resilience relationship, leading to three key contributions to Operations Management. First, the research uniquely contributes to SC resilience theories by bringing together two concepts: (i) cost of resilience, and (ii) level of resilience. Second, we propose a prototype process approach for managing resilience-cost trade-offs. This approach reveals that resilience capabilities interact across SC echelons in reinforcing, conflicting, overlapping, or collective ways, shaping how trade-offs are managed. Third, there are findings that have not yet been conceptualised in the context of AP SC design. By bridging theory and practice, this research provides a foundation for designing cost-effective resilient SCs in the rapidly expanding novel foods industry.
